#5727. These 5 Italian Exotics Are More Dependable Than The Finicky Supercars Of Yesteryear

Supercar ownership has been, and likely always will be, quite a scary proposition for newcomers, save for those who have pockets deep enough to not even care how much the next service or repair bill will cost. However, modern engineering and the cross-platform hardware that exists in many a modern supercar makes ownership a little more approachable compared to the exotics that came before them. For example, classic Ferraris like the F355 and Testarossa require engine-out servicing on an uncomfortably frequent basis, while electrical gremlins, rattling cam chains, and inadequate braking systems trouble the pre-Audi-era Lamborghinis.

Now, look at their modern counterparts. The Ferrari 458 Italia is chain-driven and capable of six-figure mileages, plus its modern DCT transmission is impressively durable and free of pricey clutch changes. Meanwhile, modern Lamborghinis share a lot of hardware with mass-market models from within the Volkswagen-Audi group as well as some other mainstream automakers, which, for buyers that know where to look, brings down servicing and maintenance costs dramatically.

To prove our point, this piece covers seven modern Italian supercars that offer a surprisingly worry-free ownership experience — from the aforementioned models through to more entry-level supercars like the Ferrari California. The supercars on this list all utilize proven powerplants that have all been on the market for at least a decade, are typically simple and robust in design, and are backed up by numerous examples with six-figure mileages still on the roads today. As a result, the Italian supercars on this list all have no known major mechanical issues, straightforward servicing and global warranty coverage, and a reputation for reliability among enthusiasts. And above all else, they are way more dependable than many pre-2000 models that preceded them.

A high-performance, limited-run Alfa Romeo and dependable, all in the same sentence? That's right. Including the 8C wasn't some sort of mistake, and this Alfa's case is actually quite easy to argue. First off, the 8C isn't totally void of faults. Alfa Romeo issued a recall in 2009 that affected the front and rear lower ball joints, and at least one 8C randomly combusted as a result of a suspected electrical gremlin. However, even $70 million 250 GTOs catch fire from time to time, so perhaps that's just part and parcel of Italian supercar ownership.

That aside, the 8C is largely based on a Maserati GranTurismo, rather than being some custom creation featuring heaps of unique parts. It's also motivated by the same Ferrari-Maserati F136 — a notoriously well-built V8 that also featured in the Ferrari F430 and 458. What this means for owners is that finding a specialist familiar with this engine shouldn't be a problem. Though the F136 is considered relatively dependable as long as basic maintenance is kept on top of.

Some of the factors that make the F136 more robust than older Ferrari V8s are chain-driven cams, a completely new, stiff aluminum block, forged pistons and a hardened-steel crankshaft. Owners also appreciate the fact that there's no engine-out servicing. We even mentioned it among the greatest engines of the last decade.

Given the super exclusive nature of these cars, most 8Cs seem to be kept as cherished weekend toys and don't see heaps of use, but the proven underpinnings mean that, given the chance, they could probably cover significant mileage without major hiccups. Compare the F136 V8 to the complex and low-production engines fitted to previous special Alfas like the '70s Montreal, and the 8C looks like quite a tempting prospect.

For all the same reasons why the 8C is great, the California is just as good. It's another grand tourer supercar that uses the F136. In this guise, the V8 produces 460 hp and 358 lb-ft of torque from a 4.3-liter displacement. One of the real benefits to the California is that it was sold with the "Ferrari Genuine Maintenance" program packaged in — alongside other contemporary Ferrari models. That provided owners with seven years' worth of free servicing, and it wasn't capped at one service per year.

Owners who exceeded the 12,500-mile-per-annum limit would also be welcome to another service as part of the program. That might seem a little redundant to a shopper considering an early model in 2026, but the peace of mind that comes with knowing Ferrari was so confident in these cars and that early maintenance was carried out to such a high level is not something to be underestimated. Older models, such as the F355 and 360, did not benefit from such a package, as it was only introduced in 2011. Also, since engine-out services on older Ferrari models can cost as much as $25,000, it's also reasonable to assume that they carry a larger risk of having experienced neglectful ownership in the past, with some owners wanting to avoid the hefty service bills.

Further bolstering the California's appeal is the positive feedback often given by current and previous owners. In fact, across a total of 13 reviews currently shown on Cars.com, the California scores 4.8 out of 5 for reliability, with many owners noting in their individual accounts that their drop-top Prancing Horse had been next to no trouble at all.

The last F136-powered Prancing Horse on this list (we promise), the 458 Italia did use a different variant of the engine — dubbed the F136FB – and the differences between it and some "lesser" variants are really quite important. Most notably, the 458's F136FB enjoys a slightly larger 4.5-liter displacement, and it also boasts a dry sump lubrication system, as opposed to the more typical wet sump system found in the California. The 458 also boasts a higher compression ratio of 12.5:1 and has its F136FB rear-mid mounted, rather than front-mid. These tweaks ensure the 458 easily walks a game of "Top Trumps," with 570 horsepower and 398 lb-ft of torque on tap.

All that makes it sound like a highly strung and technically marvelous Italian supercar, and that it is. But what's remarkable is that the 458 Italia has proven itself to be a surprisingly dependable machine, with one Japanese example having surpassed 240,000 miles so far (via AutoNext). That ludicrous example may be a one-off, but we found stories of other six-figure-mileage 458s too, demonstrating that these cars genuinely can be relied upon for long-distance or even daily driving.

Naturally, the 458 benefits from the same positives that make both the 8C and California such dependable choices, but it's also worth noting that this later mid-engined car benefits from a few extra years of development, too. Gone is the old single-clutch automated manual of the F430, and in is a more reliable dual-clutch system, which does away with the earlier car's frequent clutch replacements. Plus, a crankshaft-related recall for 2011 and 2012 model year cars fixes the issue of the engine potentially freezing up and gives owners of newer models even more peace of mind.

The Lamborghini Huracán debuted back in 2014, and continued in production for the best part of a decade, bowing out with various special editions such as the hardcore but friendly Huracán Tecnica and Sterrato, which offers pure and unfiltered joy both on and off the beaten path. It didn't look to hide its close connection with the Audi R8, the two cars sharing much of the same basic architecture, including the same naturally aspirated 5.2-liter V10. It was a proven engine by the time Lamborghini launched its Huracán, and any known issues had been addressed long before its arrival. In fact, the V10 received little in the way of complaints through the Gallardo years, too.

That V10 was also complemented with a suitably strong transmission. While the Aventador drew early criticism for clunky changes, and the Gallardo's fragile E-Gear system has a tendency to chew through clutches, the Huracán uses a proven and dependable R8 dual-clutch unit.

An ex-rental Huracán came up for sale in 2020 with 188,000 miles, which should stand as a solid testament to the model's durability (via Car and Driver). Its original transmission presumably lasted 180,000 of those miles, with almost 2,000 drivers having been at its wheel. Consistent 5,000-mile oil-service-intervals kept the V10 in rude health.

Speaking of the Huracan's reliability, independent testing has called out everything from the electrical systems through to the overall build quality as being both sound and durable. Ultimately, this Italian supercar with German blood in its veins is about as dependable as a supercar could realistically be. Contrast that with the reputation of older Lamborghinis, especially among those who are familiar with them, and it's not difficult to deduce that the Huracán presents a far more dependable ownership experience in comparison to the Raging Bulls from the past.

We recently looked at whether Maserati deserves its poor reputation or not, and judging by some pretty disappointing owner reviews, in addition to sky-high depreciation, we concluded that its bad rap is often fairly justified. That's why this one might come as a little surprise. However, the MC20 could be the supercar that bucks the trend for Maserati. It's notably simpler than some key rivals, with no all-wheel drive, hybrid, or rear-wheel-steering systems, and across long-term testing, it's actually proven to be a genuinely dependable steed. This is more than can be said for Maserati models of old, that's for sure.

Undoubtedly one of the MC20's core highlights is the 90-degree Nettuno V6 that powers it. Maserati enjoyed success in the past with similar V6 engines, and this one continues to avoid the hot-vee configuration that many of its V6 supercar rivals use to save space and reduce turbo lag. In other words, it doesn't hide its turbos down in the engine's valley — a design that has been known to accelerate wear in other engines due to excessive heat accumulation, potentially resulting in heat soak and turbo failure. That's a big plus point for long-term Maserati owners. The fact it develops 621 horsepower alongside 538 lb-ft of torque is also a positive — not everything's about dependability, after all.

That said, these are still very recent cars, so there certainly aren't any 100,000-mile-plus examples kicking about yet. Having said that, owners on enthusiast forums such as Maserati Life have boasted about covering 24,000 miles plus since the car debuted in 2022, while others managed to rack up 15,000 miles within just 12 months with zero issues, strongly suggesting that the MC20 is perfectly capable of daily duties.

#5726. GM Steps On Tesla’s EV Toes With EV1 Celebration

In a move that shocked and surprised nobody, last week Tesla CEO Elon Musk pulled the plug on his much-hyped Cybertruck. Production will end sometime next year. It may be small consolation, but at least the Cybertruck sold more units than another notorious flop in modern automotive history, General Motors’s ill-fated EV1 sedan. Was EV1 really a flop, though? In sales, yes, but GM wants everyone to know that the EV1 beat Tesla to the electrification punch in key technology milestones.

GM actually sold few, if any, EV1 units, preferring to lease the car with a focus on drivers in California. Production began in 1996 but that didn’t last long. In 2003 GM pulled the plug, recalled the vehicles, and sent them to the crusher, having produced barely more than 1,000 units overall.

Only a scant few escaped the junkyard. One of them was rescued by US filmmaker Alex Gibney, leading to his advisory role in the searing 2006 EV1 documentary “Who Killed the Electric Car?” (btw, Gibney ‘s newly released “Musk” documentary is available on streaming now).

This year marks the 30th anniversary of EV1 production, and GM is using the occasion to celebrate. Rather than shoveling all memory of the EV1 debacle into the memory hole, GM has embarked on sort of under-the-radar public relations campaign, seeking to position the car as a necessary, albeit short lived, step along the vehicle electrification journey.

In not so many words, GM also draws attention to the fact that its work on EV1 predates the launch of Tesla Motors, which came on the scene in 2003. The automaker’s Senior Writer and Editor at GM News, Chris Perkins, ran down the particulars in March, noting that EV1 was the first EV to deploy heat pumps for climate control, energy efficiency, and battery temperature management.

Perkins also takes note of the car’s regenerative braking system. “Engineers developed a system for the car that translated a driver’s brake-pedal input into an electronic signal that blended regenerative and friction braking,” Perkins wrote.

“It’s a precursor to the braking systems used in GM’s modern EVs, which also add One-Pedal Driving1 and paddle-actuated Regen-On-Demand2 capability,” he added.

EV1 also eschewed mechanical actuators in favor of fully electronic (aka by-wire) controls for the accelerator pedal, brake pedal, parking brake, and gear selector, with the power steering featuring electro-hydraulic control.

Additionally, Perkins elaborated on the regenerative braking angle in a follow-up article in August, by way of demonstrating a through line between the 1990’s technology and the automaker’s current EV lineup.

“Conceptually, the EV1’s braking system operates exactly like the braking systems in GM’s modern EVs,” Perkins wrote. “Press the brake pedal, and the car’s computers decide how much friction and regenerative braking to actuate. Should the electronic system fail, it’s connected to a mechanical backup, just as in the EV1.”

As part of the PR campaign, GM is also putting its 1994 concept sedan on display, the 1994 Impact (pictured above). “As one of the first modern, purpose-built electric vehicles from a major automaker, the Impact was a critical learning tool that shaped the final production version of the EV1,” GM emphasizes.

If you blink, you’ll miss it. The Impact is on display at the GM-sponsored Test Track at EPCOT, the Disney theme park in Bay Lake, Florida, until mid-December.

As for why all this fuss, why now, that’s a good question. Over the past several years, GM has put a jolly spin on its inability to catch up to Tesla in sales, let alone surpass it. As recently as last year, GM vigorously touted itself as #2 in EV sales in the US, second only to Tesla as a badge of honor.

Still, by August of 2025 the competition was beginning to take on a different tone, with GM pitching low-cost LFP (lithium-iron-phosphate) batteries as a near-term pathway to meeting, then beating Tesla.

The 2026 EV1 celebration elaborates upon the technology angle, underscoring GM’s claim on the pre-Tesla, 1990’s roots of innovation in the vehicle electrification field.

The new emphasis on technology also comes at a pivotal moment for EV sales in the US. The US market nosedived last fall after US President Trump and his Republican allies in Congress prematurely eliminated federal tax credits for EVs. However, activity continued to stir in some quarters, and Trump himself made the case for EVs more attractive when he decided to bomb Iran in February.

Nine months later, the price of gas remains stubbornly high, sparking renewed hopes that EV sales will rebound more quickly than first anticipated. In addition, a fresh round of innovation is on the horizon, with GM banking on its forthcoming LMR (lithium manganese-rich) battery formula to push costs down without sacrificing performance.

While Tesla is not the only competition in town, beating the startup at its own game would be a feather in GM’s cap, and Elon Musk made the effort a little easier when he canceled the Cybertruck, leaving Tesla without a foothold in the hot market for pickup trucks in the US. The automaker still has sedans, SUVs, the new Semi Class 8 truck, and the “flying” Roadster in its pocket, but the demise of the Cybertruck has left the pickup field wide open.

Meanwhile, Ford is on track to produce its new Fathom electric pickup next year starting at under $30,000, far less than the Cybertruck’s most recent starting price of $77,000 plus change. The Jeff Bezos-backed startup Slate Auto is also aiming at the affordability market with a stripped-down electric pickup starting at a base price of $26,000 and change, before accounting for add-ons.

On its part, GM is aiming for the middle ground with the 2027 Silverado electric pickup, starting at around $56,000 and reaching close to Cybertruck range at around $72,000.

Meanwhile, Rivian is also aiming upscale at close to $80,000 and up for its RIT pickup. The startup is on the move, having somehow managed to squeeze a loan guarantee of up to $4.5 billion out of the Trump administration. The funds are earmarked to expand Rivian’s production capacity with a new factory in Georgia.

Readers, what do you think? Does GM — or any other automaker — have a snowball’s chance in hell to catch up to Tesla in the US market? Drop a note in the discussion thread…

Photo: General Motors introduced the Impact concept EV in 1994, laying the groundwork for the automaker’s short-lived EV1 electric car (Impact concept; cropped, courtesy of GM).

#5725. Gloating Emails To A Newspaper Solved The Arson Spree That Hit 125 SUVs In One Night

In the early morning hours of August 22, 2003, in West Covina, California, vandals damaged one building and 125 SUVs across four dealerships and a private neighborhood with paint nd destroyed others with firebombs. The vandals spray-painted messages like "I love POLLUTION" and "SUV = TERRORISM". Most of all, they repeatedly painted the acronym "ELF," linking them to the Earth Liberation Front, a leaderless, loosely organized activist group. ELF targeted property and managed to avoid causing serious physical harm to anyone in hundreds of credited attacks from the late 1990s through the 2000s. The government branded ELF a terrorist group, partly because ELF used destructive tactics like arson, which is a common tool of militant groups. And, in fact, multiple SUVs were set on fire that night in 2003.

Either way, the government knew they were looking for passionate environmentalists. Within just a couple of weeks, the feds arrested a suspect, Josh Connole. Connole was a peace activist, vegetarian, and solar panel sales rep. He drove an EV and lived at a commune. All of those things seemed to make him a perfect fit for a particular kind of profile.

But Connole wasn't the guy. After his arrest was announced, a reporter at the LA Times received the first of multiple emails from "Tony Marsden" that read, "The police have the wrong man here. I was amongst those responsible for the SUV attacks."

Was the sender concerned about an innocent man paying for their crimes? Maybe, but some gloating was involved, too. "We left plenty of clues, none of them pointing to Josh," the message said, then added smugly, "The FBI hasn't seemed to pick up on any of them, which makes the whole ordeal very boring for us, the true culprits." To prove his involvement, he noted that he had spray-painted an equation by Leonhard Euler, an 18th-century Swiss mathematician, on one of the SUVs. That was a detail that hadn't been released to the public.

His boredom wouldn't last long, as the emails would be traced to his college, Caltech. Apparently, he couldn't be bothered to send the emails from another location. Law enforcement seized multiple computers from the school and found a cache of the email messages on one of the machines, sent right after the sender checked his own messages. The actual sender of the email, as you might have guessed, was not named "Tony Marsden." His name was William "Billy" Cottrell, and he was going for his PhD in theoretical physics at Caltech.

If Billy thought that he could successfully deny sending the emails or his involvement in the spree, that wouldn't last long. Investigators soon matched his DNA to a headband found at the scene of the crime. For Billy, the jig was up.

At first, Billy told investigators he wouldn't implicate anyone else in the spree, but later blamed the arson part of it entirely on his friends, Tyler Johnson and Michie Oe. According to Billy, whose statements are a little self-serving and should probably be taken with a grain of salt, Tyler and Michie showed up that night and convinced him to go spray-paint some SUVs with them. Billy wouldn't have seen this as an odd request, since he and Tyler had recently planned to plaster a couple of hundred SUVs with bumper stickers that said, "My SUV supports terrorism," though that plan fell through.

The three hit one dealership, then another before moving on to a private neighborhood where they vandalized some more SUVs. It was in that neighborhood where Tyler, according to Billy, set the first SUV on fire. Billy claimed that Tyler had never told him about plans to set anything on fire, and he objected when Tyler used the first firebomb. Supposedly, Tyler said it wouldn't happen again. But Tyler didn't stop, and more SUVs were set ablaze at the last dealership hit that night. In fact, a Molotov cocktail accidentally hit Billy's clothes, setting them on fire. He quickly took off his shirt, which is how his headband wound up on the ground for investigators to find.

A few emails later, police had Billy in handcuffs. Johnson and Oe were later named as unindicted co-conspirators, but had fled the country before they could be arrested.

Billy's defense team had few options. They had to draw a line between spray painting, which wasn't a federal crime, and arson, which, in this context, it was. But Billy's attorney came up with an additional defense — Asperger syndrome. Asperger syndrome is a diagnostic term, since dropped by the World Health Organization, for a form of Autism that does not include intellectual or language impairment. His attorney hired a medical professional who later diagnosed Billy with the condition.

The defense claimed that his diagnosed condition kept Billy from picking up on social cues that would have told him that Tyler was lying about stopping at just one firebombing. When it came to figuring out other people's motives, as reported by Los Angeles Magazine, his lawyer asserted that Billy's brain was like "'a slow computer' with a dial-up Internet connection." That seems like an odd way to describe the brain of a doctoral candidate researching theoretical physics. Still, Billy did fit the common, if ill-informed, stereotypes of adults with Autism spectrum disorder with high intelligence. Why didn't he bother to drive to another location to send those emails? He had to get back to his theoretical physics work.

It could be considered a questionable defense strategy, given the estimated 5 million U.S. adults with Autism Spectrum Disorder and most of them, we assume, don't go around vandalizing SUVs. The judge would rule that Asperger's couldn't be used as a defense, but that ruling didn't come until the prosecution had almost rested its case.

A jury found Billy guilty of seven counts of arson and conspiracy to commit arson. The judge sentenced him to over eight years, which included three years added because of the supposed terrorism aspect of the crime. He was also ordered to pay $3.5 million in restitution.

Billy didn't do well in prison, even getting into a fight. It seems he tried to change the channel on the TV to the news when the other inmates wanted to watch "I Love Lucy". His ordeal prompted one of his former professors to write a letter detailing the emotional effects prison conditions were having on Billy. The professor got several prominent physicists, including Stephen Hawking, to sign the letter. It turns out that Billy's case had prompted an intense interest in the scientific community, with many expressing the view that imprisoning someone of his intelligence was depriving the world of the theoretical advancements he could be making. The letter worked, and Billy would be transferred to a different prison to serve out the rest of his sentence.

Eventually, the arson counts were thrown out, and Billy's entire sentence was vacated on appeal because his Asperger's diagnosis wasn't allowed to be used as a defense. The appellate court kept his conspiracy conviction, though, and sent the case back to the trial judge, who resentenced Billy to eight years for the remaining charge, meaning he would have to serve the same amount of time.

Billy was finally released in 2011. After he got out, he finished his PhD in 2017 at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, then held postdoctoral positions at the University of Amsterdam and Stanford University. He would go on to work at Jump Trading and teach a course on cryptocurrencies at the University of Chicago. Overall, things didn't turn out too bad for him. After all, the government has vowed to seek harsh penalties for this kind of crime, and the current administration has even threatened to send perpetrators of similar crimes to El Salvador.

What about his friends? Tyler Johnson fled to Europe and eventually wound up on the island of Corsica. He got by working odd jobs and even founded a nonprofit that supplied solar-powered ovens to households in impoverished communities. He also liked to hike the mountains, which would lead to his tragic death in 2010 in an avalanche. A documentary entitled "Finding Tyler" would be filmed about him after his death.

As far as we can tell, Michie Oe has never been caught. Her name doesn't appear in any law enforcement arrest databases we can search. Whether Billy actually participated in the arson that night or was only a willing participant in the spray painting is anyone's guess. But so far, he's the only one who has paid the price for what happened.

#5724. What Democratic control of Congress means for healthcare in 2027

What Democratic control of Congress means for healthcare in 2027" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Tuesday’s forecast-busting blue wave puts wind in the sails of Democrats who have promised a stark departure from Trump-era healthcare policy—though whether or not the shifts will be incremental or seismic hinges on intra-party debates and the president’s veto.

As of noon Wednesday, Democrats had flipped seven seats in the Senate and 21 in the House, setting the party up for comfortable majorities as unexpected battleground races continue to be tallied.

Healthcare issues were a major talking point through many midterm election campaigns. In battleground Senate races, for instance, Democrats spent $65 million on ads primarily focused on healthcare, more than twice that of their next-most prominent topic. Healthcare was overall the second-most prominent issue featured in ads (as measured by spend) across the two parties, behind a push on taxation topics from Republicans.

And within those ads: promises to deliver lower costs, greater coverage and federal oversight, starting Jan. 1, 2027.

The immediate legislative impact will be seen in the bills new chamber leaders bring to the floor.

A health policy agenda circulated in September by a working group under Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.)—the House’s current minority leader and likely speaker in the next Congress—outlined immediate, “First 100 Hours” goals that include repeal of the Medicaid coverage and funding cuts of 2025’s H.R. 1 (the One Big Beautiful Bill Act) as well as restoration of enhanced Affordable Care Act premium tax credits that expired at the top of 2026 and vastly increased marketplace plan premiums.

Other 100-hours priorities outlined in the document include medical debt protections, removal of visa program fees for healthcare workers, an end to an AI prior authorization program in Traditional Medicare, restoration of withheld National Institutes of Health funding, a block on immigration enforcement operations in hospitals and guaranteed no-cost coverage of recommended vaccines regardless of changes in federal recommendations.

Additionally, the new majorities would install key Democratic policy heads to congressional committees responsible for advancing healthcare legislation and conducting oversight into government and private sector conduct. Among those new chairs would be Vermont’s Bernie Sanders, a vocal opponent of corporate interests in healthcare and the country’s chief Medicare for All advocate, who would chair the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee; and Oregon’s Ron Wyden, who as Finance Committee ranking member recently pursued oversight of Medicaid stakeholders, endorsed Sanders’ Medicare for All bill, led calls to hold “Big Insurance” accountable for administrative roadblocks to care and summarized his midterms reaction with a single word: “Subpoenas.”

Underpinning the party’s legislative leaders are a slew of new-to-office healthcare advocates. Several of those elected to Congress have backgrounds as physicians or other COVID-era public health experience. Among the standouts are Ohio Governor-elect Amy Acton, a pediatrician who was director of the state’s Department of Health and resigned early in the pandemic in protest of state leadership; and Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and Detroit’s former health director, who has made progressive health policy goals like Medicare for All a cornerstone of his campaign.

For the public and the healthcare industry, the key question is how Democrats will pursue their healthcare agenda under a divided government and lame-duck president.

Molly Turco, who covers healthcare policy at TD Cowen Washington Research Group, wrote in a Wednesday policy note that “with Trump in the [White House], passage of major reforms are very unlikely and even medium-sized policies, like rollbacks of Medicaid [state-directed payment] cuts or restoring ACA subsidies, are an uphill battle. But the midterm results and catalysts like the debt ceiling give Ds leverage.”

Consultants at BRG, in a media roundtable late last week, generally agreed with the veto hurdle, but noted that a stymied Congress still has room to write and pass bills that could become new policy in a future majority, as was the case with Medicaid work requirements pushed by Republicans during the end of the Biden administration but ultimately codified last year.

There is still an avenue for dealmaking between the parties, analysts and advisors noted, such as on areas with general bipartisan agreement (think this year’s pharmacy benefit manager reforms, or other major pain points like physician pay or surprise billing arbitration reform) as part of must-pass spending packages slated for this December and the coming years. The president, for his part, told outlets late Tuesday night that he intends to work with Democrats to pass bills he believes will benefit the country—while also highlighting his willingness to veto.

PricewaterhouseCoopers, in a Wednesday policy note, said “targeted bipartisan legislation is most likely to move. Look for action on cybersecurity, AI, price transparency, modernizing drug development and prior authorization processes. Regardless of congressional gridlock, continued regulatory implementation will shape near-term business and compliance requirements.”

Turco’s note predicts a dual messaging strategy for congressional Democrats on affordability and accountability, with the latter involving “an aggressive corporate investigation and hearings strategy.”

The TD Cowen analyst also questioned whether Democrats’ midterm over-performance and gains by progressive candidates will embolden the party to pursue and campaign on “bold” healthcare reforms like Medicare for All ahead of 2028.

Wyden’s recent endorsement of Sanders’ reform bill “is a powerful signal that even long-tenured moderates are under pressure to have a vision that reimagines [healthcare],” Turco wrote, though “many other D members are worried about blowback from M4A support that has almost no chance of being a viable policy. These members are vocal about their concerns and want to work on more realistic policies like restoring the ACA and Medicaid, building on IRA negotiations, reducing premiums/ deductibles for employer-based coverage, adding more benefits to Medicare, etc.”

Investment banking firm William Blair’s equity research team, in an election day brief, noted that Democratic governorships bring immediate impact to the healthcare industry as states make strategic decisions on how to implement, or offset, the provisions of H.R. 1.

The limited avenues for swiftly rolling back that sweeping bill mean that industry players, including Medicare Advantage plans and margin-strapped hospitals, should begin preparing for its financial headwinds, consultants and health systems heads have said. But that doesn’t mean Democrats’ strong night has dashed all hopes for rollbacks or other tweaks to ease the pain.

“While the election has changed who controls Congress, it doesn't change the financial challenges hospitals will face in 2027,” Chris Van Gorder, president and CEO of nonprofit integrated health system Scripps Health, said in a statement reacting to midterm election results. “Democrats won't have the votes to simply reverse major federal health care cuts over a presidential veto. But Congress is far from powerless. Lawmakers can use their oversight and budget authority to press for changes in how those cuts are carried out, protect critical health care funding where possible and work across party lines to ease the growing financial pressures on hospitals and impact on patients."

Even if political gridlock takes hold, Tuesday’s results ensure that affordability will be center stage in Washington, analysts said, especially as consumers’ cost pressures will likely persist well through the 2028 election cycle.

“Even where legislation stalls, don’t dismiss the headlines,” PwC advised healthcare executives. “Democratic hearings, investigations and proposed bills offer insight into the policies taking shape for 2028, while growing pressure around affordability continues to push the healthcare market toward consumer expectations. Executives who look beyond near-term political conflict, plan for multiple policy scenarios and adapt to evolving consumer demands will be better positioned for potential healthcare reform after 2028.”

On the virtual care front, ATA Action, the advocacy-focused affiliate of the American Telemedicine Association, said the election presents an opportunity to build on strong bipartisan support for telehealth and virtual care at the federal and state levels. The group plans to continue working across party lines to make Medicare telehealth policies permanent, expand digital health access and remove regulatory barriers to virtual care, Kyle Zebley, CEO of the ATA and Executive Director of ATA Action, said in a statement.

#5723. Gene Therapy Under Scrutiny After Nine Tumor Reports

— Novartis acknowledges reports in SMA patients treated with Zolgensma

Drugmaker Novartis acknowledged Thursday that there have been nine reports of tumors in children treated with its gene therapy onasemnogene abeparvovec (Zolgensma) for spinal muscular atrophy (SMA).

Two of the tumor cases were linked to the drug, the company said.

Zolgensma, an adeno-associated virus (AAV) vector-based gene therapy, was approved in 2019 to treat pediatric patients under 2 years of age with SMA and bi-allelic SMN1 mutations.

"Since first approval in 2019, Novartis has received 9 reports of tumors in patients previously treated with Zolgensma," a Novartis spokesperson wrote in an email to MedPage Today.

"Of those, two cases to date have shown evidence of vector DNA integration into the DNA of the patients. In both cases, the patients underwent treatment and continue to be monitored," the spokesperson continued. "In each case, we timely and appropriately notified health authorities and will continue to work with them on next steps."

The spokesperson did not say when tumors may have developed in the other seven cases, or when they were identified.

SMA is caused by reduced levels of the survival motor neuron (SMN) protein due to deletions or mutations in the SMN1 gene. A nearly identical gene, SMN2, produces low levels of functional SMN protein.

Onasemnogene abeparvovec uses an AAV vector to replace the SMN1 gene. Its prescribing information notes a theoretical risk of tumorigenicity from the integration of AAV vector DNA into the genome.

"The potential risk of tumors due to vector integration is currently included in the Zolgensma prescribing information," Novartis said.

Advocates recently raised concerns on social media after learning from their doctors that Novartis had received reports of tumors in patients treated with the gene therapy. SMA Europe, an umbrella organization of SMA patient groups in Europe, acknowledged the reports in a news release early Thursday.

"We understand that the relevant regulatory authorities are actively involved and are currently assessing the available evidence and determining what further steps may be needed," SMA Europe stated. "We trust in the regulatory processes established to evaluate safety signals and to take the necessary measures to protect patients and ensure the continued safety of medicines on the market."

In the U.S., the Muscular Dystrophy Association (MDA) said it was "seeking additional information, reviewing the available scientific and safety data with clinical and research experts, and has reached out to Novartis."

The MDA added that "limited information is available currently about the timing of events, nature of the tumors, and any future monitoring of treated individuals that may become appropriate."

A 2023 case report described a 16-month-old boy with SMA who was diagnosed with an epithelioid neoplasm of the spinal cord 14 months after receiving onasemnogene abeparvovec; the finding was considered inconclusive. A 2025 case report detailed a pilocytic astrocytoma in a child with SMA treated with onasemnogene abeparvovec; a molecular analysis suggested tumorigenesis was causally independent of the gene therapy.

Earlier this year, researchers identified vector integration in a brain tumor in a 5-year-old boy with severe mucopolysaccharidosis type I (Hurler syndrome) who received another AAV gene therapy, describing the case in the New England Journal of Medicine.

More than 6,000 patients have been treated with Zolgensma in clinical trials, managed access programs, and commercial treatment, Novartis said. "As part of Novartis' ongoing commitment to monitoring the safety of our medicines, we continually evaluate new safety information and assess all reported cases," the company added.

The tumor reports are not the first controversy involving Zolgensma. Soon after the therapy was approved, the FDA criticized the Novartis AveXis unit over data manipulation that affected the accuracy of animal product-testing results.

#5722. Cold Seawater Is Supplying District Heat in Esbjerg, Denmark

Esbjerg, Denmark, is using large electric heat pumps to extract heat from the North Sea and supply its district-heating network. During a two-hour winter test, seawater entered the system at 3.3°C and left at 1.2°C. The two heat pumps consumed 19.9 MW of electricity and supplied 55.2 MW of heat at a district-heating water temperature of 90°C. The difference, 35.3 MW, came from the seawater. The project team’s May 2025 operating report recorded a coefficient of performance, or COP, of 2.8. The figures describe that test, not annual average performance.

A heat pump transfers thermal energy from a colder source to a warmer destination. Its refrigerant absorbs heat at a temperature below that of the seawater, and an electrically driven compressor raises the temperature so the heat can enter the district network. Esbjerg uses carbon dioxide as its refrigerant in a high-pressure cycle. For each unit of electricity used by the compressors during the test, the plant delivered 2.8 units of heat. Resistance heating would have required 2.8 times as much electricity for the same heat output under those conditions.

The installation has a nominal heating capacity of 70 MW and began delivering heat in late 2024, as part of Esbjerg’s replacement of its retired coal-fired combined heat and power plant. The operating report describes controls for variable conditions and protection against freezing as seawater temperatures fall. The recorded COP of 2.8 was lower than the more favourable performance figures used in the original project expectations, and full guarantee testing had not been completed when the results were published. The city’s heating supply also includes a wood-chip boiler and waste-incineration heat. Emissions reductions reported for the wider replacement programme cannot be attributed in full to the seawater heat pumps.

Electricity price and heating-network temperature have a direct effect on the cost. At an illustrative electricity price of €100/MWh, compressor power at COP 2.8 costs about €36 per MWh of useful heat. That excludes seawater pumping, equipment maintenance, capital recovery, financing and heat distribution. A network able to operate at lower water temperatures generally asks the compressor to make a smaller temperature increase, which can improve COP. Older networks supplying 90°C heat face a harder operating requirement than newer, lower-temperature networks.

Esbjerg builds on decades of seawater heating experience. Monaco began using seawater heat pumps in 1963, and Stockholm has used large seawater-sourced district-heating equipment since the 1980s. Creative Energy’s Horseshoe Bay development in West Vancouver takes a different approach. Submerged heat exchangers transfer heat through a closed loop, with no seawater intake or discharge to the marina. Denmark’s Aalborg project is developing 177 MW of seawater heat-pump capacity. These installations serve different loads and use different marine arrangements, so their costs cannot be assumed to match Esbjerg’s.

Marine heat systems require more than suitable water temperatures. Engineers must address corrosion, biological fouling, intake and discharge effects, pumping requirements, maintenance access and freezing protection. The environmental assessment has to consider the local marine ecosystem and the discharge of colder water. The distribution network can be the larger financial obstacle in areas without existing pipes or concentrated heat demand. Wastewater, industrial waste heat, ground-source systems or individual air-source heat pumps may provide lower-cost heat at some sites.

Hot-water storage can add value by allowing a utility to make some heat when electricity is inexpensive and deliver it later. The available flexibility depends on storage capacity, network temperatures and heat demand. Esbjerg’s test provides direct evidence that cold seawater can support high-temperature district heating. Coastal utilities can use that evidence when comparing local heat sources, network investments and the costs of replacing combustion-based heating.

My TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines Esbjerg’s operating results, experience in Stockholm and Monaco, the Horseshoe Bay system near Vancouver, and the cost and environmental factors that determine where seawater heating is suitable.

Michael Barnard has 1545 posts and counting. See all posts by Michael Barnard

#5721. Well, Someone 3D-Printed A Whole Engine And It Actually Ran (Sort Of)

You've probably sat around a campfire at some point in your life and figured out firsthand that plastic and heat don't mix. Whether you threw an empty soda bottle or marshmallow bag in and watched it shrivel up, or propped your sandals up on the stones around the fire and witnessed your soles melting, you get it.

Plastic is a pretty good insulator, but it has a pretty low melting point. ABS has a melting point of around 440 degrees Fahrenheit, while most available PLAs melt at 340-ish degrees. If you've spent any time looking at your engine's oil or coolant temperature gauges, you'll know that a running engine is pretty stable in the low 200-degree range, but the combustion chamber can get up to 2,500 degrees during the peak of the power stroke. Plastic doesn't stand a chance, which is why most engines are crafted from cast iron or aluminum.

We've already seen what happens when you try to use a 3D-printed cylinder head; the results aren't pretty. With the kind of heat an engine sees, plastic just isn't the preferred material to work with. There are certainly some engines that have made extensive use of plastic, including the Torlon-based engines from Polimotor Research in the 1970s and 80s, but there isn't a high-enough-heat plastic to manage combustion chamber heat spikes, so a blend of metal and plastic is necessary.

YouTuber and mad scientist Alexander's Laboratory recently built and ran a pair of 3D-printed plastic engines, a single-cylinder and a parallel twin. We'll talk through both engines and their unique challenges in a second. First, we should take a step back and think about the implications of potentially building real working 3D-printed engines as prices come down and the technology both improves and becomes commonplace.

Have you ever built (or rebuilt) an engine for one of your project cars? There are just so many pieces and parts you have to buy, and there's so much measuring and clearance-checking to be done before the parts can all get bolted together. It's time-consuming and expensive, but the longest time you'll spend working on it is the shipping time to get all of the parts. Imagine if, someday, every engine in every car shared interchangeable components that could be stocked at any local auto parts store, and the rest could be 3D-printed at home. Wouldn't that be cool?

There are certainly still components that would need to be made out of metal, of course. The obvious first step would be to use metal for the combustion chamber, cylinder head, pistons, and crankshaft. You would also need to figure out a bearing system that works for the crankshaft and camshafts. Then there are things like the valves, valve springs, hardware, water pump components, and the accessory drive pullies.

Alexander is able to make most of his engines out of plastic, including the water pump and drive gears, but I'd go with metal for those on a full-scale engine, purely for longevity's sake. In the end, if you could make it work, you would have an engine significantly lighter than a comparable aluminum cylinder head and engine block unit. Recent research indicates swapping from a metal component to a 3D-printed plastic replacement cuts weight by 30% and costs by 15%. With enough research, you could add structural lattice inside some areas of components to make it even lighter, or allow better coolant flow to critical heat spots. Now this is exciting!

If you wanted to build a 3D-printed plastic engine, what steps would you need to take so it would run for more than a few seconds? As mentioned above, some metal is needed to keep it alive. Alexander strategically used machined steel for both the cylinder walls and the combustion chamber surface. This is smart, as it allows a sealing surface for the metal valves and the ability to thread in a common spark plug. The crankshaft is also metal, as is the surface of the pistons, but pretty much everything else comes straight off the printer.

In the single-cylinder-engine video above, Alexander had some issues with sparks and grounding. It's harder to get everything to ground out properly when the engine is non-conductive, of course. Once it gets running, though, it sure sounds like a pretty normal single-cylinder four-stroke engine, the kind you might find in a lawnmower or go-kart. After getting everything dialed in, Alexander piles on the throttle until the engine decides to eat itself. We don't get an indication of how long it ran, but eventually the carbon-reinforced plastic connecting rod gives up the ghost and shoots through the side of the plastic block.

Trying again with a more balanced twin-cylinder engine, Alexander might actually be on to something. Using some beefed-up components, a little more metal, and better heat management, this little 250-cc twin seems, in the video anyway, to run and work as a standard small motorcycle or scooter engine would. With a better-built engine and more care taken in its running, the twin just keeps on chugging. Maybe it's time to start developing open-source plastic engines that can run with just a few off-the-shelf components. It could be cool.

CommonSpirit Health has locked in a deal to sell three hospitals to Altru Health System, a rural North Dakota nonprofit.

The deal is contingent on regulatory review and other customary closing conditions, but is expected to close in early 2027. The pair's new definitive agreement, announced Wednesday, follows 10 months of due diligence following a letter of intent unveiled near the top of the year (see that story below). Financial details were not disclosed.

The to-be-sold facilities are CHI St. Alexius Health Bismarck, a multispecialty acute care medical center in the state’s capital, and two smaller critical access hospitals, CHI St. Alexius Health Turtle Lake and CHI St. Alexius Health Garrison.

They would join Altru's flagship acute care hospital, a critical access hospital it also purchased from CommonSpirit in March, a trauma center, a specialty hospital and 20 practices spread across northern North Dakota.

The organizations said there are no changes to patient care or day-to-day operations related to the deal. The hospitals will maintain their Catholic identity and mission.

"Through our work together over the years, we’ve developed tremendous confidence in Altru’s commitment to high-quality, compassionate care," Tim Bricker, president of CommonSpirit Health's Central Region, said in reference to prior partnerships with the health system. "We believe Altru is the right partner to build on St. Alexius’ proud legacy, honor its Catholic mission and continue serving patients and families for generations to come.”

CommonSpirit is in the midst of a sweeping operational overhaul as it looks to bolster its financial performance ahead of imminent Medicaid cuts. Those efforts have opened the $42.4 billion system to a string of hospital divestitures, including its four handoffs to Altru as well as the sale of a four-hospital Ohio system to UPMC in September.

CommonSpirit Health and Altru Health System are considering a deal to transfer three North Dakota hospitals to the latter, the organizations announced Thursday.

The pair’s signed letter of intent outlines plans to evaluate a potential deal for the facilities, a process they said would run “the next several months” before a potential definitive agreement might be struck.

In the balance are CHI St. Alexius Health Bismarck, a multispecialty acute care medical center in the state’s capital, and two smaller critical access hospitals, CHI St. Alexius Health Turtle Lake and CHI St. Alexius Health Garrison. All three are Catholic facilities within CommonSpirit’s regional healthcare system CHI St. Alexius Health.

Potential financial terms of any deal for the hospitals were not disclosed, nor were any details on whether other assets tied to the hospitals, such as clinics, would be included.

“This is a natural next step in exploring how we can continue to support strong, sustainable healthcare for the region,” Tim Bricker, president of CommonSpirit Health’s central region, which includes CHI St. Alexius Health, said in the announcement.

CommonSpirit is a $40 billion nonprofit that counted 137 hospitals in two dozen states. It’s in the midst of an operating performance turnaround initiative and, at this month’s J.P. Morgan Healthcare Conference, teased “a couple” of portfolio divestitures to be announced in the next quarter as part of the effort.

Grand Forks, North Dakota-based Altru Health System is a smaller nonprofit, with just over $700 million of revenue in 2024 from its sole acute care hospital, a specialty hospital and 20 practice locations in northeast North Dakota and northwest Minnesota. It opened a new $500 million hospital in January 2025.

The news comes hot on the heels of another deal between the systems for ownership of CHI St. Alexius Health Devils Lake, another critical access hospital. That handoff was unveiled in December and is set to close March 1.

Both deals have been described as a boon for rural communities and an opportunity for Altru to better coordinate its local care.

“Altru has a long history of serving communities across North Dakota and northwest Minnesota, and our organizations share a deep respect for the people we serve and the responsibility that comes with delivering local healthcare,” Todd Forkel, CEO of Altru, said in the announcement. “We look forward to working more closely with CommonSpirit to strengthen access to care for patients and families well into the future.”

#5719. Why Pontiac Paid The SCCA $5 For Every Trans Am It Built

Pontiac had helped launch the muscle-car era in 1963 — when it debuted the GTO package for its 1964 Pontiac Tempest LeMans coupe — and the brand followed that up with the Firebird pony car in 1967. In 1969, both saw iconic variants take the stage. The former began courting customers with a new GTO trim called The Judge, while the latter hatched the Firebird Trans Am.

Only, it wasn't called the Trans Am at first. The brand had originally tried out a variety of different ideas on the public, with "Sebring" coming out on top –- inspired, no doubt, by the country's oldest road-racing circuit, Sebring International Raceway in Sebring, Florida. Yet, when Pontiac went to register the name, it discovered Chrysler had gotten there first.

The public's next-most-popular names were "Formula" and "Trans Am," so Pontiac snapped up both. Trans Am was reserved for the most powerful member of the Firebird family, which was actually a little odd. General Motors was already running Camaros in the Sports Car Club of America's Trans Am series. Moreover, Pontiac's decision ran into a roadblock anyways. It turns out that the brand didn't have permission from the SCCA to use that moniker, at least not at first. Once the lawyers got involved, Pontiac agreed to pay the organization $5 for every Firebird Trans Am it produced.

Now, finding the exact amount forked over isn't easy, but in 1979 alone, for instance, enthusiast sites say that Pontiac made more than 117,000 Tran Ams. Royalties-wise, that works out to a non-negligible total of $585,000, which is equivalent to about $2.7 million today. Some sources say that — during some seasons — the Pontiac royalty check was all that kept the SCCA out of bankruptcy.

One of the reasons Pontiac didn't put up a fuss about the royalty deal was that it didn't think it would actually sell that many. The SCCA apparently didn't realize what was going on until 1970 or 1971, and the brand had only produced 697 Trans Ams during the model's first partial year on the market — it went on sale in April of 1969. For some context, the entire Firebird lineup, in what was considered a down year, was worth 87,709 sales during 1969.

But one of the main reasons the Trans Am was introduced was to boost demand for the Firebird family. Helping to attract enthusiast customers was a pretty comprehensive package of upgrades that would set you back $724.60 (for a total Trans Am base price that opened at about $3,600). The highlight was under the hood, where Pontiac placed a standard 400-cubic-inch V8 with a Ram Air III intake system good for 330 bhp. As an alternative, buyers could opt for a more powerful setup with 345 bhp. It's backed by the same displacement, plus high-lift cams and upgraded valves/pistons. Additionally, there were standard dynamic details such as front/rear spoilers, functional hood scoops, a ride-and-handling package, high-effort variable-ratio power steering, high-effort power front disc brakes, and dual exhaust. Of course, when it comes to exhaust outlets, two isn't always better than one.

All '69 Trans Ams were then wrapped in a Cameo White exterior accented by Tyrol Blue racing stripes. One thing that did set some apart, however, was the body style. The majority of the first-year cars – 689 -– were hardtops, but 8 were convertibles.

Currently presented by Pirelli — and originally known as the Trans American Sedan Championship — the series was just about to wrap up its 60th-anniversary season at the Circuit of the Americas when this article was written. The very first race was held in 1966, and in an interesting coincidence, it was at Sebring.

The first years of the series might have been its golden era, too. That's when it was a high-performance playground for pony cars such as the Camaro Z/28, Mustang Boss 302, Dodge Challenger T/A, and AMC Javelin. But what's ironic is that the 1969 Pontiac Firebird Trans Am, the one that first borrowed the Trans Am name from the SCCA, never raced in the series because its engine was too big for the rulebook. That said, the occasional Pontiac Trans Am did show up in the series' record books. The highlight? Sports-car master Elliot Forbes-Robinson drove his Trans Am racecar to five victories and the series championship in 1982.

There were some big names on hand as well. That first Trans Am race at Sebring was won by Jochen Rindt, who would go on to claim the 1970 Formula 1 driver's championship. The likes of A.J. Foyt, Jacky Ickx, Richard Petty, and Mark Donohue also competed in the series' early seasons. Meanwhile, after a few decades with a more international focus – Jaguar, for one, scored multiple driver's and manufacturer's championships in the early 2000s — Trans Am racing has returned to American muscle in recent years, and that's even though some folks don't think muscle cars have to be American. The 2026 field is packed with Chevrolet Camaros and Ford Mustangs.

#5718. Will RFK Jr. Face Impeachment Under New Congress?

— Dems already are discussing investigations, but impeachment would be a heavier lift, experts say

On Friday, as some public health groups continued to call for the impeachment of HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Kennedy's fate remained up in the air following the Democrats' overwhelming sweep in the congressional midterms.

"The more measles cases are reported, the further the administration digs in their heels against the solution: a full-scale federal effort to vaccinate Americans against the disease," Kayla Hancock, director of the Public Health Project at Protect Our Care, a public health group, said in a statement. "Trump and [Kennedy] would rather scare parents than protect children ... Kennedy should have resigned in disgrace long ago, but his ego is immune to shame and accepting responsibility. With the incoming Democratic Congress that actually trusts science and wants to eliminate measles once and for all, Kennedy's impeachment may be the only way out of this mess."

Kennedy's perceived lack of action on the measles epidemic, along with his questioning the safety and effectiveness of vaccines, has angered many public health advocates. His running of HHS itself, including closing down several offices and redirecting the way appropriated funds were spent -- for example, keeping the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality open but taking away most of its funding and rendering it inoperable -- also has drawn controversy.

If Kennedy doesn't decide to leave of his own accord, as Cabinet secretaries sometimes do halfway through an administration, "he's going to be on the hot seat a lot," Georges Benjamin, MD, CEO of the American Public Health Association, said in a phone interview. "Every time he does one of these illegal or immoral acts that he's continued to do over time, or says something that is ill-tempered or inappropriate ... I expect that in addition to groups like mine calling him out, he'll be called out more and more by Congress. So I think he's going to be miserable in terms of the oversight that he's going to see."

Indeed, future members of Congress have already begun talking about investigating Kennedy. Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, MD, the senator-elect from Michigan, told CNN that he was going to look into Kennedy's cuts to the FDA and CDC and how they affected the explosive diarrhea outbreak this summer that was traced to tainted lettuce.

"This is not about retribution for something past," El-Sayed told CNN. "This is about understanding what happened, holding people accountable for what they did, and then solving the problem moving forward."

The question becomes how long Kennedy will be willing to put up with the increased scrutiny, Georges said. "Obviously my dream is he's fired or quits. Is it possible they might try to impeach him? It's possible, but you've got to get a two-thirds vote [in the Senate] to do that, and whether you can get enough Republicans to come on board, I don't know."

Kennedy appears to have some administration support, at least for now. A story in Politico Thursday noted that "Emily Hilliard, senior press secretary at Kennedy's Health Department, said Kennedy 'will continue delivering President Trump's Make America Healthy Again [MAHA] agenda and advancing historic policies that put the health of the American people first.'" In an emailed statement, she said the administration "has transformed federal food and nutrition policy ... and reshaped the federal approach to scientific research and environmental health."

And Tony Lyons, who works for a number of organizations in the MAHA movement that Kennedy is aligned with, said he'd work with congressional Democrats who were open to Kennedy's plans related to things MAHA cares about.

To move forward, "we partner with absolutely everyone who's willing to partner with us -- companies who will listen, politicians who will work with us from any party, activists, influencers, MAHA moms in every corner of the country," Lyons said during a virtual call with supporters, according to The Hill.

Policy analyst Steven Grossman, JD, a former HHS official, said in a MedPage Today opinion piece Friday that although he had been thinking Kennedy would stay for the whole administration, that's no longer as likely. "Post-election, the job will quickly become a nightmare for Kennedy, as he will have to respond to hostile investigative hearings led by Democrats on the health committees. And Kennedy is unlikely to get White House help: Trump will have bigger fights to address and less political capital to spend."

"Also, if impeachment hearings were to start, Kennedy would be behind only Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as the object of Congressional attention," he added. "This situation will evolve, but I suspect Kennedy will leave (resign) rather than face congressional challenges to his own hubris."

Michael Baker, director of healthcare policy at the American Action Forum, said in an email that although Kennedy's fate at the moment is unclear, "there are both new and returning members [of Congress] that want to focus on various parts of the healthcare ecosystem. And I expect oversight of the Department of Health and Human Services and its leadership to be a top priority in that focus."

"From the most-favored-nation drug price agreements to the changes in the ACIP [Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices] and pediatric vaccine schedule to the Medicaid cuts, there is no shortage of policies that congressional committees will investigate, and I think that oversight effort happens no matter who is sitting in the secretary's (or any other official's) chair," he said.

#5717. The Velotric GoMad Electric Utility eBike — CleanTechnica Tested

Velotric has emerged as one of the largest ebike brands in the US, offering a wide range of models for buyers to choose from. Having a wide range of models with differing capabilities is increasingly a key factor for buyers when deciding which ebike to buy, as it allows them to upgrade or swap out for a different model to accommodate different stages of life.

They reached out to CleanTechnica about a review and we were excited to play with the Velotric GoMad Electric Utility bike, because it is just so darn flexible in what it can do. You can throw a set of bags on the back rack or a passenger kit to bring a friend with you. You can put a basket on the back and deliver pizzas, or you can just throw a backpack on and ride around town solo. It truly looked like the jack of all trades, so we pulled the trigger, and after a few days, it showed up.

Disclaimer: Velotric provided the GoMad to the author for the purposes of this review.

Assembling the Velotric GoMad is similar to the process for most e-bikes. It can be done with a basic set of tools that are included with the bike, and takes between 30 minutes and an hour depending on how much of a hurry you’re in.

After that, it’s a simple matter of attaching the pedals, mounting the handlebars to the stem, installing the front wheel and tire, connecting a few of the electrical connectors between the handlebars and the bike itself, airing up the tires, and you’re on your way. Ours took a few minutes longer than normal to bolt on the optional Passenger Kit

Taking in the Velotric GoMad, it is an attractive bike with great proportions. The battery is integrated into the main downtube on the frame, which makes it look slightly bloated, but in a way that fits into the overall proportions of the bike. The oversized tires help with this, making it look like it can go absolutely anywhere.

The rear hub motor kicks out plenty of power, and with a range of pedal assist modes. You can choose just how much power you need for the ride you want. You can choose from the motor being completely off, Eco, Tour, Trail, Sport, and even the full-out Boost mode that can give you exactly the support you need.

It’s perfect for when you’re carrying a load, powering up a hill, or just feeling tired. The motor is always ready to step in to provide assistance. At the upper end of its power cycle, the motor controller is more sensitive to the pedaling cadence, resulting in the motor pulsing on and off, providing for a bit of a bumpy sensation when pedaling. It’s only something you’d notice if you’re really paying attention, but it’s there.

The GoMad is designed with an integrated rear rack and a hidden storage pocket. The rack can also be converted into a seat for a second passenger with Velotric’s passenger kit. The passenger kit itself is amazing if that’s what you’re looking for, and this is further accentuated by the bike’s compact footprint. The tradeoff is that the main seat has a flat rear, which does make it slightly less comfortable than more fully built-out options.

The passenger kit comes with a set of pegs down below for the passengers’ feet to rest on, a rear grab rail for the rack, and a front handle for the passenger to hang onto as you’re boosting around town. Given the compact footprint of the bike, it feels like it was designed to be used as more of a teenager-plus-one setup, but if you want to put it to work as a husband-and-wife date night setup, its 500 pound weight capacity is more than up to the task.

I rode around on it with my wife on the back and it was very comfortable and stable for both of us. The foot pegs and the solid support bars that come with the passenger kit make it feel much safer and more comfortable for the passenger. I took a few pics of us on the bike, but, hilariously, none of them had the bike in frame and she wasn’t a fan of my one handed stunts. Of course, that’s for you to decide what you want to do with your life and how you want to set up your bike and put it to use.

The Velotric Nomad is an extremely capable bike at a mid-level price point for bikes of this quality and capability. It’s currently listed as $1,899 with a special Black Friday offer that includes a free young passenger kit.

The fact that its 750W continuous power output motor has a peak of 1,300W means it’s got plenty of pep to take even the largest and least-in-shape riders wherever they want to go. The specs across the board and the integration of the torque and cadence sensor make it feel like a very natural ride that will surprise you with just how intuitively the power is coming from the motor.

I especially love the colorways this bike comes in. They have a nice modern-looking sage that feels classy and refined, a dark amber that’s somewhere between a bright orange and bright red that looks like a pop of lipstick that really sets the whole frame off, and finally an obsidian, which is what our review bike came in.

The obsidian has a base color that looks almost black, but then when you put it in the sunlight, it has a rainbow pop of color that peeks out every once in a while. It’s not so much that it feels like it’s covered in glitter, but it’s just enough to make it feel fun.

For more information about the Velotric Nomad e-bike, head over to their official website, where you can learn all about it or purchase one for yourself.

#5716. AI Comes For Drag Racers' Jobs As GM Patents Automated Launch Control

AI is coming for all of us. Not necessarily in an apocalyptic world like "The Terminator" or "The Matrix," but by stealing jobs from truck drivers, astronauts, and even Jalopnik writers (despite what I read in the comments, I assure you we're all human beings — at least, for now). Not even drag racers are safe, thanks to a launch control system GM patented that not only automates the launch process, but even reads the countdown Christmas tree to time a perfect launch.

Patents can be wordy and cumbersome to read, but Road & Track sums this one up nicely. Some cars already have launch control systems, which can get you off the line as quickly as possible with the perfect balance of power and traction. Pair those systems with the cameras being used in cars today and the rest is a simple matter of programming.

The potential future tech uses the car's cameras to recognize the Christmas tree lights at a drag strip, and a prompt instructs the driver to activate launch control. This part works like normal, with the driver pressing the gas and brake pedals simultaneously. Once launch control is engaged, the driver removes their feet from the pedals, and the car takes over. It doesn't just use its onboard cameras to watch the lights and go on green, it initiates the launch process before the light is green, ensuring the car begins to move precisely when it's supposed to without red-lighting or launching too early. This is exactly the way I learned to do it, but a computer is going to be far more precise than my feet. I'm only human.

Automatic drag strip launch control is a fine technological achievement. It also completely misses the point of what racing is all about: human drivers testing their skill against one another. Drag racing doesn't have the braking or handling challenges of a road course or rally stage, but it still requires skill to reduce your reaction time and execute even a near-perfect launch. If you take that out of the equation by automating the entire process, what's left? Not steering into the wall? In a production car, that takes even less skill than driving down the highway. (Top Fuel dragsters and Funny Cars are a completely different story. Mad respect to them.)

Does anyone really want autonomous racing? I sure don't. In theory, a machine can always put down the perfect lap, time after time. The only time it gets exciting is when the programming goes wrong, and it steers straight into a wall. People already complain that Formula 1 is boring. It takes extraordinary driver talent to race at those speeds, but the cars are so good, so reliable, and so evenly matched that there's little difference between them. Take the driver out of the car, and it's nothing but a competition of technology. If I want to see that, I'd rather watch BattleBots. It's much more fun, and you get to watch them completely destroy each other.

I have never driven a perfect lap, and I never will. Perfection itself doesn't matter. It's the pursuit of perfection that matters. Striving to do better than we ever have before is rewarding for its own sake. It's also part of what makes us human. So I'll leave GM's drag strip launch control turned off and drop the clutch myself. I don't care that I'll run a slower time than the fully automated machine. As a certain James Bond villain once said, "There's no point in living if you can't feel alive."

#5715. Chutes & Ladders—UHC names individual MA leader; HATCo CEO steps down

Chutes & Ladders—UHC names individual MA leader; HATCo CEO steps down" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Welcome to this week's Chutes & Ladders, our roundup of hirings, firings and retirings throughout the industry. Please submit the good news—or the bad—from your shop, and we will feature it here each week.

> UnitedHealthcare has named Suha Assi as CEO of individual Medicare Advantage, per a LinkedIn post.

Assi previously spent nearly a decade as executive director for Medicare and Retirement in Tennessee, and she previously held roles based in the state for Cigna. She wrote in the post that the "relationships with our teams, providers and communities have shaped how I think about this business and, most importantly, the people we serve."

"As I step into this national role, I’m excited about what’s ahead for Medicare Advantage," she wrote. "I look forward to working alongside teams and provider partners across the country to modernize how we work together, strengthen relationships, and find new ways to deliver for our members."

> Daryl Tol, president and CEO of General Catalyst's Health Assurance Transformation Company (HATCo) is stepping down from the role, the venture capital firm's CEO Hemant Taneja shared Tuesday.

Tol had been with the firm for about four and a half years in the wake of his time as president and CEO of AdventHealth's Central Florida Division. During that time, he headed HATCo's partner and advisory network—helping grow it to nearly 40 providers, payers and other portfolio companies—and took the company's top spot partway through 2025. Of note, he helped HATCo close its acquisition of regional health system Summa Health and served as its interim CEO for much of the past year until the appointment of Jennifer Eslinger last month.

Tol is being succeeded by Reva Nohria, a founding member of the HATCo team who has been with General Catalyst since 2018. Taneja, in his announcement, said her work at both organizations has encompassed investment, company creation and strategic partnership, and that she will continue as an investor at the venture capital firm alongside her new appointment.

Tol will support a smooth leadership transition and remain in an advisory role, a representative of General Catalyst told Fierce Healthcare.

> Jennifer Shuford, M.D., is leaving her post as deputy director and chief medical officer of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Nov. 12, just four months after joining, according to a Washington Post report that was confirmed by the agency on Tuesday.

The agency told press in a statement that Shuford was departing "to spend more time with family." Her appointment was announced by President Donald Trump in April, and she joined in June.

Shuford is an infectious disease specialist who came to the federal stage from a role as commissioner of the Texas Department of State Health Services and before that, served as the state's chief epidemiologist. Notably, she was credited with heading Texas' response to a measles outbreak last year. Her departure comes as the CDC clashes with state health departments and other public health leaders over its response to a growing national measles outbreak.

Satish Pillai, M.D., is slated to fill the role in the interim as the agency seeks a replacement, the CDC said.

> Johns Hopkins Health System CEO Kevin Sowers is set to retire at the end of 2027.

Sowers has served as president and CEO of the Johns Hopkins system since 2018. He also previously spent more than 32 years as a leader within the Duke University Health System, including eight as CEO of Duke University Hospital.

The early announcement of his retirement plans gives Johns Hopkins significant time to conduct a search for a successor, with Theodore DeWeese, dean of the medical faculty and CEO of Johns Hopkins Medicine, leading the charge. Sowers will become a strategic adviser to Johns Hopkins to support the transition, the health system said.

"When I joined Johns Hopkins Medicine in 2018, I made a commitment to the organization and to myself to give 10 years of everything I had to this extraordinary place—to the talented, dedicated people who work here, and the people and communities we serve. And I intend to keep that commitment," Sowers said in a video message.

> Calley Means, a prominent senior advisor to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. closely aligned with the Make America Healthy Again Movement, resigned from his role on Thursday.

The resignation was reported by the Wall Street Journal and confirmed by Means on social media.

Media reports from the past several months described Means' frustrations seeing MAHA policy priorities delayed or blunted by others in the administration, with the journal citing sources describing him as "disillusioned." Still, his time advising the secretary notched several wins for the movement, including overhauled dietary guidelines, steps toward greater food ingredient transparency and loosened restrictions on psychedelics as potential medical treatments.

Means wrote in his confirmation post that he still holds "tremendous respect for President Trump and Bobby Kennedy" in their battles against "the entrenched, dark forces in D.C. that profit from Americans getting sick."

"More policy and cultural change has happened around these goals in the past two years than any time in history—and I know this movement is just getting started," he wrote.

> Premier Health, a five-hospital nonprofit academic system in Southwest Ohio, has appointed Rosanna Morris as its upcoming president and CEO, effective in the first quarter of 2027.

Morris is currently executive vice president and chief clinical operating officer at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, and was previously president of Beaumont Hospital-Royal Oak. She is a registered nurse by training and has more than 27 years of health leadership.

She takes over for the retiring Michael Riordan, who has led Premier Health for about half a decade. During that period, he's credited, by the system's board, with stabilizing the system's finances.

> Centivo has added two leaders to its C-suite, the health plan announced.

Lisa Bielamowicz, M.D., will join the company as chief health officer, while James Parr will step into the role of chief commercial officer. Both are veteran healthcare leaders, Centivo said.

Bielamowicz has a long career as a physician and health system consultant, and will take on the chief health officer title after advising Centivo's board of directors.

Parr has previously served as a senior adviser to employers at Lockton as well as senior vice president and head of sales at Collective Health. Parr has also held leadership roles at Cigna, per the announcement.
