Prior to joining Hims, he founded Next Generation Medicine, which combines medical education with AI technology to assist clinicians with incorporating longevity medicine. He is also the author of several peer-reviewed publications, and Vinjamoori received his MD from Harvard Medical School and his MBA from Harvard Business School.

The Global Chief Medical Officer of Hims & Hers, Pat Caroll, says “Dr. Vinjamoori has been at the leading edge of helping people feel great at every stage of life, and he brings the perfect combination of clinical expertise and dedication to consumer access to Hims & Hers.” His work will shape Hims’ clinical backbone in the sexual health, hormone health, dermatology, weight loss, and mental health fields, according to the company’s press release.

>The Melanoma Research Alliance (MRA), a nonprofit funder of melanoma research, announced that beginning on July 1, 2026, Stephanie Kauffmann will serve as the organization's Chief Executive Officer. Joining MRA in 2022 as Chief Operating Officer and President, she oversaw growth in research investment and philanthropic and corporate partnerships.

Kauffman will replace Marc Hulbert, Ph.D., who is leaving MRA to become CEO of the National Kidney Foundation. The Board recognized Dr. Hulbert’s contribution to strengthening the position of MRA as a melanoma research funding leader, and notes that he will continue to serve as a member of MRA's Scientific Advisory Panel.

According to Debra Black, Co-Founder and Chair of the Melanoma Research Alliance, in Kauffman’s previous role she “has earned the trust and respect of our Board, staff, researchers, donors, and patient community through her leadership, vision, and unwavering commitment to our mission.” Under Kauffman’s leadership, MRA plans to continue expanding their investments in groundbreaking rare melanoma research and patient centered innovation to improve conditions for patients worldwide.

>Ardent Health President and CEO Marty Bonick "has stepped down to pursue other opportunities," the for-profit health system announced this week. Replacing him immediately is Dave Caspers, who had been serving as chief operating officer.

Bonick helmed the company through a string of challenges, including the COVID-19 pandemic and its 2024 initial public offering. Board Chairman Mark Sotir noted that work in the announcement and said the former head executive had positioned Ardent "for sustained long-term growth and help[ed] build a strong foundation as the Company continues to navigate industry headwinds with a focus on disciplined execution. We wish him all the best in his next chapter."

Caspers, meanwhile, joined Ardent in March 2025 but has spent decades in operational roles. These include senior healthcare leadership positions at Walmart Health, Banner Health and Target. He's spent the past year in the weeds of Ardent's IMPACT (Improve Margins, Performance, Agility and Care Transformation) Program.

"Over the past year, I have had the privilege of working closely with Marty, whose leadership and guidance have been instrumental in laying the solid footing on which Ardent Health now stands," said Caspers, who has also joined Ardent's board. "Today, Ardent Health and our best-in-class team are well-positioned to accelerate our next phase of growth, and I am eager to build on this momentum with a continued focus on delivering high-quality care to the communities we serve.”

>Drew Altman, M.D., founding president and CEO of the influential heath policy research, polling and news nonprofit KFF, will retire from his roles at the end of this year.

He formed the organization in 1990 out of the Henry J. Kaiser Family Foundation, and has since expanded its scope to include the country's largest newsroom focused on health policy, KFF Health News.

“With two small grandkids in Sacramento and Atlanta and another on the way, after what will be almost 37 years of very hands-on leadership since I founded KFF, and with KFF at the apex of its effectiveness, and the opportunity for a perfect transition, the clock in my head is telling me it’s time,” Altman said in this week's announcement.

Following the recommendation of a search committee, KFF has unanimously appointed two in-house leaders to take on Altman's titles: Larry Levitt, currently executive vice president for health policy, as CEO; and Mollyann Brodie, Ph.D., currently executive vice president and chief operating officer, as president.

The pair have a combined six decades of experience at KFF already under their belt, and will take on board positions with their new roles. They will work with Altman to ensure a smooth transition through the end of the year, officially stepping into his shoes in January 2027

>Visory Health, a prescription savings program, has promoted two executives: Alexandra Robertson to chief growth officer, and Brittney Tierce to chief technology officer.

Robertson started as vice president of growth, driving the company's expansion and presence in more than 38,000 pharmacies nationwide. She will now oversee growth strategy, partnership development and program innovation.

"Visory is positioned to redefine what prescription access looks like for underserved populations, making affordability and access the norm, not the exception," Robertson said in a press release shared in advance with Fierce Healthcare.

Meanwhile, Tierce created the tech underlying Visory. She will now drive the tech strategy company-wide, including security, tech and AI innovation.

"Technology should be a bridge, not a barrier," Tierce said in the announcement. "My focus is raising that bar continuously by creating smarter systems, faster delivery and infrastructure that scales access to the communities we serve."

> Healthcare AI company Abridge brought on board a new chief technology officer, San Oo, as it expands its technology into more health systems. Oo joins Abridge after previously holding leadership roles at Slack and Notion, two popular workplace and productivity software tools.

At Notion, Oo set engineering goals and directions, with a strong focus on reliability, developer velocity and agentic engineering, according to an Abridge press release. At Slack, he helped build the engineering organization during the "hypergrowth years" that defined modern workplace collaboration. Earlier, he served as CTO at ShopBack, a unicorn in the Asia-Pacific region. He was also a founding member of two companies that were later acquired: Mumbo Inc., acquired by LinkedIn in 2012, and Astro Technology, acquired by Slack in 2018.

"The platforms San helped build altered the texture of work with thoughtful technology and exceptional craft that facilitate human connection,” Shiv Rao, M.D., CEO and founder of Abridge, said in a statement. “Healthcare is the next industry that needs that kind of care and platform-level rethink, and San is the rare engineering leader who's done it multiple times."

Abridge is rapidly scaling its AI scribe and clinical decision support technology. It is live in more than 270 of the largest health systems in the U.S., including Duke Health, Johns Hopkins Medicine, Sutter Health and Yale New Haven Health. The platform will support more than 100 million patient conversations in 2026.

"I've spent my career building products and platforms that people love to use that are secure and reliable. Now I want to do the same for healthcare, where the stakes are even higher,” Oo said in a statement. “Abridge already sits at the center of the most important moment in healthcare, the conversation between a clinician and a patient. The opportunity now is to extend that intelligence across the entire system."

> Alignment Healthcare has announced multiple leadership changes that it says will power up the company for long-term growth.

In an announcement, the insurtech said that CEO John Kao has also been named as chairman of the board, allowing him to work more closely with board members. Alongside this shift, previous board chair Joseph Konowiecki has been named vice chairman and as Alignment's executive vice president of corporate affairs.

In the role, Konowiecki will provide critical enterprise-wide leadership as the team looks to build scale, Alignment said in the announcement. Konowiecki is a veteran healthcare executive.

Mark Kent will also join Alignment as president of its management services organization, or MSO. Kent brings experience in value-based care and primary care to the position, having previously held leadership roles in Humana's primary care division, Alignment said.

Alignment Healthcare has also tapped Shane Hochradel as its new chief operating officer. Hochradel has held leadership positions at Elevance Health, Highmark and UnitedHealth Group, per the announcement. All three executives will report to Kao.

“Together, these leadership additions strengthen Alignment’s operating model and position the company well for sustained growth and execution at scale,” Kao said in the announcement.

> Highmark Health has tapped former UnitedHealth Group executive Heather Cianfrocco as its new chief operating officer.

In her time at UHG, Cianfrocco held multiple key leadership positions, including serving as CEO of Optum where she helmed its three core business lines: Optum Rx, Optum Health and Optum Insight. She was most recently the healthcare giant's executive vice president of governance, compliance and information security.

She announced her departure from UnitedHealth in March.

"We have boldly said that we want to be one of the organizations that solves the complex and fragmented health care system," said David Holmberg, Highmark Health CEO, in the announcement. "Heather is a seasoned, innovative health care leader who has a broad national lens, and her skills will be critical as we strive to further expand the reach of our mission and accelerate the work we are doing to transform our industry."

Highmark President Karen Hanlon will continue to lead the company's Living Health initiative, per the announcement.

> Emad Rizk will join Premier, Inc. as its new president and CEO, the company announced.

Rizk, M.D., comes to Premier from healthcare analytics company Cotiviti, where he also served as president and CEO. In the new role, Rizk will be tasked with continuing to drive Premier forward as it seeks to support better patient outcomes at a lower cost.

“I’ve seen healthcare from every angle, and I know what is at stake for Premier’s members,” said Rizk in the announcement. “Providers are being asked to do more with less in an environment that is only getting more complex. Premier has the scale, the data and the relationships to help providers make better decisions and deliver better outcomes. This is where we can make the greatest impact.”

> Alexander Billioux, M.D., is joining the executive team at Cityblock as chief health officer.

Billioux spent the last five years at UnitedHealthcare, where he most recently served as chief medical officer for government programs. He also held leadership roles at the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation and the Louisiana Office of Public Health.

In his new role, Billioux will spearhead Cityblock's clinical strategy and care operations as the company looks to continue advancing its care model.

"I've always been passionate about ensuring that the opportunity for quality healthcare is accessible for all populations. For a large part of my career, that has meant supporting members who face increasing financial and social challenges," Billioux said in the announcement. "Joining Cityblock allows me the opportunity to leverage ground-breaking technology to empower teams to deliver high-quality, comprehensive care that improves the health of vulnerable members."

> Blue Shield of California has named Hayley Park as its new senior vice president and chief pharmacy officer.

In the role, Park will lead the charge on Blue Shield's Pharmacy Care Reimagined initiative, which eschews traditional pharmacy benefit management models for an "unbundled" approach that leans on multiple solutions to offer different elements of the benefit.

Blue Shield said Park brings more than 25 years of experience to the position, and that she served most recently at Kaiser Permanente Northern California as president of pharmacy operations and services.

“What drew me to Blue Shield is that it’s a mission-driven nonprofit health plan that’s committed to improving member health and their lives—not just lowering costs for medications,” Park said. “As pharmacy care shifts to support individuals in a more connected and personalized way, I am excited to join an organization that is transforming healthcare to make it more accessible for everyone.”

Janice Nevin, M.D., will end her 12-year run as president and CEO of ChristianaCare on Sept. 1, the system's board announced.

She retires after 23 years at the organization, initially joining as its chair of family and community medicine. The physician executive is credited by the board with expanding the system's physical footprint, shepherding "significant investment in historically under-resourced areas" and strengthening its academic partnerships.

Taking up the mantle will be Jenn Schwartz, who was named executive vice president and chief strategy officer at the top of 2026. She came to ChristianaCare in 2018 to initially serve as chief legal officer. Prior to that she spent over a decade at Lourdes Health System, where she was vice president of legal affairs & general counsel as well as its executive director.

> Maui Health CEO Lynn Fulton will be stepping down on May 3 after a little over two years in the Hawaiian health system's top role. She plans to return to central Illinois to be closer to her family, according to the announcement that promises a leadership transition plan "in the coming days."

Fulton is credited with overseeing improved quality and financial stabilization during her time at the three-hospital nonprofit system.

> Tenet Healthcare Chief Information Officer Paola Arbour plans to retire at the end of this year, according to a recent regulatory filing from the for-profit hospital and ambulatory surgical center chain. She's been in the role since 2018, and plans to stick with the organization in a part-time, non-executive role through April 1, 2028 "to provide continuing transition services and support."

> Samuel Marchio was named senior vice president, chief government relations and policy officer at Ascension, per a social media post. He comes off a 15-year stint at Elevance Health (initially Anthem), where most recently served as regional vice president of federal government affairs.

> Stephen Taluja was named chief mission officer of Providence, a role that tasks him with aligning the Catholic nonprofit system's charity and service aims with ongoing strategic and organizational transformation. The appointment takes effect on June 29.

Taluja comes to the organization from a Bon Secours Mercy Health, where he is currently chief sponsorship and formation officer. He's been there in various roles since 2014, and before that led multicultural parish ministries.

> Addiction treatment provider Birches Health has added former Cigna Chief Medical Officer Doug Nemecek, M.D., to its advisory board as a senior adviser. As a senior adviser, Nemecek will work closely with the leadership team at Birches as it evolves its clinical and payer engagement strategies.

Nemecek's experience in the payer market will be key to informing this work, according to an announcement.

> Oraida Roman has been named as Aledade's new chief commercial officer, the company revealed on Wednesday. In the role, she will be tasked with leading the team's strategy around national health plan partnerships.

Roman brings 25 years of experience to the role, and will spearhead work around 200 contracts including Medicare Advantage, Medicaid and commercial plans.

> WellSpan Health President and CEO Roxanna Gapstur, Ph.D, is calling it a career after more than eight years at the nonprofit system's helm.

WellSpan's board announced the plans April 6, sharing that Gapstur will continue in the role until the transition to a replacement is complete. No specific or expected timeline was given, other than sharing that a national search for that new executive has begun.

The system, which employs 23,000 people, has grown under her tenure from eight hospitals to 12, and from $2.5 billion of revenue to $4.7 billion. Its footprint has also expanded from five counties to 12 across Pennsylvania and northern Maryland, now reaching more than 1 million patients.

The announcement credits Gapstur with bringing "clear strategic direction" that focused on quality, safety, patient experience and employee engagement. That approach brough national recognitions and designations to its facilities, plus new developments like a genomic program bringing precision medicine into patient care.

> Centene Corporation has created two new positions to lead key segments of its insurance business.

The company said in an announcement that it has named Daniel Finke as group president for markets and commercial and Michael Carson as its group president for Medicare and specialty. Both executives will report to CEO Sarah London, per Centene.

Finke is an experienced insurance executive and will be tasked with overseeing and scaling the company's Medicaid and commercial segments. He joins the insurer from Convey Health Solutions, where he was CEO, and has also previously served as president of Aetna at CVS Health.

Carson, meanwhile, will take on an expanded role in overseeing Centene's Medicare Advantage, Part D, dual-eligible and specialty populations. He joined the company as CEO of WellCare in 2024, and previously held leadership roles at Bright Healthcare and Harvard Pilgrim Health Care.

London said in the announcement that the shift recognizes Carson's significant contributions to the company and the experience that Finke brings to the table in driving operations forward.

"Their collective experience will be instrumental as we continue to strengthen performance across the portfolio and deliver sustainable, profitable growth," she said.

> Cory Mead was named CEO of HCA Florida Palms West Hospital, effective March 30. With more than a decade in leadership roles with HCA Healthcare, Mead most recently served as CEO of HCA Florida Woodmont Hospital.

> Elevance Health unveiled a slew of new leadership appointments within its Health Benefits business and Carelon, the unit leading services such as pharmacy benefits, behavioral health and value-based care enablement.

Kristy Duffey was named president of Carelon Health. The nurse practitioner-turned-executive recently helped scale care models and boost performance at Optum and CINQCARE. She'll be taking over for Peter Haytaian, who's slated to leave the role on May 4 to focus on family commitments but will remain through the end of the year as a special advisor to ease the transition, the company previously announced.

Aimée Dailey was appointed president of government business. She's already attributed with playing "a pivotal role" in expanding Elevance's government programs, and will now have responsibilities covering Medicare, Medicaid, Federal Government Solutions and Group Retiree Solutions.

Additionally, Will Feest, currently chief operating officer for Carelon, will be adding president of Carelon Insights to his title card; Darrell Oliveira was named chief financial officer for Carelon; and Jeff Plante, previously president of Carelon Insights, was dubbed chief financial officer for the Health Benefits segment.

#5714. So You've Hit A Deer With Your Car. Now What?

Fall is a magical time of year: The air is alive with the scent of pumpkin spice, the decorative gourds are presented, and, of course, the dang deer won't stay off the roads. Typical fall, right? That last one ain't no joke — just about everyone who has driven in a place with a significant deer population can tell you a tale or two about a run-in with deer. If you're in France, you really need to look out for the drunk deer.

Deer are a hazard drivers have to contend with. Sure, we could put some murder kitties in the forests, because more big cats in forests can reduce car crashes by roughly 75%. Or, we could install crossings to give creatures a safe path over big roads, like they did in California with the world's largest wildlife crossing. But short of that, accidents with deer will happen. State Farm reports that there were more than 1.6 million animal-related collisions between July 2025 and July 2026. It is a real concern.

But don't fret. If the unfortunate accident does happen, the first thing you should do is to ensure your own safety. Move off the road, and turn on your hazard lights so you're not at risk from any other vehicles. Check your vehicle only when it's safe to do so. There's no need to compound the accident by putting yourself in greater danger.

Hopefully, you are in a safer situation now, so be sure to check any passengers and yourself for injuries. Call 911 immediately if anyone is injured. At this point, you may be tempted to check on the deer. If you can see it and it's a road hazard, for safety's sake, report it. You don't want another driver to hit it. Do not attempt to approach or move it! An injured animal is a dangerous animal. If it's not visible, don't try to find it.

At this point, it's not a bad idea to take pictures of the accident in case your insurance asks for it. Your insurance may also ask for an accident report, so it's a good idea to get one. Speaking of insurance, hitting a deer is usually covered under comprehensive coverage if you have it. Swerving to miss a deer and hitting something else is typically covered by collision coverage, but don't do that.

If your vehicle is not drivable, call a tow truck. If you think your car is still drivable, you may be tempted to leave. If there is property damage or if the deer is still a hazard to others, report it. Otherwise, depending on state law, you may be okay to leave. Before you drive off, do a basic check of your vehicle to ensure that it's actually roadworthy. Take a look underneath your vehicle to see if it is leaking any fluids. If it is, do not drive it — you can cause more damage to your engine. Check that the hood is latched securely and will not come loose. Verify the headlights are still working, especially when it's dark out. Simple stuff, but it could save you trouble down the road.

There is no sure-fire way to avoid hitting a deer, but you can reduce your risk by being cautious when you're in an area with an active deer population. Slow down to a speed that will allow you a better chance of stopping before they become hood ornaments. Be especially cautious at dawn and dusk, as deer are more prone to roam at those times of day. Use extra caution when traveling near wildlife crossing signs. No, the deer aren't reading those signs and deciding to cross there – obviously, those signs declare that you are in an area known to have heavy activity. Also, remember that deer tend to travel in groups, so if you see one, others are likely nearby.

Lastly, if hitting that deer is unavoidable, your natural instinct will be to swerve to avoid the animal.  Fight the urge to do this. Swerving to miss the deer is often more dangerous, as it can cause your car to roll or result in other unwanted behavior. Quite often, the resulting crash is worse than just hitting the deer. Brake in a straight line, and brace for impact.

#5713. REDD — Picking Up Our New Tesla Model Y

REDD, the name for our new Tesla Model Y (Standard Range ’26 build, ’27 model), was inspired by the movie of the same name – Retired, Extremely Dangerous Drivers (the wife and I, of course). As mentioned previously, there is nothing wrong with our beloved 2019 Model 3. It is our bodies that are aging and less able to get in and out of our beloved little sporty Tess. So it was with mixed feelings that we arrived at the Tesla delivery centre to pick up the new car.

As always, it was a hive of activity, with deliveries taking place all around us. Quite a contrast to 7 years ago when Tesla was operating out of one cramped delivery spot near the centre of Brisbane, and the handover took less than 3 minutes. This time there were plenty of sales representatives spending their time and making sure we knew what we were doing.

On arrival, we walked past a line consisting of ICE cars being surrendered as trade-ins for an electric. As we left, a car carrier was unloading half a dozen new Model Ys. All in all, a smooth operation. While Majella was getting her phone synced and lots of information from the sales rep, I had a wander around.

The delivery centre is divided in two by a screen. On our side of the screen, I could see at least 60 new cars anxiously awaiting their new owners — like puppies at the pound, I thought. I wasn’t allowed behind the curtain where cars were being detailed and prepped. I commented to our sales rep that there didn’t seem to be many Model 3s. He told me that they had just received a Model Y shipment; the 3s were on their way. Asked about what lay behind the curtain in Tesla wonderland, he said that there were hundreds of cars “back there.”

Majella drove REDD home and I drove Tess. I am having mixed feelings. I get attached to my cars; it was difficult to sell George (my ‘64 Wolseley) and Ruby (my Hyundai Accent). But they were old and tired and their time had come. Tess, at 180,000+ kilometres still feels young. It’s me that’s getting old. The letting go is being made easier because we are selling Tess to our youngest daughter. So, we will still be in contact with the car and watch the milestones as she grows.

As we sipped our celebratory champagne, I mused at the difference between buying the Model Y in 2026 and the Model 3 in 2019. Going from the Hyundai to the Tesla was a massive leap in both design and technology — the screen, the regen braking. Our Tesla was the only one in our suburb, and there was no high-speed charging. Electric vehicles were seen as a “soon to pass” fad on the way to hydrogen cars, and a stupid decision in a country as big as Australia. In 2019, less than one percent of new cars sold had a plug, Tesla was still on a deathwatch. We had taken a risk — would it work out?

It certainly has! Owning Tess and dealing with FUD gave me a cause to champion. I started exploring this new world and writing about it — driving long trips and proving that an EV can do what it has to. CleanTechnica published my ramblings — which have now reached over 1,000 articles. People contacted me and shared their stories of private ownership. CEOs of new startups (like recently introduced Thermal Dawn) gave me interviews and insights. This might sound weird, but moving from the Model 3 to the Model Y is nowhere near as exciting. Yes, I will continue to write, but the motoring world has changed. In Australia, the Model Y has been the highest selling passenger car of all drivetrains for the past few months. In October, it even beat the refreshed Toyota RAV4. My northern Brisbane suburb is full of Tesla Model Ys. The crossover has become common.

Motoring journalists are learning slowly to accept the new kids on the block, and most of their reviews seem to indicate a modicum of tolerance and truth. Of course, we still have vested interests proclaiming that Chinese cars are destroying the Australian car industry. Read: dealerships can’t sell ICE cars and aren’t making enough money. I wonder sometimes what there will be left write about as plugins take more and more of the market, and “real” motoring journalists write the articles I normally write. Relax, I am sure there will be room for all of us for some time. Especially in the USA!

Calls continue for more charging infrastructure, which is fair enough for highway and tourist travel, but seems to totally ignore home charging. “I live in a remote town and there is nowhere to charge my car!” wails one. I could scream if he would hear me: plug it into your house power socket, you moron!

Tess sits in the carport plugged into our home battery. Majella has taken REDD to her gem club. I am sure that instead of their normal lapidary, faceting, and jewellery making, they will be exploring REDD. Four other members of the club have now got Teslas or BYDs. One of them commented that they want a Model Y for Christmas — not sure if his wife will agree.

REDD will also be the guest of honour at our upcoming Coffee, Cake, and EV morning tea in a few days’ time.

Once we have done the roadworthy and registration transfer, Tess will be off to her new home. We will get to see her at family gatherings and when we pick up the grandkidlets from school. Majella is busy buying the accessories — mats, ceiling screen (no, the new heavy tint doesn’t do much in the Australian sun), rim protectors, etc. REDD came with front and back floor mats. She is buying all-weather mats for the frunk and trunk. The dog may even get to sit in the car! Shock! Horror! And we are slowly noticing subtle differences, like the reduction in noise driving on the highway — REDD has better seals and double-glazed windows.

We may have lost some of the apps that came free with Tess (Spotify, Karaoke, connectivity), but we have gained cooling seats and a heated steering wheel. And, of course, Hardware 4, which will give us access to FSD (Supervised) for our long trips. Speaking of longer trips, the range of our Model 3 (about 300 km with some degradation) pales beside the 460 km range of the LFP batteries in REDD. LFP batteries also mean less anxiety about charging to 100% when needed. REDD is longer, wider, and taller, but, thank goodness, still fits in our garage.

Majella is missing Enhanced Autopilot, for which we paid AU$5,000 just a few years ago. The Model Y’s cruise control is not as convenient. Stay tuned for updates as we enter the next leg of our electric journey.

David Waterworth is a retired teacher who divides his time between looking after his grandchildren and trying to make sure they have a planet to live on. He is long on Tesla [NASDAQ:TSLA].

David Waterworth has 1009 posts and counting. See all posts by David Waterworth

#5712. Watch The 2027 Hyundai Tucson Get Hurled Around The Nürburgring Like A Huge Miata

There's nothing quite like watching a vehicle get driven in ways you never expected. Think Miatas on a rally stage in Finland or a bunch of smoky pickup trucks on a race track in Thailand. There's something gratifying about seeing things taken to new extremes, and we probably all have a story or two about ripping a beater or rental car in ways that most wouldn't.

But if you're a test driver, it's your duty to drive cars, trucks, and SUVs in ways most wouldn't. And if you're working for Hyundai, that means hurling a 2027 Tucson, before it goes on sale, around the Nürburgring Nordschleife — seemingly the world's most famous test track — like a huge Miata. Sure, Porsche, BMW, Audi, and Mercedes-Benz test drivers probably have a great time wringin' out their steeds on this German track's sacred surface, but we bet the Hyundai cats are having just as much (or possibly more) fun.

It isn't all a big joke, though, because manufacturers have to explore a vehicle's limits to truly poke and prod it for deficiencies. But it looks freaking epic. Man, what we'd give to sit shotgun on this stilted-up rollercoaster ride.

What makes testing cars at the Nürburgring so special? Well, for one, claiming a fastest production car record. There's a good chance that this isn't the case with the flyin' 2027 Hyundai Tucson, but hey, it's probably a good idea to keep an idea on the company's upcoming news coverage just in case.

However, more realistic: there's the fact that it's a very long (almost 13 miles) and variety-rich track with big undulations, flowing sweepers, big elevation changes, on- and off-camber bits, high-speed sections, jumps, as well as the ability to be bone-dry on one end and raining on the other. Germany's Eiffel, where the 'Ring is located, is a climate that's rich in rain that comes and goes in the blink of an eye. Testing the Tucson's suspension, brakes, and their relationship with the tires' grip here gives engineers a good idea where the limits are in a bunch of scenarios. Additionally, the high speed gives them an idea of how well the cooling system works, how well the brakes work, as well as if the engine and transmission will have any issues. If it can survive a flying lap here, it's definitely good for service in normal, everyday driving.

Plus, it helps that Hyundai maintains a facility right nearby. The brand tunes all of its high-performance N models on the 'Ring, which undergo stricter and more extensive testing than non-performance fare. The plain ol' Tucson may not get that same exact treatment (yet), but it's cool to see them still driving 'em on there like they stole 'em

#5711. Amwell bets AI boom will drive demand for its unified care platform

Amwell bets AI boom will drive demand for its unified care platform" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

As health plans and employers contend with a growing array of virtual care and AI-enabled tools, Amwell is positioning its digital health platform as the infrastructure layer for AI-enabled care.

Executives at Amwell, formerly known as American Well, touted the company's platform strategy, government contracts and higher-value clinical services as the main drivers of future growth during the company's third-quarter earnings call Tuesday.

Rising healthcare costs are pushing health plans and employers to adopt tech-enabled care solutions, but they are looking for measurable engagement and outcomes from digital health vendors, not just access, according to Ido Schoenberg, M.D., Amwell chairperson and CEO.

The proliferation of point solutions, accelerated by AI, is creating more vendor sprawl and member confusion, Schoenberg told investors and analysts during the call.

There's also a lack of proof with many digital health tools, he noted. "It is hard to see which programs work and harder still to replace one without disrupting members. That sprawl is accelerating. AI has made it faster and cheaper to build a clinical program. Investors have backed hundreds of new digital health companies this year, many of them built on AI. Our customers feel pressure to offer these programs, but each one brings its own cost, its own integration, and its own front door. The opportunity is real. So is the complexity," he said.

More patients are turning to AI for health guidance, but those interactions don’t necessarily lead them to appropriate, covered care, creating the risk of poor clinical decisions and unnecessary costs for health plans, Schoenberg said.

"This is the problem Amwell is determined to solve for our customers. We help them improve clinical and financial outcomes. We do it through activation, getting more of their members into technology-enabled care in place of conventional care that often costs more. We give our customers one platform under their brand with one integration. It provides reliable, scalable rails to bring in a program, exchange data with it, and tests whether it works. The member's experience stays consistent, simple, and engaging. A common data structure proves the outcomes and improves performance over time," he said.

As AI adoption grows, a unified care platform becomes more valuable, Schoenberg asserted.

"We are not selling an AI feature. We are the trusted platform where AI-powered care runs with clinicians in the loop," he said during the Q3 call.

Amwell's customers represent more than 90 million covered lives, and the company also serves 9.6 million beneficiaries of the Military Health System.

Amwell's platform can help drive member engagement and utilization of digital health tools, executives said.

"Most of the health plans we talk to still see engagement in the single digits. We address that with always-on engagement, outreach to members through our customers' own channels within the rules they set. When a customer switches it fully on, members use the platform at more than three times the rate we see when it's off," Schoenberg said.

The platform runs on a common data structure, he noted. "It sends a member into a program with the right information. It collects outcomes back, and it reports value in the customer's own terms, whether that customer is a health plan or an employer that the plan serves. That is how a program proves its return on investment and how it gets better over time," he said.

In response to a question from an analyst, Schoenberg suggested pricing for the solution could evolve from fixed Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) fees toward outcomes-based arrangements in which Amwell shares in the savings it produces for health plans.

Amwell executives view that platform strategy as key to the company's growth.

In Q3, Amwell reported revenue that was slightly above Wall Street's consensus and a narrower adjusted loss than analysts expected. Amwell executives also reiterated confidence in reaching positive operating cash flow and breakeven to positive adjusted EBITDA in the fourth quarter.

Amwell brought in $49 million in Q3 revenue, according to financial results published Tuesday afternoon. Revenue was down approximately 12.9% year-over-year, but $1 million above the high end of management's guidance range, according to Chief Financial Officer Mark Hirschhorn.

Subscription revenue was $23.9 million, down approximately 22.5% year-over-year and 6.8% sequentially, Hirschhorn said. “The year-over-year decline continues to reflect the previously disclosed churn we've discussed on prior earnings calls,” he added.

Amwell Medical Group (AMG) visit revenue was $23.7 million, up approximately 11.7% year over year, while AMG paid visits totaled approximately 301,000 visits, essentially flat year over year, Hirschhorn said.

Virtual primary care visits were up 41% year over year, continuing that segment's strong growth trajectory. Total platform visits were approximately 760,000 visits, down approximately 30.5% year over year—though Hirschhorn noted the decline is consistent with previously discussed portfolio changes.

The telehealth platform reported a net loss of $11.7 million during the quarter, compared to a loss of $29.3 million for the same period a year ago, Hirschhorn said. Adjusted EBITDA loss narrowed to $3.6 million from a loss of $12.7 million a year earlier.

Amwell executives are bullish on revenue growth from its own clinical services, including virtual primary care and behavioral health.

Executives also highlighted the company's government business as it delivered solid third-quarter financial performance. Amwell announced in September that the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) issued a letter of intent to deploy its platform enterprise-wide.

"I want to be precise about what this is," Schoenberg said. "The letter is not a binding contract. A definitive agreement still has to be negotiated and executed under federal procurement rules, and that work is underway."

Schoenberg noted the letter followed a "comprehensive evaluation."

"It cited scalable video consultations, interoperability, cybersecurity compliance and support for integrated care delivery," he said. "In plain terms, the capabilities the department evaluated are the ones we already run at scale for the military health system, and the department's own scale is considerable."

Amwell executives are optimistic the company will sign a contract with the VA "over the next couple of months," Hirschhorn said, with implementation beginning in 2027, but no definitive agreement exists yet.

Moreover, Schoenberg said the platform is continuing to negotiate a "direct, longer-term contract" with the Defense Health Agency (DHA).

The DHA, which oversees services for the Military Health System, renewed its contract with the telehealth platform in August 2025. In June, it called for sole contracts with Amwell and four other vendors.

DHA discontinued its payment for behavioral health and automated care services with Amwell last year. Schoenberg said the cessation was due to the Department of Defense’s cost-cutting measures—not the department’s satisfaction with the services.

Hirschhorn said that Amwell is raising its full-year revenue guidance to between $204 million to $206 million, up from $195 million to $205 million. The company now expects full-year adjusted EBITDA to be a loss in the range of $6.9 million to $7.9 million, a meaningful improvement from its prior range of a loss of $12 million to $16 million.

Amwell forecasts full-year AMG visits between 1.32 million to 1.37 million visits.

“In summary, during the third quarter, we exceeded our revenue guidance with stronger visit volumes, a stable subscription base, and a leaner cost structure that positions us to finish the year on a strong note,” Hirschhorn said.

#5710. Study Finds Evidence of Cannabis Use 2,800 Years Ago

— Findings point to consumption at least 300 years earlier than previously known use

People may have been getting high off cannabis earlier than previously thought -- at least 2,800 years ago, a new study suggests.

Archaeologists who led a dig at a monumental tomb in Siberia said they turned up evidence of the earliest known use of cannabis for psychoactive purposes.

The findings point to cannabis consumption at least 300 years earlier than previously known use in neighboring China.

Ancient drug use has long intrigued scholars. The Greek historian Herodotus wrote about inhabitants of Central Asia smoking cannabis around 440 B.C., and recent archaeologists have found the seeds in tombs across its highlands.

The team from Germany, Russia, Sweden, and Switzerland said analysis of hair in the royal tomb where cannabis seeds turned up sheds new light on the plant's role in ancient societies.

"It's extremely rare that we have both preserved plant parts and human soft tissue with the active compounds in it in the same context," said study author Gino Caspari, PhD, MSc, an archaeologist at the University of Bern.

It's not clear whether the cannabis was consumed through inhalation or ingestion, he said.

The dig took place starting in 2017 at a large burial mound at the Tunnug 1 site in the Uyuk Valley of southern Siberia, home to one of the earliest monumental tombs showing material culture of the Scythians -- ancient nomads who migrated from Central Asia to southern Russia and Ukraine.

The team, deployed "essentially out in the middle of nowhere," lived in tents for months and faced a spring-to-autumn season that variously featured swamps, snowstorms, frosts, and swarms of mosquitoes. Herds of horses ran freely across the grassy steppe.

Larger artifacts on the site include weapons in the burials, horse gear, and animal-style motifs. But the team "struck gold" as it also found tiny black spots that turned out to be cannabis seeds along with preserved human hair, Caspari said.

"It's only so often as an archaeologist that you do get to drug test a person that's been dead for almost 3,000 years," he said.

Radiocarbon dating on some of the more than 1,000 seeds helped establish the time of origin, and "they are not there by accident" but deposited within the tomb, suggesting that the plant material had significance in the community, he said.

Results were published in the journal Science.

Not all independent experts were convinced.

The hair analysis "is scientifically weak" and there's not enough evidence to tell whether cannabis was used, wrote Volker Auwaerter, PhD, head of the forensic toxicology section at the University Medical Center in Freiburg, Germany, in an email.

"For a central part of the study, the article falls far short of what would have been possible," Auwaerter said. "This matters because the hair data carry the abstract's main claims (cannabis consumption and use for its psychoactive properties)."

Today, scholars don't consider ancient accounts trustworthy without corroborating evidence. Because the cannabis plant has other uses -- seeds are pressed for oil and fibers used for cloth -- their presence alone doesn't confirm drug use.

Auwaerter, who was not part of the study, said the data didn't distinguish consumption from external exposure -- in other words, the hair could have picked up traces of weed simply by being buried together with it. He said a lab test involving forensic toxicology expertise would have been advisable and easy to arrange.

But Elisa Guerra Doce, PhD, of the University of Valladolid in Spain, who has written about use of consciousness-altering substances in European prehistory, said toxicological hair analysis was not new in archaeology and has been used to identify consumption of psychoactive substances. She was not involved in the study.

In an email, she credited the authors for showing, through their methodology, that "cannabis was not merely deposited as a funerary offering but was actually consumed by individuals associated with the burial rite."

#5709. CMS finalizes steeper Medicare physician pay cuts for 2027, moves ahead with RPM vendor restrictions

CMS finalizes steeper Medicare physician pay cuts for 2027, moves ahead with RPM vendor restrictions" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services finalized sweeping Medicare payment reforms it says will shift the program from volume-based "sick care" toward prevention, primary care and accountable care.

The 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule rule includes a roughly 2% reduction in baseline physician payment rates with targeted increases and new payment opportunities for accountable care, primary and chronic care and behavioral health. CMS finalized steeper physician payment cuts than it had proposed in July.

An unpublished PDF version of the 2,468-page final rule can be found here.

In a press release, CMS said it is "prioritizing prevention, strengthening primary care, cracking down on duplicate billing and reinforcing fiscal stewardship across Medicare."

The final rule modernizes physician payment structures to "reward health maintenance and coordinated primary care rather than disjointed, volume-based intervention," CMS said.

"Medicare should reward clinicians for keeping people healthy," HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. said in a statement. "Under President Trump’s leadership, we are putting prevention and primary care at the center of Medicare, closing payment loopholes, and cracking down on waste. This rule directs resources toward coordinated care that puts patients first. We are changing what Medicare pays for to change what our health system delivers."

Under the final rule, CMS will officially sunset the traditional Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) reporting option beginning with the CY 2031 performance period. Clinicians will have through CY 2030 to transition to the MIPS Value Pathways (MVPs), which already cover approximately 98% of clinicians, or Advanced Alternative Payment Models. This reflects two additional years of transition time compared to the proposed rule. The rule also finalizes three new MVPs focused on diabetes, hypertension and hospitalists, and requires clinicians to report at least one specialty-specific "Core Measure" starting in CY 2027.

The final 2027 PFS rule also establishes new 340B reporting requirements. Covered entities will have to report certain Medicare Part D claims involving drugs purchased through the 340B Drug Pricing Program to the Medicare Part D Claims Data 340B Repository beginning with claims with a date of service on or after Jan.1, 2027. The deadline for the first quarterly submission is delayed until Sept. 30, 2027.

For physicians, while the proposed rule includes statutory payment increases, Medicare payment rates face an overall baseline decrease for 2027 due to the expiration of a temporary 2.5% legislative increase from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) in 2026.

Under the Medicare Access and CHIP Reauthorization Act (MACRA), the CY2027 conversion factors reflect statutory updates of +0.75% for qualifying Alternative Payment Model (APM) participants and +0.25% for non-qualifying participants. The changes to the PFS conversion factors for CY 2027 include these updates as required by statute and an estimated -0.12% adjustment necessary to account for proposed changes in work RVUs for some services, according to CMS in a fact sheet.

For clinicians who don't qualify through an advanced alternative payment model, the conversion factor drops from $33.40 to $32.63, a 2.31% reduction. For qualifying APM participants, the conversion factor drops 1.83% from $33.57 to $32.95. In the draft rule issued in July, CMS projected cuts of 1.68% and 1.19%, respectively.

CMS is also addressing what it sees as overpayment and duplicate reimbursement when multiple services are delivered during the same patient encounter. Under the final rule, when an office visit and minor procedure occur on the same day, CMS will reduce payment by 20% for the lower-cost service, reducing duplication in payment by patients and the Medicare program for clinical work already covered in the procedure’s valuation.

CMS had initially proposed paying the higher-cost service in full and reducing payment for the other service by 50%.

Physician groups were quick to criticize CMS' payment changes in the final rule.

"Notwithstanding modest policy improvements to enhance value-based care through MSSP, MGMA is disappointed by CMS’s decision to finalize several destabilizing policies in the 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule," Anders Gilberg, senior vice president of government affairs at the Medical Group Management Association, said in a statement.

"Conversion factor cuts of 1.83% for qualifying APM participants and 2.31% for all other clinicians further degrade an already fragile payment system and amplify severe financial challenges caused by years of inadequate Medicare reimbursement," Gilberg said.

Compounding this ongoing reimbursement decline, CMS will cut payments by 20% when office visits billed with modifier 25 are performed on the same day as certain procedures, "interfering with physician practices’ ability to offer same-day care," he noted.

MGMA is urging Congress to intervene by immediately fixing cuts to the conversion factor, along with changes to modifier 25. "To prevent annual disruption, Congress should prioritize comprehensive MACRA reform by passing the Patients First Act," Gilberg said.

The agency is overhauling the office/outpatient evaluation and management visit complexity add-on code, HCPCS code G2211. CMS is transitioning HCPCS code G2211 from a flat add-on payment to a modifier that would increase the payment of the associated E/M code by 16%. That would maintain an equal percentage increase across all levels of E/M codes, CMS said.

The agency also finalized a new modifier that would offset the costs incurred by practitioners in accountable care organizations (ACOs) when providing longitudinal care and care coordination. The modifier would only be available for practitioners participating in a Shared Savings Program ACO or participant providers in a Long-term Enhanced ACO Design (LEAD) Model ACO and would increase payment of the associated E/M visit by 32%, CMS said.

In the final rule, CMS tightened remote patient monitoring and remote therapeutic monitoring requirements, following through on a controversial ban of third-party RPM vendors. However, CMS delayed that restriction for two years.

Beginning in 2027, as CMS outlined in the proposed rule, RTM services can only be furnished to established patients, and providers must provide a separately reportable initiating visit before billing for RPM or RTM services.

Despite intense industry pushback, CMS completed a proposal that will prevent providers from using third-party vendors or contractors for RPM services. For the purposes of billing, RPM services must be performed by clinical staff employed by the practice, according to the PFS rule. But the agency provided a two-year reprieve on that requirement as it goes into effect Jan. 1, 2029, "giving practices that rely on contractors two additional years to adapt," CMS said.

Health tech companies, providers and lawmakers pushed back on the proposal to restrict third-party vendors, urging CMS to reconsider the proposed changes to preserve patients' access to these tech-enabled services. Many rural, small, and independent practices, as well as both urban and rural health systems, rely on specialized clinical and technology partners to make remote monitoring services available to their patients.

CMS finalized changes to the Medicare Shared Savings Program, the nation’s largest value-based payment program, to "accelerate accountable care service delivery, further CMS' goal of aligning spending and value in Original Medicare, and support achieving other related strategic objectives," the agency said in a fact sheet.

The overhaul to the MSSP program aims to make ACO participation more financially attractive, encourage organizations to take on risk, expand beneficiary participation and ease some quality-reporting requirements.

The agency says the changes are projected to grow the program by adding up to 1 million assigned beneficiaries in an average year and produce $5.5 billion in net federal savings over 10 years. CMS also projects the changes will generate an overall increase in shared savings net of losses to ACOs by $1.1 billion over a decade.

The final rule changes the Shared Savings Program’s benchmarking and financial methodology to balance incentives between Level E of the BASIC track and the ENHANCED track. Under the final rule, the shared savings rate for Level E of the BASIC track increases from 50% to 60%, and it reduces the maximum weight used in calculating the positive regional adjustment for lower-spending ACOs participating under the ENHANCED track from 50% to 35%.

The agency is increasing the prior savings adjustment's scaling factor from 50% to 75%, allowing more of an ACO's previous savings to be reflected in future benchmarks.

Under the final rule, CMS will risk-adjust the 5% cap on benchmark increases, potentially allowing ACOs that care for sicker, higher-cost patients to receive larger upward adjustments.

Data shows patients aligned with an ACO are less likely to experience uncontrolled diabetes or hypertension and are more likely to receive recommended preventive care, according to CMS. In performance year 2024, 75% of the 476 participating ACOs earned shared savings totaling $4.1 billion, while generating net savings for the Medicare Trust Funds of approximately $2.5 billion compared to projected spending benchmarks.

Under the final 2027 PFS rule, approved ACOs may reduce or eliminate Part B cost-sharing for many items and services for assigned beneficiaries, directly lowering out-of-pocket costs for essential care. That change goes into effect April 1, 2027.

The rule also increases shared savings rates for eligible ACOs, provides novel incentives for first-time participants and sets more predictable spending targets. The rule also simplifies electronic health record reporting requirements, streamlines patient notice mandates and removes outdated administrative hurdles, CMS said.

#5708. Here's How Much AAA Says It Costs To Own A Car In 2026

When we consider whether we can afford a car, so much of the focus tends to be on the sticker price that we often forget that the costs don't stop once we've made our purchase. Small, everyday expenses that come alongside, like fuel, servicing, finance interest, depreciation, insurance, and tax, aren't always obvious, but the true cost of car ownership adds up over time.

With that in mind, the car valuation experts at AAA performed a study to investigate car ownership costs in 2026. It turns out that drivers are facing ongoing price increases, with the AAA 2026 Your Driving Costs study revealing that the annual cost of owning and running a new car has soared to $12,863, or $1,071.92 per month this year. That's up from an average of $11,577 or $964.78 per month in 2025.

At that rate, ownership costs can add 32.67% on top of the $39,376 sales-weighted average MSRP of new vehicles. The larger bills have been linked to surging fuel prices, faster depreciation, and higher finance interest rates. Still, your specific costs can vary greatly, depending on your car's fuel type.

Owning any car at all is getting more expensive, but the AAA study revealed something more fundamental: Electric cars cost more to own than their traditional fuel-powered and hybrid counterparts. That's largely because depreciation on EVs is worse than gas or hybrid cars. On top of that, those who drive electric cars face higher fees and finance costs. Where EVs tend to do better is in fuel expenses, as they typically cost 66% to 70% less to run than gasoline cars.

Looking at a set of average consumption figures, AAA found that regular-grade gasoline costs $4.152 per gallon on average, while electric cars charged at home averaged as little as 18 cents per kilowatt hour. EVs have seen smaller electricity rate increases, too. The AAA data shows electricity prices have jumped 7.8% since 2025, while gas costs have increased a shocking 31.8%.

Even so, owning and running EVs costs more than gas-powered models, due to higher fees, finance costs, and depreciation, with certain EVs said to depreciate about twice as fast as their gas-powered counterparts. That contributed to pushing EV ownership costs above gas-powered models across the medium sedan, compact SUV, and pickup truck segments.

Nowhere is that gap more pronounced than in the medium sedan segment, where gas-powered medium sedans cost $3,080 less to own (at $10,582 per year) than comparable EV medium sedans ($13,662). Hybrids are even cheaper (at $10,204) and cost the least to own in every category, including the medium SUV class, where EVs win back some ground against gas-powered models, costing $14,332 versus $14,431 for gasoline SUVs.

As a car owner, every mile you drive costs money, but it is entirely possible to keep costs down. One way to do this is to shop around for cheaper insurance. Compare quotes from providers, or even consider buying a car from one of the cheapest brands to insure.

If you are team gas-powered cars, getting a model with great fuel efficiency is just as important. It should be easy enough, seeing as gasoline cars are now much more efficient than they used to be, with some of the most fuel-efficient models released over the years rated to return as high as 58 mpg.

You'll also want to consider depreciation. It is one of the single largest ownership costs and can add a weighted average of $4,422 per year to the cost of running some popular models, according to the AAA study. Toyota, Subaru, and Honda are some of the best brands for value retention, but if you're after something more premium, there's always Lexus. It's the luxury car brand with the best resale value, according to CarEdge.

However, maintenance and spare parts are usually more expensive for luxury marques than mainstream brands like Toyota or Honda. Speaking of which, staying on top maintenance is yet another important part of vehicle ownership that can help keep costs low. Not only does it help prevent larger bills down the road, keeping up with car maintenance also provides a strong service history that supports resale value when it comes time to sell.

#5707. BMW Pitches Free EV Charging And You Ain’t Seen Nothing Yet

EV sales in the US are beginning to tick up again, and BMW is determined to grab a slice of the action. The German automaker has begun offering a free EV charging package to anyone who purchases a 2027 BMW i5, BMW i7, or BMW iX3. The package includes $500 in charging credits, which seems like small potatoes compared to the cost of a BMW. Still, it’s better than nothing, and it positions the company to compete in a rapidly evolving landscape that includes free charging hours.

The “free hours” trend has already emerged in the US, where Texas (of course!) is an epicenter of activity. The idea is to smooth out peak weekday demand spikes and take advantage of spare capacity on the grid by offering ratepayers an incentive to use more electricity during nighttime hours, with the leading utility Constellation being a representative example.

“When you sign up for a free night electricity plan, a smart meter monitors your energy usage by time of day,” Constellation explains. The company offers a “Free Power Hours” plan between midnight and 4 a.m. every night.

“Constellation also offers Discounted Nights & Fair Days, with discounted electricity supply rates from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m.,” the company adds.

Constellation notes that standard service charges and other fees apply. They also advise that the free plan is not a good fit for households with heavy electricity use during the day, when higher rates apply.

Still, access to EV charging at a minimal cost is a tantalizing incentive for some households. Constellation currently offers its “FreeCharge” plan between midnight and 4 a.m. to ratepayers in Pennsylvania as well as Texas.

Against this backdrop, a mere $500 EV charging credit for a BMW is not much of an incentive, at least not in states where free hours are available. The monthly lease for the 2027 BMW i5, for example, clocks in at almost $750. Purchasing the car outright will set you back almost $70,000, including the destination fee.

Still, any incentive is better than no incentive, and the new offer provides BMW an opportunity to hitch its star to the free hours trend. “The new offer, available beginning November 5, 2026, is designed to make public charging simpler, more convenient and more affordable for BMW customers,” explains BMW.

“The package includes a $300 BMW Charging Network credit that can be used at participating charging providers1, as well as a separate $200 credit for charging at IONNA locations,” the company elaborates, with IONNA referring to a consortium of EV makers (including BMW) focused on improving the driver experience at charging stations.

In addition to the $200 IONNA credit, BMW is also offering a one-year IONNA membership plan that provides for a 25% charging discount.

For the record, the BMW Charging Network includes more than 180,000 charging stations compatible with the company’s My BMW app.

Over and above the EV charging package, BMW is also among the electrification stakeholders that did not throw in the towel after last year’s EV sales crash. Despite the premature demise of the federal EV tax credit on September 30 of 2025, the number of public EV charging stations in the US has continued to increase, and charging networks have become more sophisticated and convenient.

In addition to the hookup with IONNA, for example, the BMW Charging Network includes Shell Recharge, Electrify America, ChargePoint, and EVgo among others.

“The company also has invested in Plug & Charge, which simplifies the charging experience; and ChargeScape, a collaborative effort to help manage the flow of energy between EVs and the power grid,” BMW added in a press statement last week.

ChargeScape represents another indication that Trump’s war against EVs was over before it started, tax credits or not.

ChargeScape launched three years ago as a joint venture between BMW, Ford, and the US branch of Honda. “Benefiting both EV customers and the electric utility industry in the U.S. and Canada, ChargeScape will unlock entirely new value that EVs can provide to the electric grid, while enabling EV customers to earn financial benefits through a variety of managed charging and energy-sharing services never before possible with traditional gasoline-powered vehicles,” the three automakers enthused in a press statement dated December 29, 2023.

“ChargeScape’s platform will give electric utilities access to EV battery energy across a wide pool of EVs. Participating EV customers will have the potential to earn financial benefits by charging at ‘grid-friendly’ times through flexible and managed schedules,” the partners elaborated.

“The development of this project comes at a time when electric vehicle sales and infrastructure growth are ramping up quickly,” the partners added.

That was certainly an optimistic take on the future of EV sales in the US, but that was December of 2023. Just about one year later, then-candidate Donald Trump sailed to victory on Election Day 2024, winning a second turn around the Oval Office with a plan to stop the vehicle electrification trend in its tracks.

Still, ChargeScape soldiered on. By September of 2024 the alliance was ready for launch, to be joined by Nissan just one month later. ChargeScape also added the startup Rivian to its rolls in June of this year, with an option to add bidirectional EV charging. Other automakers, including Tesla, also use the platform.

The bidirectional charging element is where things get particularly interesting. The technology emerged in the early 2000’s, enabling EV drivers to power their home from their car battery, or send electricity to the grid. Unlocking the mass market potential of bidirectional charging is a next-level challenge, and the free hours trend could help accelerate uptake. With free hours EV charging, drivers can store electricity at minimal cost during those periods, and discharge it to trim the cost of electricity for their homes during periods when higher electricity rates apply.

Ford is particularly excited about the potential for bidirectional charging to scale up. The company’s forthcoming Ford Fathom electric pickup truck comes with an internal inverter that converts the DC charge from the battery into an AC current for home use. The built-in inverter eliminates the cost of the external, wall mounted inverter otherwise needed for bidirectional charging at home.

Photo: BMW is sweetening the EV charging pot with a $500 charging credit on its 2027 i5, i7, and iX3 electric cars in the US (courtesy of BMW).

#5706. Retatrutide Is One Click Away. That Doesn't Make it Safe.

— Promising data on the real drug tell us little about what's in a gray-market vial

A few clicks, a credit card, and a package arrives at your door. The same technology that has expanded access to information and consumer goods has also made it easier than ever for unregulated products to reach consumers while masquerading as legitimate medicine.

As an endocrinologist who treats obesity and diabetes, I have watched new therapies transform care for a complex chronic disease. I also regularly have patients asking about products they found online, on social media, at a medical spa, or through friends and family. Their curiosity and desire for affordable treatment options make sense. But their safety depends on knowing what a product actually is, and whether it has been tested to the standards we expect of any medicine.

Those standards exist for good reason. Before a complex medication reaches patients, it goes through years of laboratory research and progressively larger clinical trials that establish whether it works, for which patients, at what dose, and with what risks. It is then produced by an approved manufacturer under strict quality controls, in facilities subject to inspection, and monitored for safety after it reaches the market. This system allows a physician to safely prescribe a drug for a specific condition, and a patient to trust what is in their syringe.

Semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound) went through that process and were approved by FDA. But products sold online or at medical spas using the same ingredient names, semaglutide and tirzepatide, do not automatically carry the same safeguards.

Their success has fueled excitement about what comes next.

Retatrutide, often marketed online as "Reta" or "GLP-3," is the latest example. (Side note: the nickname is a misnomer. The molecule acts on three hormone receptors -- GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon -- making it more accurately a "triple-G" agonist.) Results from phase 3 clinical trials in obesity and type 2 diabetes were recently presented at the European Association for the Study of Diabetes meeting in Milan, with simultaneous publication in the New England Journal of Medicine and The Lancet. The results are impressive, but retatrutide remains investigational and is not approved for any use.

Just as important, the retatrutide studied in those trials is not what is being sold online. Clinical trial participants receive drugs made to exacting specifications, at carefully defined doses and escalation schedules, under close medical monitoring. A gray-market vial labeled "retatrutide" may or may not contain the actual molecule. It may contain more or less than the label claims, or impurities and contaminants no one has tested for. And because there is no established dose for a product of unknown content, buyers are left to mix and inject based on guesswork from online forums. Promising data on the real drug tell us little about what is in that gray-market vial.

The FDA's position is explicit: federal law does not permit retatrutide to be compounded or sold. The agency notes that retatrutide is not an ingredient in any FDA-approved drug and has not been shown to be safe and effective for any condition. Calling a product "compounded retatrutide" does not make it an approved or lawful treatment, and a "for research use only" label does not make it safe. The FDA urges consumers not to buy these products, warning that their quality is unknown and they may harm patients' health.

The agency has also taken enforcement action. In a March 2026 warning letter to Gram Peptides, FDA identified products marketed as retatrutide as unapproved new drugs and said introducing them into interstate commerce violated federal law. It warned that injectables can cause serious harm because they bypass the body's key defenses against toxins and microorganisms. No professional-looking website or glowing testimonial can confirm a product's identity, strength, purity, or sterility.

We, as clinicians, must help patients navigate this landscape without judgment. We need to create a space where patients feel comfortable bringing advertisements and questions into the exam room, where we can review the evidence together and address access issues.

My advice to my patients is clear: do not buy or use retatrutide until it is FDA approved and available from the legitimate manufacturer. In the meantime, I encourage them to ask me or another provider which FDA-approved treatments may fit their needs and how to obtain them through a licensed pharmacy. If investigational treatments interest them, I encourage them to ask about legitimate clinical trials.

Technology can support informed healthcare decisions, but it cannot replace medical guidance. The next step toward better health should begin with a patient-doctor conversation -- not an online checkout.

Fairview Health Services Partners with hellocare.ai to Expand Enterprise Virtual Care and Bring Connected Care to the NICU" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Minneapolis, MN and Clearwater, FL — Fairview Health Services and hellocare.ai today announced an enterprise partnership to expand virtual care capabilities across Fairview’s inpatient environments, including a dedicated deployment designed to connect NICU patients, families, and care teams.

As part of the initiative, Fairview is deploying hellocare.ai Module on AI-Assisted Virtual Nursing and Telehealth and AI-Assisted Virtual Sitting through fixed intelligent room devices across inpatient settings. Fairview is also deploying hellocare.ai mobile carts to extend telehealth capabilities wherever virtual clinical support is needed.

Together, these technologies create a flexible enterprise virtual care infrastructure that enables remote clinicians to connect directly with patients and bedside teams, supports virtual nursing workflows, expands patient observation capabilities, and provides on-demand telehealth access throughout the hospital.

“Technology has the greatest impact when it makes care more accessible to our patients while supporting the care teams delivering it,” said Sameer Badlani, MD, Executive Vice President, Chief Digital & AI Officer and Chief New Markets Officer at Fairview. “By creating a scalable virtual care infrastructure across our inpatient environments, we can bring clinical expertise closer to the bedside and continue exploring new ways to use digital technology and AI to improve the care experience.”

Fairview is also deploying hellocare.ai Module on NICU – Family Visits, Baby Observation and Virtual Consults across its NICUs, extending the virtual care experience to some of the health system’s most vulnerable patients and their families.

The NICU solution enables authorized family members to securely connect with and see their baby remotely when they cannot physically be at the bedside, helping families remain connected throughout the NICU journey. The same platform enables virtual consultations, allowing specialists and other members of the care team to remotely connect with the NICU bedside and collaborate on patient care.

“For families with a baby in the NICU, staying connected is incredibly important,” said Darlene Spiegelberg, MAN, BSN, RN, Executive Vice President, Chief Nursing Executive and Acute Operations Officer at Fairview. “This technology gives us another way to bring families closer to their babies while also strengthening collaboration between bedside nurses, specialists, and the broader care team. Expanding our virtual care capabilities also gives our care teams additional tools to deliver safe, high-quality care to patients.”

hellocare.ai’s enterprise platform brings virtual nursing, telehealth, virtual sitting, AI-assisted patient observation, and specialized clinical workflows onto a unified technology platform designed to integrate into existing hospital operations.

“We are proud to partner with Fairview on an enterprise virtual care strategy that extends from the inpatient room to the NICU,” said Labinot Bytyqi, Founder and CEO of hellocare.ai. “Fairview is demonstrating how a unified virtual care platform can support clinicians, improve patient safety, and create meaningful connections between patients, families, and care teams. The NICU deployment is especially meaningful because technology can help families remain part of their baby’s journey even when they cannot physically be at the bedside.”

The enterprise deployment reflects Fairview’s continued investment in digital care models designed to support clinicians, improve patient and family experiences, and expand access to care across the health system.

Fairview Health Services is a Minnesota-based nonprofit health system providing a broad range of hospital, primary care, specialty care, pharmacy, and other healthcare services. Fairview is committed to improving the health of the communities it serves through high-quality care, innovation, research, education, and new approaches to healthcare delivery.

hellocare.ai is a leading provider of AI assisted virtual care solutions. Headquartered in Clearwater, Florida, the company supports more than 100 health systems across the United States and is rapidly expanding globally. hellocare.ai helps health systems deliver high quality, patient centered care while improving clinical efficiency and staff wellbeing. Its fully integrated platform includes AI Assisted Virtual Nursing, Virtual Sitting, Patient Engagement, Digital Whiteboards, Digital Room Signage, Ambient Documentation, and Hospital at Home.

For more information, schedule a demo via hellocare.ai
