#5704. 5 Classic Pony Cars And Their Modern Equivalents

Imagining a collage of objects of American culture, the mind conjures up images of things like sports stadiums, a drive-thru menu, the Wall Street Bull, the Hollywood sign, blue jeans, apple pie, and likely, some kind of car. Cars, our car dependency, and the American love for V8 engines are integral to our culture, and there are no cars to demonstrate this better than the pony car family. While very similar, there are some differences between a muscle car and a pony car.

To put it simply, the muscle car and the pony car are two sides of the same coin. The muscle car was bigger and purely focused on looking cool and going fast, with not much thought to anything else. The pony car took all that was fun about the muscle car, including the good looks and exciting performance, and made it all a bit easier to live with, often by being smaller than its muscle car counterparts. The Mustang started the pony car trend, but it wasn't the only one to do it. Since those early days in the 1960s, we've seen different takes from different manufacturers, including models like the Chevrolet Camaro, the Dodge Challenger, and even some from the hands of Carroll Shelby. Many of these models have stuck around to the modern day. The spirit of the pony car is old, but it is far from gone.

The Chevrolet Camaro and the Ford Mustang have been in a constant battle for the pony car crown since the 1960s. As they chug on and on, new trims and upgrades grace each car, and in 1969, we saw a Camaro born of the pure rebellious nature a pony car should represent. The legend of the ZL1 starts with a man called Fred Gibb. Gibb was a Chevrolet dealer who was particularly sick of the brand's internal practices. The Corvette was the monarch of the Chevrolet lineup, and Chevy wanted to keep it that way. It adamantly ensured that no performance car other than the Corvette could be fitted with an engine with over 400 cubic inches of displacement. Gibb was sick of this favoritism, and he knew the Camaro could be so much more. So, he did something about it.

Gibb contacted Chevy's Central Office Production Order, a division charged with custom orders for mundane civil and municipal services, building things like taxi cabs or police cars. Ordering from COPO was something like a deli sandwich counter for cars with no questions asked. You could mix and match parts, and that's exactly what Gibb wanted. He ordered 50 Camaros stripped down for light weight and fitted with 430-horsepower, 427-cubic-inch V8s sourced from Chevy's Can-Am race cars. Chevrolet quickly wised up to Gibb's loophole and shut down production, but the original ZL1 remains the stuff of pony car legend.

The ZL1 is Chevy's story of childhood rebellion, and even though Chevy didn't see the greatness of a high-powered stripped-down Camaro originally, it eventually came around to the idea. To see just how far the company has come from its Corvette-rules-all philosophy, we can look at the most recent, and final, example of the ZL1 from 2024.

What would have been blasphemy in 1969 was now standard procedure, as the 2024 ZL1 was powered by a pushrod V8 pulled straight from the C7 generation Corvette making 650 horsepower thanks to some help from a supercharger. Keeping classic pony car character, the ZL1 sends all that power strictly to the rear wheels, and it can be distributed via either a 10-speed automatic or a six speed manual transmission. If you really want to turn things up, you can opt for the 1LE package, which throws in some extra upgrades, and you don't have to go through COPO to do it. The 1LE adds some stickier tires, carbon fiber everywhere, adjustable suspension, and a rear seat delete. It's Chevrolet's love letter to a car it originally didn't want to exist.

So, the Camaro has its defiant ZL1 package, but what does the Mustang have to match it? The answer is the Shelby GT500, whose original iteration came before the ZL1 in 1967. If you know a thing or two about Ford performance cars, you'll recognize the name Shelby. Before Carroll Shelby ever had a Mustang with his name on it, he was busy stuffing his nimble European-esque Cobras with massive Ford engines that had no business being there and helping Ford beat Ferrari at Le Mans. After that former achievement, in 1967, Shelby convinced Ford to put the Le Mans-based and Le Mans-winning 428 V8 into the Mustang. And so, the GT500 was born.

Prior to the GT500, Ford had already made the GT350, which was raucously fast but a bit unpolished. The GT500 took the GT350 recipe, smoothed out the edges, and eliminated the almost homemade character. By no means did this mean that the GT500 was a tame car, though. Covered in aggressive aerodynamic body panels of fiberglass for lighter weight, the GT500's V8 made 355 horsepower, and could cover the quarter mile in 15 seconds, ripping past the line at 95 mph. It was a race-bred Mustang for the road, a hot-rodder's garage build in a suit and a Stetson, and it was one of the wickedly cool cars that made Carroll Shelby a legend.

Fast forward to 53 years later, the Shelby GT500 nameplate lived on. Although the newest S650 generation of Mustang drops the GT500 trim in favor of the Dark Horse SC, the S550 received the Shelby treatment for the 2020 model. As with the original, the 2020 GT500 is very clearly not your average Mustang. If the massive hood bulge, aggressive wing, and imposing front fascia aren't enough to convince you this car means business, the exhaust note certainly should. Thanks to its cross-plane crankshaft, the GT500 produces an all-American muscle car growl with a throaty bass.

Under the hood is a 5.2-liter V8, christened "Predator" by Ford, making a whopping 760 horsepower, thanks, in part, to the Eaton-supplied supercharger, which makes 12 psi of boost. The GT500 has brains to match the brawn as well. Power is distributed by a Tremec seven-speed dual clutch automatic. Operated by paddles, your pulls go straight to the transmission controller without a detour through the powertrain control module, massively improving response. It also uses what's called magnetorheological dampers. These units are filled with a liquid, and that liquid is littered with particles of iron. Also housed in the dampers are sets of electromagnets, whose currents influence and manipulate the iron particles to adjust the fluid viscosity, thereby changing the damping and ride character. The GT500 takes all the brutish charm of the original and adds the best of the modern world's fun and fancy tricks.

By 1970, the pony car race was already on, with Ford and Chevrolet battling for supremacy in this new market. Dodge was stuck on the sidelines. It knew it needed to get into the game, and it needed to do it fast. When the first Challenger debuted in 1970, it was clear that Chrysler and Dodge had taken an approach that was a bit of a headscratcher. Rather than making a purpose built pony car, the Challenger was a jack of all trades, attempting to swipe customers from all corners of the performance market.

Regardless of what it wanted to be, the original Challenger was certainly something to behold. It was exciting just to look at, with its muscular haunches and angry face, but all that car did translate to a lot of weight, 3,890 pounds to be exact. Dodge reasoned that it had to be big to make a statement on the road but also to maximize interior space, which it felt was lacking in its competitors' entries. While Dodge got what it wished for in a comfortable and commanding car, the driving dynamics suffered heavily, literally, from the Challenger's heft. Understeer was unavoidable, thanks to its weight, a sore point for the joking boat comparisons Dodge products still endure today. However, the R/T model was fitted with a pushrod V8 that made a whopping 425 horsepower. That alone made it extremely desirable and easy to forgive.

More than 50 years after the release of the original Dodge Challenger, the nameplate had solidified itself as one of America's most rowdy pony cars. Over the years, the Challenger got more powerful and more ridiculous. In 2015, we got the Hellcat, a 707-horsepower supercharged beast that shot the Challenger into legend status, with each subsequent version being somehow more obscene.

Much to our delight, it seems like Dodge wants to bring back the Hellcat V8, but the Demon SRT 170 is currently the final entry in the Hellcat family tree. The elephant, or Demon in the room, is the car's 1,025-horsepower output, making its V8 one of the most powerful 8-cylinder engines ever made. How does a road car get that, you ask? The answer is a 6.2-liter V8 with a supercharger and a hunger for E85 fuel with 170-proof ethanol, hence its name. So powerful is the Demon, that the rear axle and driveshaft had to be upgraded to safely handle its horses and 945 pound-feet of torque. Its eight-speed gearbox is specially designed with a transmission brake for drag racing, allowing rocket-like launches for the quarter mile, with Dodge claiming a 0-to-60 time of just 1.66 seconds. In truth, the Demon 170 goes beyond the original understanding of what a pony car can be. It is a quarter-mile drag racer with a warranty and a price tag guaranteeing the Challenger a place in the history books.

By 1967, Ford was already two years into its newfound stride with the Mustang. Chevrolet was behind, and likely a bit annoyed, because the Mustang had scalped customers from Chevrolet's Corvair market. Chevy had gambled on a car that focused more on lightness, agility, and introducing turbocharging to the masses in the Corvair, and the Mustang served as a rude awakening that American buyers merely wanted something that looked cool and drove fast. Chevy quickly caught up though, and released the new Camaro in 1967.

Compared to the almost European-looking Corvair, the Camaro was an entirely different beast. Chevrolet went all-out for the aggressive look, with the car measuring up at 185 inches long, much of which was taken up by a massive hood. Its grille was flat and wide, and higher trim models like the SS included extra cosmetic enhancements, along with performance upgrades. The SS, standing for Super Sport, featured the biggest V8s in the Camaro lineup, with the crowning version being the L78 396, making 375 horsepower, all of which was sent to the rear wheels. Suspension was upgraded as well, making the SS a truly well-rounded opponent for the Ford's Mustang, and helping the nameplate dig in for what would become a years-long pony car rivalry.

Fast forward to 2024, and the Camaro SS nameplate was still going, but not for much longer. Introduced in 2016, the sixth-generation Camaro would prove to be the last entry in Chevrolet's pony car lineage, at least for now, with the 2024 model year being the last of that last generation. The SS lived on until the very end, though, and in its final form, it was truly something special, bridging the gap between entry-level Camaros and top-trim monsters like the ZL1. Even as a mid-level Camaro, the car still boasted 455 horsepower straight from a no-frills V8.

The V8 in question came with 6.2 liters of displacement, no forced induction, and a pushrod cam setup. To get the most out of the SS, though, you could opt for the 1LE performance package. This added a ton of fun bits and pieces like exclusive black wheels, Recaro racing seats, powerful Brembo brakes, and an adjustable exhaust system that could take the car's roaring V8 siren song from rebellious to rambunctious. Perhaps the coolest thing about the sixth-generation SS, though, was that it could be had not only with a six speed manual transmission, but also with a soft-top body style, giving you wind in the hair and a V8 soundtrack for the ears.

By 1969, the Ford Mustang had fallen into stride as the king of the pony car market and one of Ford's most beloved models. The lineup had grown to envelope entry-level Mustangs all the way up to things like the Boss 429. There was seemingly a Mustang for everyone, and in 1969, Ford decided to enter a new trim called the Mach 1 to serve as a middle-ground ambassador for the Mustang family. The Mach 1 sat in the goldilocks zone of Mustang performance — not too little to be fun, but not too much to be ridiculous, and that was all thanks to its engine.

The Mach 1 had six engine options, with the two most exciting options being the Cobra Jet V8s at the top of the line. This duo of engines both put out 335 horses and were identical in every way except for one using a ram-air function. Despite only one engine option actually needing it, both cars wore a hood scoop that contributed to the car's flashy looks (though only the ram-air model's scoop was functional). Despite its handsome face, the Mach 1 weighed 3,607 pounds, and 59.3% of that weight was on the front wheels. As a rear wheel drive car, this made putting the power down a bit of an issue and detracted from traction and stability. Still, the Mach 1 blended the best of each side of the Mustang spectrum, and it remained undeniably cool.

52 years after the release of the original Mach 1, we saw the final and most recent version of the trim on the S550 generation mustang. A lot has changed in 52 years, but the Mach 1's purpose and place on the Mustang food chain remained the same. When it came out in 2021, the Mach 1 actually replaced three middle ground trim levels in the GT350, the Mustang Bullitt, and the Mustang GT with Performance Package 2. This left a lot of open ground to cover for the Mach 1, with Ford trying to make a modern pony car you could live with, commute in, and even take on the track.

Trying to achieve that perfect blend, the Mach 1 ends up pulling lots of parts from the bins of the three cars it replaced. At the heart of the Mach 1 is a 5.0-liter V8 making 480 horsepower, the same engine that powered the Bullitt. Putting that power to the pavement is a Tremec TR-3160 six-speed manual transmission, sourced from the GT350, with an automatic rev-matching system for perfect downshifts, although it can be disabled for expert drivers. The Mach 1 borrows its front and rear subframes from the GT350 as well, and it uses Ford's fancy adjustable magnetorheological dampers for pinpoint ride control. The underbody also features tons of carved out air channels to help cool anything that gets hot, including the six piston Brembo brakes.

#5703. A New $1.5 Billion Wind Farm Will Play In Peoria

It ain’t over ’til it’s over, but the proposed $1.5 billion, 500-megawatt Four Creeks wind farm in Peoria County, Illinois has just passed a key step in the approval process. The new milestone is yet another indication that the domestic wind industry will continue to play a key role in the US energy transition, regardless of the topsy-turvy energy policy articulated by US President Donald Trump.

If you’re somewhat shocked to hear word of a new wind farm proposal in the US, join the club. The President has spent considerable time, energy, and taxpayer dollars in a Herculean effort to keep new wind turbines from cropping up around the US under his watch. However, his efforts have earned only mixed success so far.

Offshore wind turbines keep slipping through the cracks, even though virtually every offshore wind farm in the US is subject to federal authority. Opportunities for wind power also persist on land, where the President’s direct authority is limited to projects on federal property.

Trump attempted to work around that obstacle in August of 2025, when he weaponized an otherwise routine wind project review process that applies to projects on non-federal property. The change in policy threw at least 155 onshore wind projects totaling 45 gigawatts into limbo, prompting a lawsuit from a coalition of clean energy organizations and wind energy developers.

In July of this year, Attorneys General in 19 states intervened in support of the lawsuit. The participants included Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Illinois, Maine, Massachusetts, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, and Washington State.

Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul, who co-led the intervention, notes that federal law does require wind developers to submit proposals for wind turbines more than 200 feet tall to the Federal Aviation Administration, which then refers the project to DoD to check for any conflicts with military operations and related activities. Raoul further notes that the normal process involves collaborating on mitigation measures to resolve any conflicts.

That all ground to a halt in August of 2025, when DoD dropped the ball on its part of the process. “Officials ceased countersigning mitigation agreements, stopped sending completed agreements to developers for signature, and delayed or halted communications with developers about mitigation,” Raoul explained in a press statement in July.

The abrupt change in policy impacted at least nine wind projects in Illinois alone. According to Raoul’s office the nine projects represent $4.3 billion in private investment, or more.

Separately, on June 16 of this year the same coalition of state Attorneys General won the final resolution of a series of legal challenges to an Executive Order issued in January of 2025, in which Trump ordered a halt to all federal approvals for wind projects.

The DoD lawsuit is heading down the same path, at least so far. On August 6, a federal judge with the US District Court for the District of Oregon ordered DoD to resume its normal wind turbine review process while the case continues to wind its way through the courts.

DoD has been slow-walking the process since then, reportedly approving just 11 projects since August. However, the US branch of the global clean energy developer Repsol already saw the writing on the wall. On August 14, just one week after the Oregon decision came down, Repsol Renewables began submitting paperwork for the proposed Four Creeks Wind project.

“Repsol Renewables has identified northwest Peoria County as suitable for wind development because of a robust wind resource, its proximity to the existing electric transmission system with available capacity, compatibility with existing land use, and minimal anticipated environmental impacts,” Repsol summarized, with existing land use referring to provisions in the Peoria County Code that permit commercial wind farms in certain agricultural districts.

Although the wind farm involves a total of 27,000 acres on private land, each of the project’s 113 turbines will only account for less than one acre. The bulk of the land is dedicated to required setbacks as well as adequate spacing between the turbines.

Things are moving along at a relatively fast clip so far. On November 6, Peoria public radio station WCBU reported that the land use committee of the Peoria County Board recommended the Four Creeks project by a 6-3 vote. The project almost appeared to be dead in September when the Zoning Board of Appeals issued a 4-1 denial, but the Zoning Board also voted to include conditions for consideration by the full Peoria County Board at its meeting on November 5. The County Board approved the Four Creeks proposal on a split vote of 12-5 alongside a list of 36 restrictions mainly governing construction and operations.

Wind fans, don’t break out the champagne just yet. Repsol still has to apply for construction permits, and the entire process could take up to five years or so before shovels meet ground.

If and when Four Creeks materializes, Repsol is prepared to pour more than $193 million into the coffers of the Princeville, Brimfield, Williamsfield, and Stark County School Districts, with an additional $44.7 million in total property tax revenues for Peoria County and associated jurisdictions.

Repsol also draws attention to more than $69.4 million in total property tax revenues earmarked for libraries, fire districts, Illinois Central College, local road authorities, and the Greater Metro Airport Authority among other community resources.

Local property owners will also rake in millions of dollars in escalating lease payments.

As for objections to the new wind farm, WCBU reporter Joe Deacon highlighted remarks by Peoria County Board member Terry Ruhland, who acknowledged those who spoke against the  project at a public meeting.

“I don’t know how many people are in this room; I won’t even guess. But there is at least 179,000 people in Peoria County who are not in this room,” Rhuland said.

“Of that 179 [thousand], for every school kid who deserves the best education we can give them, and for every family that’s struggling to pay their utility bills, I’m going to vote yes,” Ruhland added.

Perhaps Ruhland was also thinking of Laborers Local 165, which has been working with Repsol for more than a year on developing a local workforce for the project. In a hearing before the Zoning Board in September, union representative Dane Simpson asserted that each wind turbine would account for approximately 3,000 hours of work.

Image: The global energy developer Repsol is on track to construct a 500-megawatt wind farm in Peoria County, Illinois, regardless of last year’s sharp U-turn in federal energy policy (screenshot, courtesy of Repsol).

#5702. Avanlee Care, platform for family caregivers, raises $3.5M, targeting Medicare Advantage plans

Avanlee Care, platform for family caregivers, raises $3.5M, targeting Medicare Advantage plans" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Avanlee Care, a platform to engage family caregivers, has clinched $3.5 million in seed funding, Fierce Healthcare has learned.

The round was led by BEA Venture Fund, with participation from angel investor Esther Dyson, who is Avanlee’s board chair, Chrysalis Ventures and FairBridge VC. Avanlee will use the capital, which brings its total raised to $6 million, to expand across the Medicare Advantage market.

Avanlee Care helps MA plans and other organizations engage caregivers within their member populations, enabling caregivers to take action and organizations to measure the impact. On the Avanlee platform, caregivers can schedule appointments, manage medications, connect with retailers, communicate with their plan and provider, get vaccination reminders and search for providers. Meanwhile, payers get insight into caregiver burnout and member health trend data.

“Avanlee Care is addressing an enormous and underutilized resource within healthcare,” Melissa Bradley, founder and managing partner of BEA Venture Fund, said in a comment. “As healthcare organizations look for more effective ways to improve engagement and outcomes, Avanlee is offering the infrastructure to make caregivers part of that strategy. We believe that creates a significant opportunity to improve both the caregiver experience and healthcare outcomes at scale.”

Founded in 2020, Avanlee began as a direct-to-consumer app, since transitioning into the enterprise space. It is fully integrated with Mark Cuban Cost Plus Drugs as its lead pharmacy partner for discounted medications, and is in discussions with a national, undisclosed MA plan to bring its platform to members with an assigned caregiver. As part of an initial potential pilot with this plan, thousands of members with an assigned caregiver would participate in Avanlee, with a broader expansion planned for mid-2027. Additionally, Avanlee is working toward a separate unnamed integration with a national pharmacy partner for delivering medications.

“We are excited to work with Avanlee Care. We share a common mission: to provide lower costs on prescribed medications, saving money for the unpaid family caregiver and their loved one, the care-receiver,” Mark Cuban, co-founder of Cost Plus Drug Company, told Fierce Healthcare.

Nearly 1 in 4 Americans provide ongoing care for an adult or child with a complex medical condition or a disability, coordinating medications, appointments, transportation, food and other needs. Yet by overlooking the person managing a member’s care and day-to-day living, plans’ efforts to engage MA members are less effective, Avanlee executives argue.

“Caregivers spend an astronomical amount of time having to juggle their career, their families, and suddenly now I’m thrust into this role of I’m a caregiver for my mom … so saving time is huge,” Avanlee Christine, co-founder and CEO of Avanlee Care, told Fierce Healthcare exclusively. Christine, who grew up with a grandfather with Parkinson’s and dementia, was inspired to build the platform that could have supported her mom when she was caregiving.

Avanlee offers caregiver wellness tools on its platform, which 59% of past users have engaged with. Over half of consistent users also reported a decrease in overall stress. In its DTC days, Avanlee supported thousands of families, claiming it saved their caregivers thousands of hours. The wellness tools include a weekly questionnaire on stress and educational resources on topics such as estate planning, life planning and legal services. Caregivers can add other relatives to the platform for extra visibility or support, and Avanlee also facilitates grocery delivery through an integration with Walmart (their pricing applies). “If the caregiver fails, the one ultimately receiving care fails,” Christine said.

This stress survey becomes a key data stream for Avanlee plan partners, allowing them to evaluate caregiver burnout. Avanlee's platform also provides payers with insights about appointment bookings, home health services and medication adherence.

There’s a reason Avanlee is targeting MA to start. Nearly two-thirds of caregivers say MA makes caregiving duties easier to manage than traditional Medicare, according to one survey. Avanlee is also interested in eventually expanding to dual-eligibles. "There's a lot of tailwinds in caregiving for both Medicare and Medicaid and those dually eligible populations,” Eric Scott, Avanlee’s chief growth officer, said.

In order to streamline scheduling, Avanlee is seeking MA partners that allow it to also tap into their provider networks. Avanlee can automatically schedule appointments when prompted by a health plan, such as annual wellness visits or cancer screenings. Caregivers can also manually add their existing appointments to get reminders. In the near future, Avanlee plans to let caregivers book ad hoc appointments for needs beyond those specifically requested by the health plan.

Avanlee charges payers per-member-per-month and is available at no direct cost to the caregiver. It behooves plans to support this population, Christine argues, not only because of their influence over member outcomes but also because they could become a loyal future customer base. “You want to build a relationship with that adult daughter or son because you take such good care of their mom,” Christine said.

Avanlee is incorporating AI to reduce friction for caregivers, like summarizing caregiver notes recorded via audio, recommending providers based on caregiver preferences and matching users’ questions with curated resources. It also makes recommendations to caregivers based on a number of insights, including what medications a member is taking, what conditions they have and what their social needs are. These AI features are powered by AWS Bedrock, with requests handled within Avanlee’s cloud environment rather than being sent to a third-party model provider.

“How do we make it the new norm in healthcare that these people are part of healthcare for mom or dad on day one,” Christine said.

#5701. 7 Sleek Sports Cars Ranked Worst To Best By Drag Coefficient

Equipping a sports car with a big and powerful engine is all well and good. But if the car in question is designed like a cinder block, then it's just wasting the engine's potential. As a car speeds up, the air resistance around it increases. And a car with a sleeker design can slip through the air with less resistance, thus granting it better performance. That, in a very basic nutshell, is why aerodynamics matter.

Now, drag coefficient (Cd) isn't the be-all and end-all when it comes to measuring a car's aerodynamics as a whole. Something like drag area, which combines that metric with frontal area measurements, provides a more complete picture. Nevertheless, drag coefficient scores still provide a solid impression as to just how slippery a car is — and such figures are more readily available from automakers, too.

Sleek designs certainly aren't reserved exclusively for performance models; economy cars like Honda's little hybrid that could, the Insight, can also be marvelously slippery. But this article will be focusing on some of the sleekest sports and performance cars out from across the last century, covering old-school favorites such as the Tatra T87 with modern marvels like Volkswagen's XL1.

This Czechoslavkian masterpiece is a genuinely fascinating piece of design. Before moving onto the aerodynamic aspects of the T87, it's first worth covering what else makes it such an intriguing automobile. Motivation is sourced from a rear-engined 2.9-liter V8, which kicked out an impressive-for-the-era 85 horsepower. Back in the '40s, that was a serious amount of power to be dealing with, and Tatra ensured its effectiveness by complimenting it with a seriously slippery design.

German Zeppelins provided plenty of influence behind the T87's iconic shape, and the end result was a drag coefficient of just 0.36 Cd. This enabled the 85-horse V8 to propel the T87 to an impressive 100 mph, although the handling characteristics of a rear-engined machine with independent swing-axle suspension resulted in a fair number of accidents. Rumor has it that, due to so many Nazi officers meeting their maker in T87 accidents, the car was actually banned for use – but the accuracy of these claims has been contested over the years. Still, it all adds to the fascinating history of Tatra's aerodynamic masterpiece.

Production spanned from 1936 to 1950, albeit with a gap during the war years. Despite such a wide production window, though, just over 3,000 T87s were ever built. It proved to be a significant influence to Ferdinand Porsche, and today, it's a cherished classic that attracts collectors willing to pay over $100,000.

The Huayra replaced the awesome Zonda in 2011, and it boasted a design that was just as striking. It was a million-dollar masterpiece at launch, packing a 720-horsepower twin-turbocharged 6.0-liter V12, capable of propelling it along to a top speed of 224 mph. Aerodynamic trickery helps the Italian to remain stable at speed, with front- and rear-mounted flaps that rise and fall to alter downforce levels.

It's important to remember that a supercar like this needs to be comfortable performing through the corners as well as the straight lines. Here's where that active aero really proves its relevancy. Those four flaps allow the Huayra to transform itself depending on the given requirements. While flat, the Huayra boasts a drag coefficient of just 0.31 Cd (as proven by a Mercedes wind tunnel). But they can also flip up to assist the car with braking and keep it planted through the corners.

Much like Pagani did with the Zonda, as the Huayra began to age, the automaker began to produce numerous special editions. Among them was a rolling $7.3 million air piece dubbed the Codalunga. The svelte model sports various ducts and diffusers, plus a longtail design – which is a known method of reducing the amount of drag a car's body produces. However, the Codalunga has not been individually tested in a wind tunnel, so whether it beats the standard Huayra's 0.31 Cd isn't officially known.

While on the topic of longtail designs, it seems appropriate to mention the McLaren Speedtail. This car categorically proves the effectiveness of such a design, with a drag coefficient of just under 0.29 Cd. The British firm from Woking knows a thing or two about churning out slippery supercars, but this Speedtail is something of a caricature; it sits 3 feet longer than the F1, and it's even longer than the F1 GTR Longtail. Helping it cut through the air as precisely as possible is a narrow frontal area, numerous concealed ducts, a complete lack of rear-view mirrors, and front wheels that are almost entirely enclosed.

Of course, a sleek design still needs to be complimented with a mighty power train if impressive performance is the end goal. And with a turbocharged 4.0-liter V8 that combines its efforts with a single electric motor to produce 1,035 horsepower, the Speedtail recipe is certainly a comprehensive one. Combined with a dry weight of just 3,153 pounds, that's enough to see the Speedtail achieve a top speed of 250 mph. Plus, it'll crack 186 mph in just shy of half the time required by its forefather, the mighty F1.

As impressive as the McLaren Speedtail's design is, what's arguably far more impressive is that a $44,245 Corvette from 2005 can match the $2.25 million British hypercar's drag coefficient. With a drag coefficient of just 0.28 Cd, the C6 Chevy is surprisingly slippery. This wasn't a one-hit-wonder for Chevrolet, either, as previous generations had also proven to be remarkably aerodynamic as well. But the C6 manages to outdo them all (albeit only marginally). The C4 boasted a drag coefficient of 0.34 Cd, while the C5 sat at 0.29 Cd. It's worth noting that later generations – including the current C8 — also sit behind the C6's rating.

It's no wonder that people think the C6 is still the best Corvette to date. Regardless of whether you agree or not, it's hard to find real fault with the C6. It combined a brilliantly efficient design with supercar-rivaling performance; the most powerful iteration was the 638-horsepower ZR1, which could top 200 mph. Even the base models were serious performers thanks to an LS1 lurking beneath that low-slung hood. These cars were affordable when new, and they're still great bang-for-buck choices today, with entry-level coupes and convertibles both available for sub-$25,000 – proving that slippery sports cars don't exclusively belong in six-figure price brackets.

Electric cars and hybrids pay a lot of attention to aerodynamics, as being able to slip through the air with minimal resistance is a particularly effective way of increasing a vehicle's range. That's led to buyers of electrified vehicles becoming understandably obsessed with realistic and effective ranges. It should come as no surprise, then, that BMW's bold hybridized i8 sports a drag coefficient of just 0.26 Cd.

That drag coefficient proves that the i8's striking design isn't all about stealing the attention of passers by, in fact, it's really quite clever. The various slices and slashes between those layered body panels help to direct airflow into the car's various radiators, which allows the i8 to disregard active aero. Even the cockpit itself is teardrop-shaped to reduce drag, while the flared rear pillars help keep the visuals sweet without damaging any aerodynamic benefits.

With a turbocharged 1.5-liter inline-three engine and single electric motor tackling the task of motivation, the i8's power train recipe could not be more different from that of the aforementioned Corvette. However, just like the C6, the BMW i8 now finds itself at a very tempting price point, with early examples now changing hands for sub-$40,000.

This one's probably something of a surprise, as unlike so many of the other mentions on this list, the Nissan GT-R doesn't exactly look immensely slippery. It's not particularly low-slung, it doesn't incorporate an obvious longtail design, nothing else about it is clearly geared toward aerodynamics — plus, there's a great big spoiler adorning the trunk. However, that hasn't stopped the GT-R from being a technological marvel with a drag coefficient of only 0.26 Cd. Yep, this chunky model with heaps of boost and gaping grills matches the rating of BMW's slippery little eco-minded coupe.

The secrets of the GT-R low drag coefficient are actually somewhat hidden. It sports an almost completely flat floor, a functional diffuser which helps to channel airflow efficiency, and a slightly tapered rear overhang. Also helping to direct the air in an effective manner are what Nissan describes as "aero-blades" adorning the front fenders, while the narrow fender vents help to provide valuable downforce at the front, too.

Throughout its impressive 18-year tenure, the R35 GT-R saw the power from its twin-turbocharged 3.8-liter V6 rise to genuine supercar levels. And the clever aero tweaks it received over those years helped drivers to make the most of that strength. It came incredibly close to cracking the 7-minute barrier on the Nurburgring, peaking with a time of 7:08.679 in its 2013 Nismo guise — breaking the world record for fastest volume production car in the process.

All of the cars featured upon this list are aerodynamically impressive, and they certainly sit a long way removed from the least aerodynamic cars ever made. However, the Volkswagen XL1 stands in a class of its own. The sole purpose of this striking little hybridized-diesel inline-three-powered sports car was to be as mightily efficient as possible.

The headline number here is a drag coefficient of just 0.19 Cd. To get this number down so far, it combines many of the other engineering techniques used by other cars on this list. It very obviously sports a teardrop profile like the i8, allowing the smoothest possible path for airflow. Like the GT-R, the car's floor is completely flat, preventing the underside from pushing against the wind. And — going above and beyond the Speedtail in this regard – covered rear wheels assist the XL1 in achieving its remarkably low drag coefficient.

It wasn't just aerodynamic efficiency that Volkswagen was chasing with the XL1. It was also designed to be immensely frugal on fuel, to the point where a Honda Insight or Toyota Prius might look like a big-block Chevy from the '70s in comparison. On the European combined test cycle, Volkswagen managed to achieve a frankly mind-boggling 313 mpg, a feat helped by the model's incredibly low curb weight (courtesy of magnesium wheels and a carbon-fiber monocoque chassis).

#5700. Tesla Hasn’t Had A Successful New Product Launch Since JB Straubel Stepped Down As CTO

As has been widely reported, Tesla is about to end Cybertruck production. The Cybertruck has been a shocking failure. I’m sure there are more detailed analyses out there somewhere, but this short response on X from Ben McCombe that Tina Casey included in her article on the matter sums it up very well:

“Installed tooling to build 125k Cybertrucks a year.

“Made just $100m in gross profits from sales.

That’s pretty wild. A net project loss of around $2 billion. Now, I have to admit that I haven’t fact checked the numbers here, but what we know for certain is that Tesla planned to produce a lot of Cybertrucks per year and ended up producing a small fraction of that target. In fact, the annual sales target for the Cybertruck was higher than 125,000 — it was 250,000, with a goal of getting up to 500,000!

The Cybertruck was hyped up as having more reservations than any vehicle in history and was supposedly going to shatter records and transform the market. I warned people on many occasions that the reservation total was not a real reservation total and was definitely not a reliable indicator of demand because a) a reservation only required a $100 refundable deposit, and b) a ton of people made reservations after Elon Musk said that you could lock in the price of lifetime Full Self Driving when making a reservation (so, you’d only have to pay $6,000 for FSD no matter how much the cost of it went up in the following years). Anyway, the Cybertruck had other issues as well when it finally arrived. It cost about twice as much as it was supposed to cost and it had about half as much range as it was supposed to have. In other words, it was not even close to the vehicle it was supposed to be — its range per dollar cost was about ¼ what it was supposed to be.

The Cybertruck was supposed to be the next big thing after the Tesla Model Y. It was supposed to disrupt the gigantic US pickup truck market. The Model S was a superb and widely acclaimed car, if a bit more expensive than the mass market could afford. The Model S did in fact compete superbly well with the leaders in its segment, the BMW 7 Series and Mercedes S-Class. The Tesla Model X brought a similar offering in a larger package with some fun extra elements (falcon-wing doors, self-presenting doors, a third row). The Tesla Model 3 then completely shook the automotive world as a tremendous market phenomenon and perhaps the biggest product launch in history (in terms of total revenue). The Tesla Model Y was basically the Model 3 in a more popular crossover package and eventually became a much higher selling vehicle. In fact, it became the highest selling vehicle model of any kind in multiple years. Then JB Straubel stepped down as CTO.

Due to their EV passions, JB Straubel and Elon Musk were introduced to each other and had lunch together to talk about electric airplanes (Elon’s dream) and then electric cars (because JB talked more sense into Elon). Then the two of them were introduced to Marc Tarpenning and Martin Eberhard, who had founded Tesla Motors and just barely got started on the idea. After a while, Tarpenning and Eberhard left the company, and Musk and Straubel truly led its development and growth into an automotive superpower (as briefly described above). Since JB Straubel stepped down from his role as CTO of Tesla, however, if one thinks about it, it’s hard to identify any successful product launch from the company or much significant improvement at all.

Straubel left his CTO position in July 2019. The Model Y was unveiled in March 2019 and was about ⅔ the same as the Model 3. It would seem that getting the Model Y designed and prepared for launch was the last big project Straubel worked on. (Note that the Semi was unveiled in November 2017 but was long delayed due to battery supply, according to Elon Musk.) Since the Model Y, what significant product launch have we seen from Tesla? There was the Cybertruck, as we’ve already discussed. That was unveiled in November 2019. When you think about the timing now, did Straubel disagree strongly with Musk on the Cybertruck and decide it was time to move on when Musk pushed forward with his idea for an electric truck? It took another 4+ years for Tesla to start delivering the Cybertruck, in contrast to Model Y deliveries starting in January 2020, less than a year after the model was unveiled. More recently, the Cybercab has been developed, unveiled, and is now in production. A consumer car smaller and cheaper than the Model 3 was never developed and unveiled — just a stripped down, decontented Model 3 — and there basically haven’t been any other product unveilings since Straubel left his role as CTO. Elon Musk has published a couple of somewhat scattered, rambling “master plans,” but we haven’t gotten any significant new products aside from the Cybertruck and the just arriving Cybercab.

Even looking over on the energy storage side of things, the Tesla Megapack was launched in July 2019, the month Straubel stepped down from his role as CTO. Did Straubel just decide he had done enough once he had finished the Megapack launch and gotten the Model Y essentially ready for market? Did he have conflicts with Musk on where to take the company from there?

Yes, there’s been incremental product development and refreshed versions of Tesla cars and energy storage systems. There are still plenty of engineers working on improving things. However, there doesn’t seem to be the same leadership in new product development, and there also isn’t the same practical, moderating element that Straubel seemingly provided to Musk’s more wild, grandiose, sci-fi inspired dreams and ideas.

Perhaps this is all misunderstanding the roles of the two men to some extent. Perhaps things would not be much different if Straubel had stayed in the CTO role and had the same influence he had before leaving. He is still on the board of directors. (What that actually means is unclear, though.) Perhaps Tesla’s success and business would still be primarily based on the Model 3 and Model Y, without new transformative products. Or perhaps we would have had a more normal pickup truck from Tesla, an electric van, better batteries, a better market rollout of the Semi, and other products. Perhaps the Cybertruck, an epic product failure, never would have been shown to the product and hyped up unrealistically with specs and figures disconnected from what was going to be possible. Perhaps we’d have a Model C (affordable, compact Tesla) rather than a Cybercab. Perhaps Tesla would be a very different company.

Who knows? We don’t know the ins and outs of JB Straubel and Elon Musk’s relationship, or how much Straubel actually led Tesla in his CTO role. We don’t know how much Straubel tampered down Musk’s worst instincts or guided product development. We still really don’t even know why Straubel left. According to Tesla, it was so that he could focus more time on Redwood Materials, but why wasn’t that business within the umbrella of Tesla in the first place? Vertical integration has long been a key element of the company. Who knows? There’s a lot we don’t know and never will. However, what we do know is that since JB Straubel stepped down from his role as CTO of Tesla, we haven’t seen a significant, successful new product launch at the company. We’ll have to wait a bit longer to see if the Cybercab is one, and whether that sets a new, positive course for the future of the company or not.

#5699. Lp(a)-Lowering Pelacarsen Shows Huge Disconnect With Cardiovascular Outcomes

— After disappointing Lp(a) HORIZON trial, eyes turn to next-gen siRNA therapies

Lowering lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a), did not translate into better cardiovascular outcomes in a secondary prevention population, at least not with pelacarsen in the Lp(a) HORIZON trial.

Among people with elevated lipoprotein(a) and pre-existing cardiovascular disease (CVD), pelacarsen was no help for reducing the primary endpoint of cardiovascular death, nonfatal stroke, nonfatal myocardial infarction (MI), or urgent coronary revascularization over nearly 5 years (HR 1.02 compared with placebo, 95% CI 0.90-1.15), reported Steven Nissen, MD, of the Cleveland Clinic, at the American Heart Association (AHA) annual meeting in Chicago.

No matter how the investigators sliced and diced the data, it was the same story: analysis of people with especially high lipoprotein(a), 90 mg/dL or higher, also yielded no benefit (HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.87-1.15); pelacarsen similarly showed no efficacy regarding a modified cardiovascular endpoint not counting revascularizations, another composite endpoint including coronary heart disease rather than cardiovascular deaths, and the individual outcomes of MI, stroke, urgent revascularization, and cardiovascular death.

Beyond these "completely neutral" results, "tolerability issues were certainly very prominent" with pelacarsen, Nissen added during an AHA press conference, citing rates of adverse events leading to drug discontinuation of 20.6% with pelacarsen versus 7.5% with placebo.

Nissen stressed that it may be the end of the road for pelacarsen, but not the lipoprotein(a) hypothesis.

"The Lp(a) HORIZON trial is not the end of the story. Ongoing trials are studying different populations, like primary prevention, aortic stenosis, and different therapies, and siRNA, several siRNAs. A single trial does not provide definitive evidence of a lack of benefit of lowering lipoprotein(a) as a strategy to reduce cardiovascular risk," he said.

Lipoprotein(a) is a genetically determined risk factor for atherosclerotic CVD and aortic stenosis. It is a highly atherogenic particle considered unmodifiable with diet or physical activity, unlike LDL cholesterol. Estimates suggest one in five people worldwide have high lipoprotein(a).

Pelacarsen was an antisense oligonucleotide made to degrade the hepatic mRNA coding for apolipoprotein(a), an intermediate to the production of lipoprotein(a).

In Lp(a) HORIZON, pelacarsen did drastically reduce lipoprotein(a) and LDL cholesterol by an estimated 77.7% and 13.3%, respectively, relative to placebo. This was on top of existing secondary prevention therapies that had gotten baseline LDL cholesterol to a median 64.6 mg/dL and systolic blood pressure to 125 mmHg on average.

"Was there no room left for improvement? To the credit of the investigators, what was done was actually optimization of what we know to do already: optimize the LDL, optimize the blood pressure. If we do that, was there just no room left in these patients to further reduce the risk?" posed panelist Donald Lloyd-Jones, MD, ScM, of Boston University.

"Like Dr. Nissen, I personally would not recommend that we abandon considering Lp(a) as a potential causal risk factor or as a therapeutic target until we have a lot more data available in different patient populations, certainly in younger individuals and primary prevention populations, over longer periods of time and with ... different chemical strategies to try to inhibit this molecule," said Lloyd-Jones, a past president of the AHA.

Nissen noted that the siRNA therapies in development are potentially more tolerable and more effective while requiring less frequent administration. Already advancing to large-scale cardiovascular outcome trials, for example, are lepodisiran and olpasiran, with others further back in the pipeline.

There's also evidence that the now-familiar PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies reduce Lp(a) along with LDL cholesterol, which may partly explain some of their benefit in CVD risk reduction, according to Lloyd-Jones.

"We don't fully understand the biology here, and I think we need to continue to take a deeper dive into that biology so that we fully understand what it is about Lp(a) that serves as a marker of risk and potentially as a better target for our future therapies," he said.

"I really think you cannot close the door with a single negative trial," Nissen emphasized. "It's going to be my mission to try to convince the people that pay the bills, which is industry sponsors, not to pull the plug on trials because we really need to understand more."

Lp(a) HORIZON trial was a phase III cardiovascular outcomes trial conducted in nearly 800 sites in 42 countries. Eligible participants had a cardiovascular event 3 months to 10 years prior to enrollment and lipoprotein(a) levels 70 mg/dL or greater. They underwent a risk factor optimization period to ensure use of secondary prevention therapies.

Nissen's group had 8,350 individuals randomized 1:1 to pelacarsen 80 mg or placebo self-administered once monthly subcutaneously.

Mean age was just under 60, with about 27% of participants being women and 78% white. Median lipoprotein(a) was 236 nmol/L and hsCRP 0.8 mg/L. Nearly 80% of the cohort were on high-intensity statins.

Follow-up reached a median 57 months in the trial.

Nissen reported that his group sought to conduct additional exploratory analyses on account of the "unexpected" results of Lp(a) HORIZON.

In this extension report, there was still no argument to be made for pelacarsen's efficacy even after accounting for treatment adherence, first and repeated adverse events, and magnitude of 3-month lipoprotein(a) reductions, among other analyses.

Lp(a) HORIZON trial was simultaneously published in the New England Journal of Medicine and its extension report separately released in NEJM Evidence.

Clover Health boosts outlook amid continued membership growth, financial momentum in Q3" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Clover Health is continuing to see strong traction in its Medicare Advantage plan, with membership growing 49% year-over-year in the third quarter to approximately 157,000 members.

Alongside continued membership growth, executives touted the company’s star ratings from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services for payment year 2028.

“We are incredibly proud that our flagship PPO plan achieved five stars for payment year 2028, making it the largest five-star PPO contract in the country,” Andrew Toy, Clover Health CEO, said during Wednesday’s earnings call. “Additionally, our HMO plan achieved four and a half stars, meaning 100% of Clover members are enrolled in plans rated at least four and a half stars for payment year 2028.”

Toy said the ratings give Clover “continued flexibility to invest” in benefits and affordable care access for members, adding that the company’s HEDIS quality performance remains “industry leading.”

“And that is why we're proud that for the third year in a row, we rank number one nationally among comparable PPO plans on core HEDIS measures,” Toy said. “At the same time, we have not built Clover around optimizing to stars ratings. We are built to manage true clinical quality and total cost of care. That distinction matters.”

Toy also announced that Clover’s board appointed interim CFO Clay Thornton as its permanent CFO.

The company posted $130 million in profit, up 77% year-over-year, and total revenue of $759 million, up 53% year-over-year, according to financial results published Wednesday afternoon.

Given its performance thus far, Thorton told investors Clover now projects full-year revenue of between $2.97 billion and $3 billion and adjusted EBITDA of $75 million to $85 million. It also expects membership in Medicare Advantage to average between 157,000 and 158,000, per Thornton.

“With the performance we have delivered to date and our updated guidance, we expect 2026 to mark Clover's first full year of GAAP net income profitability,” Thornton said.

Toy said the company’s next chapter is “proving that our model can scale further” as it expands deeper into core markets and new ones, adding that “AI is a significant part” of how it scales.

“Critically, we believe that AI has reset the playing field in health plan operations, even relatively modern systems and workflows built for a pre-AI world can now be rebuilt faster with AI, accelerated with better data, and utilize far more intelligence,” he said. “We are taking advantage of this by applying AI across Clover to make the plan far more efficient to operate as we scale. AI also creates an opportunity to deliver a much better service experience for seniors.”

Among its capabilities, Clover Assistant helps providers identify diseases earlier, surfaces treatment gaps and “turns years of fragmented medical history into actionable information at the point of care,” Toy said.

“That's the opportunity we see across Clover,” he said. “Not simply using AI to do the same work at lower cost, but using it to deliver better care, better service and better operations at scale.”

#5697. Here's Why The Electric Dirt Bikes From Tractor Supply Aren't Street Legal

Unless you've been living under the proverbial rock for the last decade, you're sure to have seen the myriad inexpensive electric dirt bikes ripping around city streets and countryside alike. With inexpensive lithium batteries and compact, lightweight electric motors providing wheel-standing torque with a twist of the wrist, these things tend to be both quick and incredibly fun to ride. When it comes to fun-per-dollar, it's difficult to argue that these don't peg the needle squarely in the as-much-as-you-want zone. However, to keep costs low, manufacturers tend to skip most of the equipment and paperwork you would need for them to be legally plated and ridden on the street.

Most of these electric dirt bikes come fresh off the boat from China. You've heard of the big names, like Surron or Talaria, I'm sure. Even American electric motorcycle brand Zero's XE and XB off-road motorcycles are built in China. These days there are dozens of other manufacturers building (or white-label reselling) these machines for distribution through just about every online retailer you can think of.

Take, for example, mini-bike maker Tractor Supply, which offers full-size GoTrax and Drift Hero electric motorcycles on its website, ranging from 800-watt (about 1-horsepower) yard bikes for little kids on up to the 7,000-watt (9-ish horsepower) GoTrax K2. That one is allegedly good for 50 miles per hour and up to 45 miles of range. Depending how far your commute is, and the roads you ride on every day, that could be the makings of an incredibly efficient and fun daily-rider. You know, if it weren't for those pesky laws. So why aren't they street legal, and can you do anything to make them legal?

While some manufacturers go through the costly process of registering their machines with the U.S. Department of Transportation and obtaining the correct paperwork to make street-legal electric dirt bikes, the vast majority (including those sold at Tractor Supply) do not. There's a long history of off-road-only dirt bikes, so this doesn't just apply to the electric ones, but riding illegal electric dirt bikes on the street seems to have grown in popularity in recent years.

An off-road vehicle is not typically equipped with a standardized vehicle identification number, and thus can't be tracked or registered as a normal motorcycle would. Without a VIN you can't get your bike registered, plated, or properly insured for legal street riding. Many of these off-road-use-only bikes lack the standard equipment necessary for street legality as well. To be federally street-legal, and therefore considered a motorcycle, requires a DOT-legal headlight, functioning brake lights, mirrors, a horn (audible from 200 feet away), and DOT-legal tires.

At the end of the day, there's a reason street-legal motorcycles are typically more expensive than a non-street-legal dirt bike. It has always been this way, even for gasoline-powered motorcycles. Take, for example, Honda's gas-powered CRF300 lineup. The CRF300L Rally is street legal, with all the requisite components necessary to be so, and it starts at $6,499 plus $600 destination. The off-road-only CRF300F, meanwhile, is $1,700 less total, at just $5,099 plus $300 destination. It makes sense that Honda would charge a premium for a bike that has significantly more components, and that's before you get to the hoops Honda needs jump through  to file the correct DOT paperwork. Any old fly-by-night Chinese electric dirt-bike startup can just ship you a bike without any of that at a fraction of the cost.

There isn't really a short answer to the question of how to make an electric dirt bike fully street legal, aside from "It depends." Before doing anything to make your off-road electric motorcycle into a street-legal machine, you should consult your local laws because this is hardly a nationally settled matter. The first step in your journey should be to contact your state's Department of Motor Vehicles to get a list of required equipment. Some states allow a more lax interpretation of the law, skipping some of those federally mandated parts. On the flip side, some states are strict, and depending on what model you've purchased, it may not even be possible.

It's tough to say there's a blanket appropriate method of installing all of these components on every kind of bike, but everything required by law should be reasonably easy to install in a home garage with standard mechanic's hand tools. There are thousands of options to choose from in the motorcycle aftermarket. Fork-mounted front light kits, easy-fit rear lights, handlebar-mount mirrors, and the like are the work of an afternoon. Depending on your motorcycle choice, however, you may need to upgrade your 12-volt battery system to accommodate the extra load of the add-ons.

Once you've made the appropriate modifications and gathered the appropriate paperwork for the DMV, you can submit your motorcycle for inspection. Usually this is quite easy, and you'll be assigned an inspector to insure each component is installed and functions properly for state standards. At that point you'll be able to apply for registration and a license plate.

Or, buy a street-legal one in the first place.

#5696. CMS’ final 2027 outpatient pay rule brings hospitals little relief on 340B, site-neutral changes

CMS’ final 2027 outpatient pay rule brings hospitals little relief on 340B, site-neutral changes" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services on Tuesday finalized its annual outpatient hospital payments rule with a lower-than-proposed rate bump and its major, industry-opposed policy shifts moderated, but largely intact.

The 2027 Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment (OPPS) and Ambulatory Surgical Center (ASC) Payment Systems rule outlines a 2.3% reimbursement increase for those meeting applicable quality reporting requirements. That’s below the proposed 2.4% increase and reflects a 3.2% projected hospital market basket increase and a 0.9 percentage point productivity adjustment.

The agency is also moving forward with a substantial and controversial cut in 340B drug reimbursements, though not quite to the extent that it initially proposed.

The final rule adjusts these drug payments down from the current bar of average sales price (ASP) plus 6% to ASP minus 28%, as opposed to the proposed 33.4% below ASP. To make the reimbursement change budget neutral as required by statute, OPPS payments for non-drug services will be boosted by 7.5%.

CMS said it tweaked the proposed 340B reimbursement cut based on 340B ceiling price data from the Health Resources and Services Administration, with the baseline reductions informed by a drug acquisition cost survey it conducted earlier this year. Those changes will reduce Original Medicare drug payments by $4.35 billion and the drug payments from beneficiaries by $1.1 billion (or $900 on average per beneficiary who receives an affected drug from a hospital outpatient department) in the policy’s first year, CMS said.

The rate adjustment did little to calm hospital industry groups who’d railed against the 340B reimbursement changes as a threat to safety-net care and a gift to for-profit hospitals that do not participate in the subsidy program but would benefit from the budget-neutral offset. The American Hospital Association, the Association of American Medical Colleges and America’s Essential Hospitals each condemned the finalized policy in reaction statements, with the latter two issuing more forceful rebukes.

“CMS has based its reimbursement to 340B hospitals on the results of a hasty and faulty survey, failing to follow the clear requirements of the Medicare statute,” AAMC Chief Health Care Officer Jonathan Jaffery, M.D., said. “The drug payment cuts disproportionately affect and target non-profit and public hospitals serving low-income patients, while redistributing billions of dollars to hospitals that do not share the same safety-net and academic missions. These cuts threaten access to critical services made possible by the 340B program and will lead to worse health outcomes for patients.”

“Rather than strengthening and preserving safety net funding, CMS is instead prioritizing hospitals that do not serve the safety net and nodding to the pharmaceutical industry's interests,” AEH’s statement reads. “These cuts are landing at a time when essential hospitals and their mission are more important than ever, as millions of people risk losing their Medicaid coverage in the coming months.”

The Federation of American Hospitals, which represents for-profit hospitals that do not participate in 340B, struck a different tone, calling the rulemaking “a win for patients, taxpayers and the hospitals that communities depend on.”

“By bringing Medicare drug payments more in line with actual costs, this reform will lower seniors’ out-of-pocket expenses and redirect billions in Medicare dollars where they’re needed most—supporting access to care for patients served by small and rural hospitals across the country,” Charlene MacDonald, the group’s president and CEO, said in a statement. “We applaud the Administration for advancing a smarter, fairer approach to Medicare payment.”

Additionally, CMS finalized an increase in an annual OPPS conversion factor to non-drug items and services, speeding up the agency’s effort to offset a prior $7.8 billion recoupment to 340B hospitals it was forced to make after previously reducing 340B rates contrary to law. But while this accelerated payback—often described by non-340B hospitals as a clawback—was proposed as an increase from 0.5% to 3%, the final rule brings the conversion factor to 2%.

AHA Senior Vice President of Public Policy Analysis and Development Ashley Thompson described both 340B policy changes together as a “continued assault” on the subsidy program that “will further stress hospitals’ ability to care for their patients.” AAMC’s Jaffery said the combined policies’ impact “will be devastating to patients,” and that his group “remains committed to pursuing all available avenues to reverse these payment cuts.”

Further rankling the hospital industry was the final rule’s continued push toward site-neutral payment policy and a phase-out of the inpatient-only list.

For the former, the agency will apply Physician Fee Schedule payment rates for some imaging services to off-campus provider-based departments. In line with the proposed rule, CMS said it expects the plan to trigger first-year reductions in Medicare Part B expenditures and beneficiary cost-sharing obligations of $260 million and $70 million, while also reducing a market incentive for provider consolidation.

Meanwhile, CMS finalized its proposal to remove 647 services from the inpatient-only list, allowing them to be delivered and paid for in the lower-cost outpatient setting.

“Both policies are misguided,” AHA’s Thompson said, “and overlook the unique role hospital outpatient departments play in delivering care to patients in communities nationwide. Hospital outpatient departments treat sicker and more complex groups of patients than independent physician practices, including those with higher rates of disability and who are more likely to come from low-income and rural communities.”

CMS’ fact sheet on the 1,270-page annual rule also noted various changes to quality reporting programs for hospital outpatient departments and ASCs, a proposal to require prior authorization for eight botulinum toxin injection codes CMS said it has seen a jump in claim volume, and new permission for accreditation organizations to assess hospitals’ compliance with EMTALA (the Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act of 1986).

“CMS is committed to spending taxpayer funds wisely and efficiently, so [that] America’s seniors can continue getting the care they need,” CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., said in a release. “By right-sizing payments and rooting out waste, today’s reforms will drive affordability in Medicare for current beneficiaries while ensuring it will still be there to serve their children and grandchildren.”

#5695. Even California’s Biggest Ports Aren’t Betting On Hydrogen For Ships

California has been one of hydrogen’s most enthusiastic supporters for two decades. The state has subsidized hydrogen vehicles, backed refueling networks, supported fuel-cell buses and trucks, invested in hydrogen production and kept the technology prominent in its zero-emission transportation policies. Los Angeles and Long Beach, the two enormous ports that anchor America’s Pacific container trade, have been part of that enthusiasm. So when these ports produce a comprehensive assessment of future marine fuels and leave hydrogen out of their detailed deep-sea shipping plans, it deserves attention well beyond California.

The Clean Marine Fuel Feasibility Assessment, released in October, is the product of a substantial examination of shipping fleets, carrier preferences, fuel availability and infrastructure costs. The ports recommend developing commercial methanol bunkering demonstrations, continuing existing ship-to-ship LNG bunkering arrangements and avoiding major new fuel terminals until demand becomes credible. Hydrogen, the molecule that California has spent so much money promoting for transportation, did not make the cut for detailed quantitative deep-sea fuel planning.

This isn’t a state government announcing the end of hydrogen subsidies. It is arguably more revealing. Two commercially important institutions have examined what the ships serving them are likely to use, considered the infrastructure they would have to provide and declined to spend the next decade preparing a major hydrogen bunkering business.

California’s hydrogen story has repeatedly confused technical possibility with commercial demand. Fuel-cell passenger cars proved they could operate, but struggled with expensive fuel, unreliable stations and battery-electric competition. Hydrogen buses and trucks have faced many of the same issues, often compounded by the economics of supplying fuel to fleets. Ports have supported hydrogen demonstrations because eliminating diesel exhaust matters enormously to nearby communities, but a successful demonstration does not establish that the resulting system is the best commercial solution.

Deep-sea shipping adds a particularly difficult set of constraints. A container vessel requires immense amounts of energy over long voyages. Hydrogen’s low volumetric energy density, expensive handling and demanding onboard storage make the fuel system difficult to accommodate economically. The problem extends beyond the ship to production, transportation, storage and bunkering equipment. There is little reason for a port authority to build a hydrogen fuel network when shipping lines are not ordering a commercially significant fleet that would use it.

The ports’ survey reinforces the commercial judgment. Of 38 shipping lines contacted, 19 responded. Nine expressed varying degrees of interest or commitment concerning methanol, but only one did so for hydrogen. That is a survey of carrier intentions, rather than binding fuel contracts, and the researchers examined other evidence as well. Still, it is difficult to turn one interested carrier into a compelling investment case for expensive hydrogen infrastructure.

The contrast with methanol is instructive. Methanol is a liquid under ordinary conditions and fits into a mature global chemical-handling industry. Existing storage and bunkering equipment can be adapted instead of requiring an entirely new cryogenic or high-pressure fuel network. Long Beach is already offering a $1 million incentive for an initial commercial-scale methanol bunkering operation, an approach that can test operational feasibility without committing to an enormous permanent facility.

I have a personal interest in that choice because I had to correct my own shipping-fuel forecast. Last year, I published Mea Culpa: Biomethanol Will Be A Major Shipping Fuel. I had previously given too much weight to vegetable-oil-derived fuels for shipping and insufficient weight to aviation’s competition for those feedstocks. I had also underestimated how far cheaper batteries could displace marine fuel demand. My revised assessment favours electricity for inland and short-sea shipping, with sustainable biomethanol becoming a primary liquid fuel for the remaining deep-sea requirement. The ports’ decision is consistent with preparing infrastructure for that possibility, although it does not establish that their future fuel supplies will be renewable.

The distinction is important because methanol is not inherently a climate solution. It can be manufactured from natural gas, coal, biomass or electricity-based production pathways, and those routes have radically different greenhouse gas consequences. California’s ports can build a technically successful methanol bunkering service without achieving substantial shipping decarbonization if the fuel delivered is fossil-based. That question belongs alongside the commercial case, not behind it.

LNG presents another caution. The ports are accommodating existing LNG-capable ships without recommending major new shoreside LNG infrastructure. It is a conservative capital decision, although fossil LNG’s climate case remains weak when methane leakage and engine slip are included. Reductions in sulfur and particulate emissions are useful, but they are not the same as meaningful lifecycle greenhouse gas reductions.

The larger significance of the study is the change in what gets taken seriously. For years, California’s hydrogen ambitions helped keep the molecule at the centre of transportation discussions. At Los Angeles and Long Beach, the planning process has produced a different hierarchy. Existing demand and affordable infrastructure determine the near-term investment choices. Hydrogen enthusiasm has not produced enough evidence to justify a deep-sea bunkering buildout.

There are weaknesses in the ports’ assessment, including the separation between bunkering readiness and verified emissions reductions, and the question of how electrification will change future fuel demand. Those deserve more scrutiny than a short article can provide. But the decision to leave hydrogen outside detailed deep-sea fuel planning is already consequential. California’s most important maritime gateways have applied a commercial filter that much of the state’s transportation hydrogen strategy has resisted.

My full TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines the ports’ fuel research, infrastructure costs, commercial demand estimates and emissions evidence, including where the study’s conclusions are sound and where its assumptions need more scrutiny.

#5694. 1968 Chevy Camaro Convertible For Sale With 83,414 Miles Shown Brings Supercharged V8 To Play

Much to your chagrin, the powers that be at General Motors are not bringing back Chevrolet's Camaro anytime soon. For those of you who didn't buy enough of the new ones to let the bean counters sign off on the next generation of the muscle car, you only have yourself to blame — and you'll have to get one of the previous six generations. Instead of defaulting to a more recent year, though, why not go into the car's deep past and get a classic? Something like this first-generation Supercharged 383-Powered 1968 Chevrolet Camaro Convertible.

On offer with Bring a Trailer, this 1968 is a second-year model of the first-gen Camaro with a few upgrades. The engine was swapped in 2004 with a BluePrint Engines 383 cubic-inch stroker V8. That particular engine is a favorite engine among enthusiasts and to further capitalize on the power it provides, the engine was fitted with a ProCharger supercharger system.

Per the listing, that power is directed to a 3-speed automatic transmission and a limited-slip 10-bolt rear-end. A dyno sheet shows a peak output of 375 horsepower and 417 pound-feet of torque, a considerable improvement over an original 1968 Camaro SS convertible equipped with the 350, which had an output of 295 hp and 380 lb-ft of torque.

The original factory color, according to its Fisher body tag, was Seafrost Green, which was considered a rare color option, but it now wears an exterior coat of red paint. For the interior, the front buckets and rear bench seats are wrapped in black vinyl. The same goes for the convertible top. A "retro-look" stereo provides access to tunes.

It's important to note that this Camaro is back up on BaT after its June 2026 sale/no-sale. The auction ended with a sale price of $43,250, but it didn't go through because of an engine vibration issue, which has seemingly been solved here with a new harmonic balancer, flexplate, and starter. Also serviced at that time were the starter, fuel pump and regulator, tires, and the front brake components. This upgraded, flashy, chrome-laden ride currently shows 83k miles on the odometer, but the BaT listing says "total mileage unknown." It also comes with a clean Montana title.
