#5569. Ryan Serhant Reveals the Turning Point That Made Him a Real Estate Star—and How He Thinks Agents Can Cash In on AI

Before Ryan Serhant became a recognizable face in real estate, he was one of thousands of agents showing up to an open casting call—and declaring himself the best in the universe.

The opportunity would put him on “Million Dollar Listing” and turn him into what he described as a “walking billboard,” giving him a platform he was determined to make count.

Speaking at NAR NXT 2026 in New Orleans, Serhant reflected on that career-changing break, the relentless social media strategy that followed, and why he believes agents should now be looking to artificial intelligence to help build their businesses.

His message to agents navigating an uncertain market was straightforward: “Markets don’t dictate your income. They dictate your strategy.”

For Serhant, learning where to direct his energy was part of that process. He recalled spending too much time early in his career stressing about things he could not control, including what might happen in the months ahead.

Instead, he encouraged agents to focus on the work they can tackle now. The future will arrive regardless, and worrying about it does little to move a business forward.

"One of the mistakes in the beginning of my career was stressing about what I can't control," he said. Agents should "attack" what they can control "without worrying about the future."

Branding himself a "futurist," he added, “At the end of the day, no one knows what they are doing."

Serhant acknowledged that his first few years were difficult and suggested that getting started as an agent is even harder today. His own breakthrough came after he attended an open casting call for “Million Dollar Listing” in 2010, joining roughly 3,000 real estate agents in Times Square.

He recalled not fully knowing what he would be doing there. But when asked why he had come, he delivered an answer that left little room for self-doubt: “I’m the greatest real estate agent in the universe.”

Serhant revealed the season was filmed with four people, but only three made the cut.

Once the show aired, he recognized that the exposure had given him an opportunity to distinguish himself—and he felt compelled to capitalize on it.

“Once the show came out, I became a walking billboard,” he said.

He also acknowledged the role timing played in his rise. He was finding his footing professionally as both cable TV and social media offered opportunities to reach potential customers.

“I need to meet my customer where my customer is,” he said.

That approach led him to embrace Instagram in its early days, posting photographs of listings with himself in the images. He recalled posting every two to three hours, steadily building an audience that could become familiar with him before ever meeting him.

The goal was to establish a presence on people’s phones, creating recognition that could carry into an eventual conversation or business relationship.

Today, Serhant said, helping other agents succeed has become a source of excitement in its own right.

“It makes me tick. I enjoy it. I love it,” he said of teaching others.

Having encountered a wide range of challenges throughout his career, he described watching his agents win as the work that now gets him most excited.

He also emphasized his belief in investing in the future, describing Serhant’s mission as helping the world move forward.

For agents considering what that future looks like, artificial intelligence was a central part of his advice.

“The excitement within AI isn’t just language. It’s in creating work,” he said.

Serhant encouraged agents to identify administrative tasks that technology could reduce, freeing up time for the activities that depend on human connection and creativity.

“Humans should be doing only what humans do, which is meeting and creating,” he said.

He pointed to negotiation support and homeownership information as potential uses, while urging agents to think beyond individual tasks and consider how AI could help generate more business.

The measures that matter, he suggested, include increasing transactions per agent and improving gross profit. In that framing, the value of adopting AI lies in what it enables an agent to accomplish.

But he also shared an anecdote illustrating how the technology can influence a client’s decisions.

Serhant recalled a buyer pulling out of a $50 million deal after asking ChatGPT whether they were paying too much and receiving an affirmative answer.

The account underscored a challenge for agents: Clients can now arrive with AI-generated conclusions that affect their willingness to move forward with a purchase.

His advice was to use the technology as support in their own work.

Across his reflections on TV, social media, and AI, Serhant returned to the importance of approaching opportunities with a willingness to act.

“I learned that optimists are successful," he said.

#5568. Selling Your Home? What You Should Know About Price Cuts vs. Rate Buydowns.

In today’s market, a growing number of sellers are opting to do something called a price cut – especially when their house has been on the market for a while without any bites.

According to HousingWire Data as many as 4 in 10 (43%) sellers are going this route – that’s the highest it’s been in 4 years. But what if there’s another (potentially better option) for your bottom line? And it’s just as appealing, if not more so, to today’s buyers?

First, let’s set the stage on why some compromise may be necessary in today’s market.

In September, Redfin says there were 63% more sellers than buyers in the market. And with so many sellers active and relatively few buyers by comparison, those purchasers are realizing they have more power. And as mortgage rates continue to put a squeeze on their budgets, they’re leaning in and using it.

One of the most common negotiation points? The price.

That’s because they want to feel like they’re getting a deal and they want to see their monthly payment drop. And since buyers can’t control rates, the price feels like the most obvious lever to pull.

But the savviest sellers realize being flexible doesn’t always mean a lower price, paying for a buyer’s rate buydown might work better.

A buydown is money paid at closing to lower the buyer’s mortgage rate. When you pay it as the seller, you are paying some of the buyer’s interest ahead of time, so the buyer gets a lower rate and monthly payment. And that’s especially appealing to today’s buyers.

Temporary buydowns lower the rate for the first few years, then it goes back to the full rate. The more years a buydown covers, the more it costs. These work well for buyers who expect to refinance within a certain amount of time.

A permanent buydown lowers the rate for the whole loan. These are paid for with “discount points.” One point costs 1% of the loan. According to FICO, each point generally lowers the rate by about a quarter of a percent. This type of buydown works well for buyers who plan to stay in the home for a long time.

And here’s why these can be a win-win for both buyers and sellers. Rate buydowns help sellers stand out in a crowded market and they can have a bigger impact on your buyer than a price cut would.

Here’s an example to show you what that could look like.

Let’s say you’re willing to make a $10,000 concession to help get the deal done. Take a look at these three ways to spend that money and the impact they could have on a buyer’s $420,000, 30-year fixed loan at 7%:

It’s the same $10,000 from the seller. But a 2-1 buydown saves the buyer about eight times more each month in the first year.

And since most buyers shop by monthly payment, that’s what grabs their attention.

That’s what makes a rate buydown worth considering. Instead of reducing your asking price, you may be able to use that same money to have a bigger impact on your buyer’s monthly payments. And depending on what matters most to that buyer, the immediate savings could be more appealing than a price reduction.

The key is working with your agent and the buyer’s lender to compare the options and see which one makes the most sense.

Loan programs cap how much a seller can pay toward a buyer’s costs.

Money toward buydowns doesn’t limit what else a buyer may ask a seller to pay for. Buyers may still ask for repairs or other concessions.

Putting the buydown offer in your listing lets agents and buyers know it’s an option.

Your agent can run scenarios on buydowns and other costs of selling in advance so you’re prepared when an offer comes in.

As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Home sellers need to be realistic about local market conditions, which could require price discounts and other incentives to attract buyers.”

And sellers who offer solutions like buydowns can make meaningful impact where home buyers need it most: in their wallets.

When you're looking for ways to make your house more appealing to buyers, a price reduction isn't your only option. A mortgage rate buydown could help a buyer save more each month, especially in the early years of their loan.Talk to your agent or a trusted lender which incentives could make the biggest difference for buyers in our market, while still protecting your bottom line.

#5567. ‘We Used House-Sitting To Plan Our Cross-Country Move—Until Life Got In the Way’

When Rebecca Dharmapalan and her partner began planning their big move from Oakland, CA, to Brooklyn, NY, they wanted to get a real feel for the neighborhoods before committing, so they turned to house-sitting to test-drive their future life.

"A cross-country move is a big financial bet, and I didn’t want us to make it on a hunch," Dharmapalan tells Realtor.com®.

The 30-year-old Californian had lived in New York City before, but her partner, Nekhi, had visited only once and was hesitant to uproot his life on the West Coast.

Dharmapalan concluded that the best way to get Nekhi on board would be to live in the Big Apple for some time, trying different neighborhoods on for size. But doing so through conventional routes, such as sublets and hotels, would have cost the young couple thousands of dollars a month.

"And every dollar spent trying out the city was a dollar we wouldn’t have for the real move," notes Dharmapalan.

Their workaround was TrustedHousesitters—a global pet-sitting platform operating in 180 countries. The online exchange connects pet owners with pet and house sitters.

Both homeowners and sitters pay an annual subscription fee, ranging from $129 to $259, to access the marketplace, but no money changes hands for individual stays.

As part of the arrangement, homeowners get vetted in-home pet care while traveling, and sitters get free lodging for weeks or months at a time.

"The homeowner can go away with the peace of mind knowing their pet's been looked after by a sitter who's doing it for love rather than money,  and the sitter can enjoy a unique homestay and the companionship of pets," TrustedHousesitters CEO Mathew Prior tells Realtor.com.

"That's probably what makes it such an attractive opportunity for people who are looking to relocate. And indeed, a lot of our sitters, anecdotally we hear, are actually using the platform for that."

Deciding where to live in New York City carries heavy financial stakes. As of September, the median monthly asking rent in the borough stood at $4,197, up nearly 5% from a year ago, according to the latest Realtor.com quarterly rent report.

To afford the typical rental home without becoming house-poor, tenants in Brooklyn would need to earn a gross household income of nearly $12,500 per month, or $167,880 per year.

For comparison, the median asking rent in the San Francisco-Oakland area, where Dharmapalan is from, was just over $3,000 a month in September.

Dharmapalan and her partner had done sits through TrustedHousesitters in the past during brief getaways in California, and now they decided to use house-sitting as a budget-friendly way to live like locals in different parts of Brooklyn in preparation for a relocation.

Over the course of several months, Dharmapalan and her partner booked two extended sits. The first was in Fort Greene, where they looked after a Chihuahua mix named Slug. The second was in Crown Heights, where their four-legged charges included two dogs, Ziggy and Venus, and two cats, Moon and Cosmo.

"House-sitting let us really sink into a neighborhood for weeks. Then, we were able to move on without a major financial hit," says Dharmapalan. "Our total travel cost was less than half of what a single month of accommodations would have run. We came out of it with our savings intact and had decided on the Crown Heights neighborhood."

Before arriving, the couple favored Fort Greene, which had everything they wanted on paper. But living in the community and speaking to longtime residents made them realize that it was not the right place for them.

"Crown Heights was the opposite," she says. "From the moment we arrived, it felt right, and we decided that’s where we wanted to live. It reminded us of the cultural richness and diversity we love in Oakland.

"Every afternoon we walked Venus and Ziggy to Brower Park and watched Shoot Hoops Not Guns, a youth basketball and violence prevention organization, running games while the whole neighborhood hummed around us, which is something you don’t get from a listing or a weekend visit."

The 30-year-old is convinced that if she and her partner came to town for a hotel stay, they could not have gotten to know the two neighborhoods as well as they did through house-sitting.

"With a hotel, you are just a visitor. With a sit, you have a set of keys, a real neighborhood, and a pet who needs walking at least twice a day," says Dharmapalan. "Those walks turned into real conversations with longtime residents.

"In Fort Greene, neighbors told us how much the area had changed with gentrification. That generational perspective was one of the most valuable parts of the experience, and we only got it because we were there long enough, and walking a local dog, to earn those conversations."

While pet-sitting in Crown Heights, the couple found a Bengali corner cafe that became part of Dharmapalan's morning routine, with hot samosas and chai on the way to the gym, and they learned which bodega made the best breakfast sandwiches.

"We lived on a normal budget, too, including groceries, eating out locally once or twice a week, and public transit," says Dharmapalan. "That told us far more about what life there would actually cost and feel like than a vacation would."

Beyond picking a neighborhood, living inside someone's home clarified the couple's property wishlist, from carefully chosen wallpaper to hardwood floors, walkability, access to green spaces, and a sense of community.

According to Prior, Dharmapalan's experience is representative of how thousands of TrustedHousesitters clients anecdotally are using pet-sitting to test housing markets before deciding where to rent or buy.

"That means you're less likely to make an expensive mistake," says the company CEO.

Ultimately, the Oakland couple had to pull the plug on their planned Brooklyn relocation after Dharmapalan's partner got a job offer in Pasadena, CA, keeping them on the West Coast.

However, Dharmapalan views their Brooklyn house-sitting experiment as an undeniable win for them.

"It honestly makes me even more glad we tested Brooklyn the way we did," she says. "We could’ve spent thousands on sublets or hotels, or rushed into a lease or a purchase and lost that money. Because we house-sat, we got a real feel for life in Fort Greene and Crown Heights without ruining our savings."

Dharmapalan and Nekhi are now using TrustedHousesitters to look for their next home in Los Angeles.

Founded in 2010 in the U.K., TrustedHousesitters now boasts 240,000 members worldwide. Prior, the CEO, says that the platform is in high demand among two distinct demographics: Gen Z and young millennials looking to relocate to a new city for work and potentially hoping to purchase their first house, along with empty nesters eyeing a change of scenery.

The average house-sitting stay lasts 10 days, and it's common for sitters to move between different neighborhoods within the same market, often gravitating toward lesser-known corners and suburbs.

"What you get is a real immersion in a local area," says Prior. "You're staying in a house, it's occupied, and with the community around you. So you're not just seeing the center of the city, the glamorous bits, you're seeing the real city."

Seattle, San Francisco, Portland, OR, Denver, and Brooklyn currently stand out as the five busiest house-sitting hubs in the U.S., according to TrustedHousesitters' data.

Meanwhile, markets seeing the fastest growth in bookings include Santa Monica, CA, Minneapolis, and Philadelphia.

"For people who are looking at a new area, you can't go for two nights and expect to understand it," contends Prior. " You have to spend some time."

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5566. How Traton Homes Is Designing for Multigenerational Living

The Presley model's guest suite at The Tillery in Marietta, Georgia.

Today’s buyers are asking their homes to work harder over time. At Traton Homes, main-level guest suites have become an important part of that flexibility, providing space for overnight visitors today and potentially aging parents, caregivers, or other family members in the future.

Director of design Angi Sago explains how evolving household needs are influencing the builder’s approach to floor plans, entertaining spaces, and long-term livability.

Traton offers a variety of floor plans featuring a guest suite on the main. What does that tell you about how buyer priorities are changing?

Buyers are increasingly looking for homes that offer flexibility to accommodate their families’ changing needs. A private guest suite on the main level provides a comfortable space for visiting family and friends, but it also offers the opportunity to accommodate aging parents, whether for extended visits or as a more permanent living arrangement in the future. It’s a feature that adds both immediate convenience and long-term value.

Who are these suites designed for; aging parents, adult children, long-term guests, or a combination?

The Presley model home at The Tillery in Marietta, Georgia.

While these suites certainly provide a wonderful space for overnight guests, we find that many buyers are thinking about aging parents and the possibility of multigenerational living. Having a private guest bedroom with en-suite bath on the main level gives homeowners peace of mind knowing they have a comfortable and accessible space for loved ones, whether they are visiting or eventually become part of the household.

How has demand for multigenerational or guest-friendly living influenced Traton’s floor plans over the past few years?

Traton has recognized the appeal of main-level guest suites for many years, and we’ve incorporated them into our home designs for quite some time. These floor plans have consistently been popular because they offer homeowners flexibility in how they use their space. As families’ needs continue to evolve, we believe this versatility is becoming even more valuable to today’s buyers.

What separates a well-designed guest suite from simply putting an extra bedroom and bathroom on the first floor?

Are buyers looking for spaces that can change purpose over time, such as moving from a guest suite to an aging-in-place bedroom or caregiver space?

Absolutely. Flexibility is one of the greatest advantages of a main-level guest suite. A space that initially serves as a bedroom for visiting friends and family can eventually accommodate an aging parent or caregiver. Buyers appreciate knowing their home can adapt to different stages of life without requiring significant changes to the floor plan.

Beyond the guest suite, what design features are becoming more important for homeowners who regularly entertain or host overnight visitors?

Spaces that make entertaining easier and more enjoyable continue to be popular. Butler’s pantries are especially appealing because they can double as a beverage or bar area while providing additional storage and serving space. Keeping rooms are another desirable feature, offering a comfortable, informal gathering area where family and friends can relax and spend time together. Buyers appreciate having spaces that encourage connection while allowing for different types of entertaining.

The Abney model at Linden Grove in Powder Springs, Georgia.

Traton’s floor plans with owner’s suites are offered at various price points. How do expectations for hosting and flexible living differ between by price point, if at all?

Interestingly, we see many of the same priorities across price points. Regardless of price point, homeowners want comfortable, functional spaces where they can welcome family and friends. The primary difference is often the amount of space available for entertaining and the additional features a larger home can accommodate. While buyers of our more expansive homes may have more gathering areas, the desire for a private guest suite and flexible living spaces is equally important to buyers of our more moderately sized plans.

Are buyers willing to give up square footage elsewhere in the home to get a main-level guest suite, larger pantry, loft, or other flexible space?

We find that a main-level guest suite is typically a feature buyers either prioritize from the beginning or don’t necessarily need. Rather than sacrificing square footage elsewhere, buyers tend to gravitate toward floor plans that already incorporate the spaces that matter most to their lifestyle. That’s why offering a variety of thoughtfully designed floor plans is so important. It allows buyers to select a home that best fits their individual needs and preferences.

Looking ahead, how do you expect changing family structures and the way people live together to influence Traton’s next generation of floor plans?

As housing costs continue to put pressure on household budgets, we anticipate that multigenerational living will become an important consideration for home buyers. Sharing a home can offer financial advantages while allowing families to stay connected and support one another. We believe buyers will continue to place a premium on flexible floor plans that provide both shared gathering spaces and private retreats, allowing multiple generations to live comfortably under one roof. At Traton, our goal is to continue designing homes that reflect how families live today while anticipating how their needs may change in the years ahead.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5565. EXCLUSIVE: Real Estate Leader Shelton Wilder Reveals the Design Trends Set To Define Luxury Living in 2027

Real estate powerhouse Shelton Wilder has revealed that luxury homes in 2027 could be getting a warmer, more personal makeover—with an emphasis on spaces that feel as good to live in as they look.

From richer wood finishes to rooms designed for relaxation, Wilder opens up about what she expects buyers to seek in homes while speaking exclusively to Realtor.com®.

For homeowners preparing to sell, however, that doesn't necessarily mean taking on an expensive renovation to keep up.

Instead, her predictions point to a preference for thoughtful design, practical amenities, and improvements that suit the property itself.

When it comes to the look of luxury homes in the coming year, Wilder anticipates a continued focus on natural finishes and enduring appeal.

“We're going to see luxury homes continue moving toward warmth, character, and timeless design. Buyers want homes that feel beautiful but also comfortable and livable,” she says.

“We're seeing more natural materials, beautiful wood tones, interesting stone, layered textures, and architectural details that give a home personality.”

That interest in distinctive finishes comes with an eye toward longevity. Buyers aren't simply looking for a space that reflects the latest aesthetic, according to Wilder; they're considering how well its design will age.

“They are becoming much more thoughtful about quality and craftsmanship. They want something that feels special, but they also don't want a home that's going to look dated in five years,” she explains.

“For me, the best luxury design isn't about following every trend. It's about creating a home that feels authentic to its architecture and will stand the test of time.”

Wilder also sees room for more individuality, although she cautions against interpreting that shift as a wholesale embrace of bright colors.

"I don't necessarily think that means everyone suddenly wants brightly colored walls or really bold interiors. I think buyers are craving more personality and warmth,” she says of the move away from neutral, minimalist spaces.

For some homes, that personality may come through in the finishes and fixtures rather than a dramatic change in wall color.

“There's a difference between a home that's neutral and one that feels completely devoid of personality.”

The key, in her view, is to let the property's architecture guide those choices instead of applying the same look to every home.

“I always tell sellers that design should complement the architecture of the home. A Spanish home should feel different from a midcentury modern, and both should feel different from a contemporary coastal property,” she says.

“In 2027, we'll continue to see more individuality in design, but the homes that really resonate with buyers will still feel cohesive and timeless.”

Wilder's outlook extends beyond a home's appearance. She expects buyers to place importance on features that fit their routines, whether that means room to entertain or somewhere quiet to work.

“Buyers are prioritizing how a home actually supports their lifestyle. Beautiful finishes are wonderful, but functionality is just as important,” she says.

In Los Angeles, that includes outdoor spaces that serve as an extension of the home.

Dedicated spaces for exercise and relaxation are also drawing attention

“Wellness is another big one. We're seeing more interest in home gyms, saunas, cold plunges, spalike bathrooms, and spaces dedicated to health and relaxation,” she says.

But the wish list isn't limited to amenities that might headline a listing. Wilder also highlights the value of a layout that works and enough space to accommodate daily life.

“Luxury buyers are looking for homes that make their everyday lives easier, not just homes that look impressive in photographs.”

For homeowners hoping to attract those buyers in 2027, Wilder recommends considering smaller improvements before committing to a major project.

“I always tell sellers that you don't necessarily need to spend a fortune to make a significant impact. Sometimes the smartest updates are fresh paint, updated lighting, refinished floors, beautiful landscaping, and professional staging,” she says.

A costly remodel, particularly one tailored to the seller's personal preferences, may not deliver the desired result.

“Where I see sellers get into trouble is spending a lot of money on highly personalized renovations right before listing. A major kitchen or bathroom remodel can be incredibly expensive, and there's no guarantee the next buyer is going to have the same taste,” Wilder explains.

Her advice is to assess the likely audience for the home before deciding where to spend.

“Before making those investments, I would absolutely talk to a real estate professional who understands your specific neighborhood and buyer pool,” she says.

“The goal is to make strategic improvements that will appeal to the widest group of qualified buyers and help maximize your return.”

Asked which emerging Los Angeles design trend could spread nationally in 2027, Wilder points to spaces that help residents unwind and recover.

“The biggest one is the integration of wellness into everyday home design,” she says. The significance lies in how homeowners use those features as part of their routines.

“What's interesting to me is that these features are becoming part of how people actually live, rather than just amenities to show off when entertaining,” she explains.

“That's going to continue spreading across the country because people are increasingly thinking about their homes as places where they can recharge, take care of themselves, and spend meaningful time with family.”

“Indoor-outdoor living continues to be huge in Los Angeles. Buyers love a great backyard, a pool, covered entertaining areas, and spaces where they can really enjoy the California sun year-round,” Wilder explains.

#5562. This $9.5 Million Pasadena Estate Looks 100 Years Old—Until You Step Inside

A vine-covered Mediterranean estate in Pasadena, CA that looks as though it has stood for a century or more, is actually just 16 years old, and it/s now on the market for $9.5 million.

Located at 1466 San Pasqual Street, the home was designed by architect John Barber to blend in with its neighbors—landmark homes that are roughly six times its age.

The home is represented by Brent Chang of Compass.

Behind automatic driveway gates, the exterior borrows many of the period architectural elements used by Wallace Neff and Marston & Van Pelt, defining names in Southern California’s early 20th-century residential architecture. The result was convincing enough that the house was once the lone new builds featured on a Pasadena Heritage tour of Spanish Revival homes from the 1920s and '30s.

Inside, however, the floor plan is decidedly modern. The main house offers 9- to 11-foot ceilings throughout, a two-story entry, a two-story family room and two staircases. French doors open to outdoor patios and a fireplace.

The open kitchen includes a breakfast area, pantry and butler’s pantry, while a library features its own fireplace and bar. There are two primary suites, each with a walk-in closet and private water closet, plus three additional suites and upper-level laundry.

The estate last sold in 2015 for $6.4 million, according to property records. Two years later, a 2,120-square-foot pool house was added. It includes two bedrooms, two bathrooms, a kitchen and a lounge with a wall of stacking glass doors that opens to the pool and spa.

The pool house’s lower level holds a game room with an automatic screen and projector, cubby bunk beds, a bathroom, laundry and separate front and rear entrances.

All together, the property spans 9,150 square feet with seven bedrooms and eight bathrooms on a 0.73 acre lot.

The grounds include a circular drive, three automatic gates, multiple lawns, gardens and patios. A secure rear driveway leads to a secondary motor court with a garage that fits four cars.

And behind all the period details are a set of thoroughly modern systems, including 400-amp electrical service, copper plumbing, a whole-house water filter, a fire sprinkler system and two water heaters which were installed in 2022.

#5561. Kyndryl shares surge 30% on hyperscaler-related revenue growth

Shares of Kyndryl Holdings Inc. jumped 30% today after it reported better-than-expected earnings for the second quarter of its 2027 fiscal year.

Kyndryl generated $3.9 billion in sales during the three months ended Sept. 30. That represents a 1.9% decrease from a year earlier, but the company still managed to top the consensus estimate by about $50 million. It attributed the top-line surprise to its Kyndryl Consult business.

Kyndryl, a former IBM Corp. unit, once generated nearly all its revenue from managing other companies’ technology infrastructure. In 2022, it launched Kyndryl Consult to take on more strategic, higher-margin professional services deals.

The unit’s revenue grew 4.2% year-over-year in the second quarter. Kyndryl didn’t share a specific quarterly revenue number, but divulged that the unit earned a total of $3.6 billion over the past 12 months.

Kyndryl Consult’s signings, a measure of future revenue, jumped 19% over the past year. That momentum may have contributed to the company’s stock rally today.

Many of the projects that Kyndryl Consult takes on involve artificial intelligence. The unit can help customers build AI agent ensembles and set up training data generation pipelines. Additionally, it can advise clients about business decisions such as how they should allocate their AI budgets.

Kyndryl offers a software platform called Bridge to companies that buy its AI services. It enables AI agents to access business data from an organization’s internal systems. Additionally, Bridge monitors those agents to ensure they adhere to safety requirements.

The public cloud is another major focus of Kyndryl’s growth efforts. The company’s hyperscale-related revenue topped $500 million in the second quarter, which amounts to a 27% year-over-year increase.

“Strong signings and continued growth in Kyndryl Consult and hyperscaler-related revenue reinforce our confidence in our fiscal 2027 outlook,” said Kyndryl Chief Executive Officer Martin Schroeter. “Our performance reflects demand for Kyndryl’s AI-led modernization capabilities and deep mission-critical expertise that help customers evolve their complex technology environments, strengthen cybersecurity and achieve measurable business outcomes.”

The company delivered an adjusted net income of $92 million, which breaks down to 42 cents per share. Analysts expected 41 cents per share. The sum excludes a $38 million workforce reduction charge the company took in the second quarter. It’s part of a broader cost-cutting initiative that is set to save up to $500 million annually starting from Kyndryl’s 2028 fiscal year.

For the current fiscal year, the company is forecasting an adjusted pretax income of $600 million to $700 million. Kyndryl expects its revenue to be flat or increase by up to 2%.

#5560. ‘It’s Insane’: Building Tech CEO Slams L.A.’s Return to Wood Framing After Deadly Wildfires

The country—maybe even the world—is at a crossroads in building construction due to climate change, and one CEO is disappointed about where things are going.

"Ninety-five percent of this community is rebuilding with wood," Ken Calligar says of Los Angeles County, which still trying to rebuild after the devastating 2025 Palisades and Alatadena wildfires. "It's insane."

"Unfortunately, that means they have designed in the next disaster," the founder and CEO of building technology company RSG-3D tells Realtor.com. "Builders say 'If we have to design in resiliency into a house, then no one can afford the house.' That's just baloney."

A former Wall Street investment banker who acquired disaster-resilient technology manufacturer Insteel Panelmex in 2018, Calligar has spent the past decade trying to get people to build differently. (The difference between "resilient" and "resistant" is complex, but Calligar prefers the term "resilient.")

Renamed RSG 3-D, his company manufactures framing panels made of steel wire and expanded polystyrene wrapped in concrete skins that can be molded into any shape and are practically indestructible—impervious to hurricanes, earthquakes, and fires.

Unsurprisingly, Calligar's firm has been busy in Los Angeles since the fires—but not busy enough as far as he is concerned.

He points out that not only are most destroyed residential buildings in the area being rebuilt with flammable materials—but they are now larger and closer together, increasing the chances that a conflagration can spread from one home to the next.

"A six-year-old could have said this wasn't a good idea," he says. "These towns are so vulnerable, they have no idea. To me, it's so obvious what the solution is."

In 2011, Calligar was doing a deep dive into building technologies for a start-up he was advising. The start-up didn't last, but Calligar's intense interest in creating buildings that could survive disasters did.

"Since the 1980, we have had decades of increasing frequency of natural disasters and the costs have gone up dramatically," he says. "In the 1980s, there averaged about four natural disasters a year. In the 2020s, we’re averaging about 23."

Beyond fires, there is an increasing frequency of other types of natural disasters—hurricanes, floods, tornadoes, shoreline erosion, extreme heat and cold. According to the 2026 Realtor.com Housing and Climate Risk Report, 23.1% of U.S. homes are vulnerable to severe or extreme climate risk from wind, flood, or wildfire, culminating in $11.2 trillion in risk exposure.

Then there is the human compulsion to build in risk-prone zones. "We like our views, our mountains and our seashores, and the population has been building in more vulnerable areas," says Calligar.

Homeowners are already paying the price in higher HOA fees, rising insurance premiums, elevated mortgage delinquency rates, and even in the inability to find insurance coverage at all.

"When disaster strikes, shoppers retrench, but the effect is short-lived," says the report. "Following the January 2025 LA wildfires, buyer interest in high-risk homes dropped 10%, yet fully recovered within one month."

"Waterfront access, mountain views, and river retreats matter more than the risk that comes with them."

Another alarming report says that California could lose up to 75% of its beaches either seasonally or permanently by 2100. Highly developed areas face "especially severe losses."

Calligar agrees—not only that homeowners want what they want and what they want isn't always good—but that builders keep making the same builds that have proven ineffective and even downright dangerous.

He notes one destroyed home in L.A. that burned down again during its rebuild. Someone had broken into the construction site to steal copper wire and sparked a fire. According to Calligar, the home was "all wood framed."

"The U.S. residential world is the only technology that hasn’t changed in the last half century," he adds. "It's actually gone backwards. The wood is worse, the productivity of the workers is worse, the quality of the builds is worse."

"If you refuse to learn, you're going to get the lesson again."

Some people, however, have learned. Jonathan Scott of the Property Brothers led the rebuilding of fiancée actress Zooey Deschanel's childhood home in Pacific Palisades. The 100-year-old Spanish Revival house was rebuilt to look exactly as it had before the fires—only this time it's using RSG 3-D technology.

"When Zooey’s parents walk in, this will feel like the original home," the HGTV reality star told KTLA. "All of these things we’ve thought about to make sure this house never ever burns down again. They’ll never have to go through what they went through last January."

"He is not connected to us financially," Calligar stresses of Scott's plentiful touting of RSG-3D technology in the press. "He's just a very happy client."

Calligar, who is currently working on about a dozen Los Angeles building projects, has three times that number scheduled for next year. "The demand is off the charts," he says. "It's a question of how much we can handle. We're still a small company, we can’t be everywhere."

Nor are his projects limited to L.A. Partners are using the technology in six states and in 20 international countries.

He says the notion that it costs significantly more to build a resilient home are a myth—and that using RSG-3D is "cost competitive against inferior building systems." Plus, additional costs can usually be absorbed with savings in energy and operating costs, and lower insurance premiums.

"You pull out way ahead, we've done the math," he says.

Another bonus? Homes can be built faster using the technology, since the panels are easy to erect, and don't require heavy machinery. Those concerned about aesthetics need not be, says Calligar. The panels are architecturally flexible, and can be curved or domed for any shape.

"Because of the strength of the system, you can do a lot more architecturally than you can with wood," he says. "We've got a lot of cool architecture."

Those sold on the idea of a disaster-resilient house can get it done with the firm's "trained ecosystem" of builders, architects, and engineers.

He compares RSG-3D technology to vaccines, and how they extended the human lifecycle.

"What we're trying to do is eradicate the diseases that are harming everyone," he says. "And extend the [building] lifecycle by centuries, by selecting the right materials."

He points to the Egyptian pyramids, erected with practically indestructible limestone and granite, and still standing tall after 4,500 years.

"If they'd done that with wood, we wouldn’t even know about them, they'd be muck in the sand," he says. "It's a good lesson in doing things right."

#5558. Phaze raises $8.75M to give AI agents remote access to powerful workstations

If autonomous artificial intelligence agents are really going to become the future of the enterprise then they’re going to need to have a computer of their own so they can get on with their work without disturbing anyone else.

The founders of the remote desktop firm Parsec Technologies Inc. have come up with a new offering that’s designed to give those agents the computer access they need. Their new startup is called Phaze Inc., and it has just launched its offering after raising $8.75 million in seed funding from Andreessen Horowitz. Today’s round also saw participation from Index, NextView, Makers and Lerer Hippeau.

Phaze has developed a high-performance remote desktop platform that’s designed to accommodate both humans and AI agent workers, giving them access to powerful computers, including high-end workstations. With its platform, those users can control a distant workstation with the same low-latency responsiveness and visual fidelity they’d get if they were accessing hardware locally.

The startup says it’s trying to solve a couple of glaring efficiency problems at many enterprises. One issue is the emergence of computer-use agents that like to hijack worker’s screens while automating mundane business tasks, reducing human productivity.

Another challenge is that many enterprises invest in powerful workstations capable of rendering complex 3D graphics and compiling massive codebases that can cost upwards of $10,000. Those machines are needed, but many information technology departments tend to have a policy of assigning one machine to each employee, which means that expensive hardware is often left sitting idle if that person goes out for lunch, sits in a meeting or takes a few days off.

Phaze’s solution is to transform those workstations into a shared pool of elastic compute, allowing anyone at an organization to access it via its proprietary low-latency streaming technology when they need it. This streaming tech is backed by a specially developed Model Context Protocol server that allows computer use agents to log into and operate expensive workstations the same way a human employee would.

The result: Instead of working exclusively through expensive and brittle application programming interfaces, agents can access a computer directly and navigate its operating system, launch applications and get work done.

Phaze co-founder and Chief Executive Benjy Boxer said the platform also supports human-to-agent collaboration, so they can work together to get more complex tasks done. For instance, an automated IT support bot might work to diagnose problems when new tickets are created, and then pass the session to a human engineer if the solution is more nuanced than what it’s authorized to do by itself.

“The computer sitting on your desk shouldn’t determine what compute you can access,” Boxer said. “People need powerful workstations to do their jobs, and now AI agents need computers they can actually operate. We’re building the access layer that lets either one connect to the machine they need, wherever it happens to be.”

By transforming expensive workstations into shared infrastructure, administrators can assign their computing resources dynamically to whoever needs access as people’s and agent’s workflows fluctuate. The workstations themselves can be sat on a desk, installed in a data center, or locked away in a cupboard. Wherever they’re located, organizations will be able to get maximum efficiency out of them.

Phaze’s job now is to convince enterprises of the benefits of its platform, and Boxer said the money from today’s round will be used to accelerate its go-to-market plans and onboard new customers. The startup will also look to expand its engineering team and develop more features.

Andreessen Horowitz General Partner Martin Casado think Phaze is likely to see a lot of interest in its remote access platform, because workstations are too expensive to be left sitting idle for hours at a time. “Phaze is turning those machines into shared infrastructure for people and AI agents,” he said. “Benjy and the team have been building in this space for more than a decade and they bring that experience to a new era of remote access and machine management.”

#5557. Ocient raises $100 million as agentic AI drives growth in large-scale analytics

Ocient Inc., the maker of a speedy data analytics platform, today said it has raised $100 million in a Series C funding to expand its agentic artificial intelligence analytics business.

That business is fueled by growing demand from national security organizations and telecommunications providers seeking to analyze massive datasets without sampling. The new round brings the Chicago-based company’s total funding to $260 million.

Ocient said it expects revenue to more than triple in its current fiscal year, which ends in January, after doubling revenue the previous year. The company said the new financing will accelerate delivery of its OcientAIQ Solutions, which enable AI agents and human analysts to query petabyte-scale datasets.

Chief Executive John Morris said much of the growth is coming from new customers in national security and telecommunications, particularly organizations using the platform to consolidate cybersecurity information.

“They’ve been accustomed to having to sample data coming off the network,” Morris said. “They don’t have anything that can handle the ingest rates, nor that can store at an affordable price tens of petabytes of data.”

Ocient’s original business focused on high-performance analytics, but the emergence of AI agents has expanded its potential market. Increasingly, software agents rather than human analysts are querying its systems, driving higher utilization and creating demand for more comprehensive datasets.

The OcientAIQ Unified Data Platform combines ingestion, analytics, governance and agent orchestration. Its architecture minimizes data movement and uses forward error correction instead of conventional replication to provide data protection with reduced storage overhead.

“The architecture is designed not to move data around constantly as most architectures do, and to have nothing replicated,” Morris said.

The company competes with Snowflake Inc., Databricks Inc. and open-source analytics implementations, although its technology frequently complements existing platforms rather than replacing them, the CEO said.

Cybersecurity has emerged as a particularly promising market. Ocient provides the underlying data infrastructure that enables security tools and AI agents to analyze network activity across complete historical datasets, potentially identifying threats that conventional sampling would miss.

However, Morris said the company isn’t positioned as a cybersecurity tool. “We don’t do the detection algorithms and the sort of things that the companies in that space do,” Morris said.

Government and defense customers account for a substantial portion of Ocient’s business. The company recently established a dedicated national security subsidiary to serve those markets.

Morris said the new funding should be sufficient to help Ocient reach breakeven, although he declined to provide a timetable. Ocient plans to direct much of the investment toward hiring sales and customer delivery personnel while continuing engineering development.

The company is also seeing increasing demand for on-premises deployments as customers seek greater control over costs and sensitive information. “Most of our opportunities now are on-prem because they’re either repatriating for cost reasons or for data sovereignty and data protection issues,” Morris said.

The company is also looking to expand geographically, particularly in Europe, Asia-Pacific and Latin America, while pursuing additional cybersecurity customers.

The round was co-led by Boka Capital Ltd. and OCA Ventures LLC, with participation from previous investors Greycroft Partners LLC, In-Q-Tel Inc., Blue Bear Capital LLC, Buoyant Ventures Management LLC, PSP Partners LLC’s PSP Growth fund and Pritzker Group Venture Capital LLC.

#5556. A Former 1900s Lakeside Resort in Georgia Is for Sale as an $8.85 Million Private Retreat

Owning waterfront property is one thing. Owning the entire lake is another.

The lake, created from a dam on Ichawaynochaway Creek, is just part of the 1,442-acre property in Leary, GA listed for $8.85 million.

"When you're on the water, it's about 250 acres of private water in this famous mill pond. You own the whole [thing]. You own everything," explains listing agent Jon Kohler with Jon Kohler Associates.

“When you're out in a boat, you're not used to being the only one in this enormous lake. It probably takes five or six hours to go around the whole thing. It’s huge.”

“It's just fascinating. There's really nothing else like it, nor can there ever be again,” Kohler says. “You control it. You're the only boat that's able to duck hunt, fish, there.”

Cordray's Mill was once a resort property with a dance hall, swimming lake, and more, dating back to the early 1900s and continuing at least through the 1960s.

“There are a couple of remnant guest homes from the era when it was a resort, it was one of the first resorts in Georgia,” he says. “People would come from all over for events and whatnot.”

One structure is a converted church that is now a four bedroom and 1.5 bathroom house, in addition other living spaces.

“There's a house back where the mill pond house used to stand. There's a house on the lake, but back during its heyday, there were all types of structures, stores, shops, everything,” Kohler says.

The two houses have a total of six bedrooms and two bathrooms.

Another structure is a converted grain silo with one bedroom and a bathroom.

“It's one of those great ideas that not many people are able to pull off because the walls are rounded. It’s a really quaint little home.”

But the draw isn’t all of the places for people to stay, it’s about the activities.

“My favorite thing is the diversity of the habitats. You have almost every great habitat that Southwest Georgia has, but on one property,” Kohler explains, adding there is irrigated farmland and timberland in addition to the lake and waterfront.

The trophy whitetail deer make the property something special.

“I see it being owned by somebody that wants something that no one else has, which is the diversity and really the trophy deer hunting and the trophy deer habitat,” he says.

“Just a wildness factor that most places don't offer. [The perfect buyer is] somebody that really just wants to have the best of the best trophy whitetail, a lot of turkeys, and top it off with waterfowl, in an abundance greater than what most places offer.”

The property could also meet another need, a social storm property, which is a term Kohler trademarked several years ago.

“We recognized a trend that people were buying land for the lack of better word in case s**t hit the fan,” he said with a laugh, comparing the term to a prepper's property.

“This property is an ideal social storm property as well as a legacy sporting estate. I see most of these great places, but I had no idea a place like that existed. It's like a unicorn.

"You have 250 acres of water backed up in one of the largest private lakes in southeast United States all to yourself.”

Tiffani Sherman is an experienced freelance writer based in the Tampa, Florida area who covers real estate, personal finance, travel, and more for a variety of print and online publications. #5555. IBM, AMD and Oak Ridge join forces to launch quantum computing error-correction platform

IBM Corp., Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and the Quantum Science Center at Oak Ridge National Laboratory today announced a new quantum error-correction platform that integrates quantum and high-performance computing.

Gaining high performance and correctness in quantum computing requires protecting quantum information from noise. In many cases, researchers have paired quantum computers with classical computers to achieve superior performance for running industry-relevant problems. The challenge today is scaling up these advances with classical computing.

Today’s physical quantum qubits make errors roughly once every few hundred operations. Without correction, errors compound rapidly, rendering long or complex calculations completely untenable. Game-changing algorithms such as Shor’s algorithm for factoring or for molecular-scale simulations in chemistry require billions of error-free operations.

This launch uses a co-design platform for quantum error correction using IBM’s quantum computers, including the 120-qubit Nighthawk with ORNL’s Umbra High-Performance Computing system powered by AMD’s Instinct MI355X graphics processing units and 5th Gen EPYC central processing units.

“ORNL’s strength in high-performance computing, combined with the expertise of our QSC partners – like IBM and AMD – creates an opportunity to push the boundaries of what is possible,” said Director of the Quantum Science Center Travis Humble. “With Umbra, we will now test new ideas, evaluate approaches at scale, and build the foundation for more reliable quantum computers.”

Jay Gambetta, an IBM Fellow and director of IBM Research, added that the biggest contributor to today’s research is no longer whether error correction will work on quantum hardware, but how to accelerate and optimize it to build systems scientists can use to tackle problems.

IBM said the Nighthawk’s square-lattice connectivity enables industry-leading speed and real-time control to test error-correction techniques. GPU accelerators, such as AMD’s nodes in the Umbra system, can help with this fine-tuning. The co-design platform connected at Oak Ridge will help explore quantum as part of a broader artificial intelligence and scientific computing infrastructure.

“This new co-design platform for quantum error correction allows us to evaluate different approaches and determine the architectures, software and workflows that will scale,” said Gambetta.

Researchers can measure qubits mid-calculation and act on the results in real time, set the exact timing for the signals that protect the qubits from noise, and see exactly what the hardware ran while working with raw measurement signals. This will provide error-correction research with the raw data needed for the next generation of approaches to build sophisticated capabilities for large systems running real code.

Earlier this year, IBM and ORNL unveiled results showing how workloads running on both quantum and classical computers and the Frontier supercomputer can simulate real magnetic materials and calculate molecular configurations of a promising material for fusion fuel.

The simulation of magnetic materials could lead to breakthroughs in superconductors, more efficient batteries and novel drugs. A promising fusion fuel could provide a stepping stone to abundant energy superior to nuclear fission, which powers current nuclear power plants.

#5554. Compass ‘Welcomes’ Open Real Estate, Sees Record Quarterly Earnings

As Open Real Estate makes headlines around the future of listing flow and control, Compass CEO Robert Reffkin addressed the initiative in the company’s third quarter earnings call, saying Compass “welcome(s) this change.”

Reffkin said that Open Real Estate’s plan “actually validates” Compass’s messaging over recent years, and he is “excited to see the four of them lead in this way and just see others join.”

In terms of whether or not Compass itself would join the initiative, Reffkin said “there’s definitely a path.”

“Compass International Holdings is definitely excited that there will be a national real estate listing service that will return the power back to the creator of the listing, the homeowner and their trusted agent, and that is good news for all agents and for all their clients, and we’re looking forward to seeing if there’s a way for us to be involved,” he continued.

Compass reported a “record” quarter, beating out expectations it set for itself in Q2. Reffkin touted the firm’s success amid an array of market challenges, from increasing mortgage rates to decreasing home sales.

Compass’s adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization) of $306 million for Q3 surpassed the company’s original expectations of $275 million to $305. While down from $363 million in Q2, EBITDA rose from $94 million in Q3 2025 to set a new Q3 record.

Other Q3 records for Compass include revenue, which came in at $3.9 billion for Q3. While this marks a dip from last quarter’s $4.31 billion, it represents a whopping 111% year-over-year increase from $1.85 billion in Q3 2025. Pro forma revenue was up 11.6% year-over-year from $3.49 billion.

Net income was also at a record Q3 level, coming in at $62 million. While down from $92 million in Q2, the increase is significant compared to the $4 million net loss year over year. The company has now been net income positive for three consecutive quarters.

Much of the quarter’s success was attributed to improvements in Compass’s operating expenses (OPEX), which were down 6% year-over-year. Free cash flow was also improved at $240 million in Q3, which the company noted was a record for any quarter or year in its history.

CFO Scott Wahlers said that bettering the company’s OPEX came from “just good old-fashioned tightening our belt” in a market that is experiencing challenges from “worse than normal seasonality.”

Looking at the brokerage business, gross transaction volume for Coldwell Banker, Compass, Corcoran and Sotheby’s International Realty came in at $138.9 billion, down from $155.2 billion in Q2 but up 96.5% year-over-year from $70.7 billion in Q3 2025. Pro forma, transaction volume was up 7.5% year-over-year to $133.1 billion.

Brokerage transactions were up 106.4% year-over-year, from 67,887 in Q3 2025 to  140,118 this quarter. Pro forma, transactions were actually down 0.3% year-over-year, but this is compared to a 1.8% decrease across the entirety of the U.S. residential real estate market (as sourced from NAR’s existing home sales data).

For franchise business, gross transaction volume was at $108.9 billion, a 1,181% year-over-year increase from $8.5 billion in Q3 2025. Pro forma, transaction volume was up 2.3% year-over-year to $104.2 billion. Franchise transactions were up a whopping 2,073% year-over-year, from 8,825 in Q3 2025 to 191,809 this quarter. Pro forma, transactions actually decreased 3.6% year-over-year.

Reffkin also called out some business that will be coming in from Wall Street due to bonuses from working with and investing in AI.

“(Wall Street) will have record bonuses coming in the months ahead, and that will lead to more transactions,” he said. “There are a number of partners on Wall Street who have asked me for an introduction to our agents, and I have made those introductions.”

The mortgage business improved as well, credited to Compass’s acquisitions. Total mortgage transactions were up 406% year-over-year to 38,757 (up from 7,666 in Q3 2025). This was also up pro forma by 1.7% year-over-year. Loan volume was $3.30 billion, up 9.9% year-over-year on a pro forma basis.

Compass just recently inked a deal with fintech company Rate to unite the two companies’ mortgage ventures—Guaranteed Rate Affinity and OriginPoint—under the OriginPoint brand. The merger shifts OriginPoint up to a top 10 mortgage lender, which Reffin said is “incredible after such a short amount of time.”

“Longer term, we want to be a top five retail lender,” he added.

Agent retention and recruiting also improved for Compass due to what the company and Reffkin outlined as a strong value prop and industry positioning. For agents producing more than $20,000 in gross commission income, retention is above 98%.

Recruiting-wise, brokerage agents specifically increased by 2,292 in Q3, and total agent count grew by 6,390.

Reffkin also attributed Compass’ Q3 success to the rollout of its “Home” platform, an end-to-end proprietary technology for real estate professionals.

Across Coldwell Banker, Corcoran and Sotheby’s International Realty, Compass stated it saw 33,950 agents adopt the available platform, bringing the total number of users across the full company to 68,349 agents. The plan remains to roll out the platform to the full portfolio of Compass brands in Q1 2027.

Through the platform, all participating agents will have access to the company’s Private Exclusive and Coming Soon inventory.

In talking about Compass’s platform, Reffkin dove into the company’s “See It First” campaign, calling it “part of a rebranding exercise.”

“I think some of our competitors have tried to brand the listings that we have as hidden, clearly,” he explained. “All of our listings are available to all agents and to all buyers, and when you call them See It First, then it’s pretty clear we just want you to see it first on our site, which is a natural thing for a company to want to be able to do.”

Reffkin reported that the company will take a conservative approach in the months ahead as the market continues to be challenged.

“There are reasons to be optimistic, but obviously we’re not planning for that,” he said. “We continue to focus on costs and plan for being conservative. But I think what can help in our favor (is) one, we have more inventory right now than any point since…2019. ..More inventory means you can create more sales.”

When asked about future merger-and-acquisition opportunities, Reffkin indicated the door is open.

“We continue to be a company that wants to support great operators and continue to have those conversations.”

Compass stated it expects a Q4 revenue of $3.150 billion to $3.350 billion, and a Q4 adjusted EBITDA of $100 million to $130 million. For the full year of 2026, the company stated it expects free cash flow to be positive, and OPEX of $2.71 billion to $2.73 billion.

Maria Patterson contributed to this report.

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5553. Exclusive: StrongestLayer launches tools to verify payment requests and block hidden AI instructions

Artificial intelligence email security startup StrongestLayer Inc. today launched two products aimed at email that can move money or manipulate an AI assistant.

The first product, Intent Workflows, can hold payment, payroll and executive account requests for verification before anyone acts on them. Alongside it comes AI Instruction Intercept, which stops hidden instructions in a message before an assistant such as Microsoft Corp.’s Microsoft 365 Copilot reads them

Intent Workflows targets attacks that carry no malware or suspicious link. In vendor email compromise, a criminal takes over a real supplier’s mailbox and sends new bank details inside an existing thread.

StrongestLayer went through 32,052 attacks that got past existing defenses at 45 organizations in the second quarter. Only 3.6% were payment or bank-change requests. Under a loss model built on the Factor Analysis of Information Risk framework, that small slice accounted for more than 98% of the estimated financial exposure. Sender authentication checks were little help, since 94% of those messages passed them.

Traditional email security asks whether a message looks bad, according to Alan LeFort, StrongestLayer’s co-founder and chief executive. “The costliest attacks are built to look fine,” he said. His company looks at what a message is trying to make happen, which for a wire transfer means “verifying the action instead of betting on a verdict.”

StrongestLayer’s detection still screens every message. Intent Workflows adds a hold for the smaller set of requests that can’t be reversed, with each customer deciding whether those requests wait for verification or go to the security team or a process owner.

Customers can also let a request through with a policy banner, which appears only on tracked requests and spells out the company’s own rule, such as “Bank change: call the number on file.” Payments in scope are held whatever the verdict, so a hijacked vendor account can’t get one through by sounding legitimate.

The software compares each payment request with the payee’s history, and customers pick the threshold, whether that is every payment or only those over $5,000. If nothing has changed, the payment owner confirms in one click, in Microsoft Teams or by email. Any change, or a new vendor, means a call to a phone number already on file, and the email isn’t released until the outcome is logged.

Payroll changes are verified the same way, and executive password, multifactor authentication and account recovery resets go to the identity or security team first, even when the request comes in through the help desk.

The release also takes on a newer problem. Researchers at Aim Security Ltd. found the EchoLeak flaw in Microsoft 365 Copilot last year, and one crafted email was all it took to get the assistant leaking data.

AI Instruction Intercept reads each message first. A reasoning model checks it for hidden instructions against the customer’s own business context, and only after that does the email reach Copilot, Google LLC’s Gemini or a security classifier. Suspect messages are quarantined by default with an explanation of what each instruction was after.

Email is the one route to an AI assistant that “any outsider can use,” said Joshua Bass, StrongestLayer’s co-founder and chief product officer. He argues the inbox is the first place to stop prompt injection, since all an attacker needs is an address.

Both products are available now for Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace and run alongside a company’s existing email security.

#5552. This Off-Grid ‘Treehouse’ Is Perched 60 Feet in the Air—and Built From Shipping Containers

If you've ever dreamed of sleeping among the trees, a property in the Epworth, GA, forest might be just the place.

"The structure itself is very unique. It's a steel watchtower built to commercial grade but for residential purposes, purely for leisurely enjoyment, for getaways, for the adventurer at heart," says listing agent Logan Fitts with Mountain Sotheby's International Realty.

Listed for $1.2 million, the 60-foot-high tower sits on 14.31 acres of land adjacent to the Chattahoochee National Forest with about 3,000 feet of river frontage.

"I was definitely awestruck first by the property itself, the river frontage, the waterfalls on the property, all of the hemlock trees dispersed throughout the property," Fitts says. "But then when we went to the top of the property where the watchtower was, I was in total awe."

Two shipping containers are perched atop the tower, creating the living space.

"The main structure is the bedroom efficiency with a bed, sitting area, stove, kitchenette. There's a landing between and then across is the bathroom area with a full shower, toilet, and double vanity," he explains. "Then there's a spiral staircase to the rooftop fire pit and lounge area."

And while there is a lift for things like suitcases and packages, people need to walk up 82 steel-grated stairs, which Fitts admits can be a bit daunting.

"I was actually nervous going up the tower for the first time because it's high and it is an experience. But once I did it, I said, 'This is what real mountain experiences are like. This is something that people remember for the rest of their lives.'"

"You are surrounded by just foliage, so when you're at the top, you just see a full panoramic view of the mountains and valley across one way, and you hear the roaring river on the property down below. You can actually see the waterfall," Fitts says.

"It's like a glass birdhouse at the top of this mountain, and you feel like you're definitely elevated and away from everything, but still connected to nature."

To get to the property itself requires a four-wheel-drive vehicle, because some of the roads are gravel and visitors need to cross the Jacks River, literally.

"Anyone with a four-wheel-drive or some type of ground clearance should have zero issue forging the river," Fitts explains, adding that the river is shallow at the access point. "It's not scary if you've done it before, and once you do it, it's like 'OK, now I'm an adventurer.'"

The current owner has had the place for about a decade and completed the tower house in 2023. Since then, it has been a short-term rental, bringing in about $92,000 annually during a nine-month rental period.

The owner would "love to pass it to someone that would take it, create a new legacy, and maybe make it even better," Fitts says.

"I think more than anything, he wants a true outdoors lover to really appreciate this property and not just see a metal dwelling in the middle of the forest. He built it for people to really enjoy nature, embrace nature, and take care of nature."

While the property itself is off-grid with solar power, a well, septic system, and generator, it’s not physically far from civilization.

"Probably the property is maybe 30 minutes from downtown Blue Ridge," Fitts says, adding it just feels remote. "Once you're there, you're in a totally different world. Your neighbors are trees and wildlife."

#5551. What the World Series can teach real estate agents about focus

ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA – OCT. 28: William Contreras, No. 24 of the Milwaukee Brewers, poses with the Willie Mays World Series Most Valuable Player award after defeating the Tampa Bay Rays in the 2026 World Series at Tropicana Field on Oct. 28, 2026, in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Mindfulness for real estate isn’t about calm. It’s about hearing clients under pressure. See what baseball teaches brokers about training attention.

The Milwaukee Brewers just won the World Series, and while I love baseball, I’ve been watching with a question that has very little to do with it: What happens to your attention when the outcome matters more than you can afford to think about?

Nobody at the plate can win a championship with the swing they wish they’d taken last inning. The players can only deal with the pitch (or batter) in front of them.

That sounds obvious until you notice how often we walk into a seller conversation still arguing with the deal that fell apart yesterday.

What’s interesting to me is that baseball has stopped treating this as a personality trait. Both the Rays and the Brewers have extensive mental performance training programs (as do all Major League ball clubs), but most brokerages treat mental health as a wellness issue, not a performance one.

Whatever name your office gives this kind of work, baseball has made it somebody’s job.

What makes this baseball tale useful to brokers and team leaders, though, is how much resistance the work still meets in a sport that has every reason to embrace it.

Andy McCullough’s recent reporting in The Athletic examines meditation in Major League Baseball, and I found the takeaways instructive.

For over two decades, most teams have invested in behavioral science and expanded their mental-performance staffs. It’s a sport that measures everything, with tens of millions of dollars on every roster, and it has decided the mental side is worth paying for.

What I find fascinating is that even as the evidence piles up, many players remain skeptical. Some call it “woo-woo.” One of the game’s best pitchers says he doesn’t need it. Coaches avoid the word “meditation” altogether because, as one put it, it intimidates people, and if you push it, they’ll tune you out.

My favorite part of the Athletic piece was this: The San Francisco Giants brought in a consultant, titled “Breathing Specialist,” and the players made jokes about it. The next season, the same man did the same work but with a new title: “Human Performance Coach,” and the resistance started to fall away.

By the time he left, about 15 players regularly attended his sessions (complete with Tibetan singing bowls). He concluded that the stigma had more to do with the title than the practice.

I don’t call it meditation when I train real estate teams either. But that doesn’t mean you can’t intentionally sharpen the skills involved.

When the market tightens, brokerages usually prescribe more activity: more calls, more door knocks, more open houses. We can count activity, so we reach for it. Ballplayers do the same thing when they skip the mental work and take extra swings.

The trouble is that pressure narrows attention, and narrowed attention is as poor a state for a batter with two on, two outs, behind two, in the bottom of the ninth as it is for a seasoned agent on a listing appointment, a price-reduction conversation or a buyer about to walk.

Don’t get confused. This kind of performance coaching is not about caring less about the result; it’s about letting go of the need to make it happen. A hitter can care enormously about winning the World Series and still recognize that thinking about winning doesn’t help him see the next pitch.

The same is true when a seller is deciding whether to take your advice. You need the listing, but needing it more isn’t any more effective than gripping and swinging the bat harder.

The goal isn’t calm, either. Mental-performance people who work with ballplayers talk about finding a usable level of activation for the task, since too much overwhelms you and too little leaves you flat. I’m not trying to produce agents who feel peaceful about losing business. I’m trying to help them notice when fear has taken over the conversation so that they can let it go and hear the client again.

There’s sports research worth knowing here. One study of Division I basketball players found that higher measured mindfulness predicted better free-throw percentages in games, a 5.75-point delta, to be exact. A separate training study found something more useful: under high stress, the gap between athletes who trained their attention and those who didn’t was larger than under low stress.

I won’t tell you a practice will add a specific number to your agents’ closing rates. Nobody can honestly promise that, and even baseball struggles to quantify the benefit. What I will tell you is that the moments that make or break an agent’s year are high-pressure, and training for them is a performance issue, not a wellness perk.

In each World Series game, every player must let the last pitch go before the next one arrives. Your agents face the same job on a smaller stage every week.

You don’t need agents who identify as meditators. You need agents who can hear what a client is saying while a deal they “need” is coming apart. That capacity deserves practice before the conversation, not a reminder to calm down halfway through it.

Aaron Hendon is the Managing Broker for Christine & Company with eXp and a mindfulness teacher. Connect with Aaron on Instagram and LinkedIn.
